item.content:encoded:
The present phase of the Ukraine war confirms, with a clarity that is almost didactic, a structure I had already attempted to fictionalise across the trilogy Umbrella, Shark, and Phone: namely, a triadic or dialectical relation between warfighting technologies, the pathologies of the human mind, and the apparatus of civilian life. War is not merely one domain among others; it is the determining moment of temporalisation itself, the vector along which technological necessity advances. Civilian technology emerges as the apparent negation of war—its pacified, domestic, intimate form—while mental pathology registers the unresolved contradiction between the two, inscribing within the organism the stresses of a system it cannot metabolise.

This is not a sequence but a simultaneity: war persists as a condition (a war omnes contra omnes), peace is only its local and temporary negation, and technology mediates both while producing the very dislocations it claims to heal. Freud’s observation about the train and the telephone—mobility producing separation, communication compensating for it—becomes here a general law. The system creates its own wounds and then supplies their prosthetic remedies. The Ukraine theatre now renders this dialectic explicit. As the BBC report puts it, “1,500 to 2,000km inside Russian territory is no longer the ‘peaceful rear’,” while the commander of Ukraine’s unmanned systems boasts that his forces are “taking the war to their territory so that they feel it too.” What is at stake is not simply reach, but the abolition of the distinction between front and hinterland, combatant and civilian environment.

The drone is the instrument of this abolition, and it is not properly understood as a weapon in the traditional sense. It is at once sensor, platform, delivery system, verification device, and broadcast medium. Each strike is filmed, logged, counted; each death becomes a datum. The commander speaks openly of a “kill plan,” of exceeding monthly quotas, of requiring video proof for each casualty. This is not merely brutality; it is gamification in its most literal and terminal sense. The battlefield has been subsumed into a scoring system, the enemy rendered as targets within a quantified environment, the operator positioned as both combatant and player. The interface—joysticks, screens, live feeds—is continuous with civilian gaming culture, logistics dashboards, and social media analytics. War has not borrowed from these domains; they all derive from the same underlying architecture.

Dromodronology names this condition: total surveillance disaggregated into innumerable nodes, total force projection fragmented into cheap, proliferating vectors, and the spectacle no longer representing violence but constituting it in real time. The drone does not simply deliver the bomb; it transforms the bomb. The classical bomb was an event, punctual and catastrophic, dividing time into before and after. The drone is the bomb temporalised, distributed across duration. It hovers, searches, transmits, returns as image, circulates as affect. It is the bomb that has not gone off because it has fissioned into the entire environment of anticipation, targeting, verification and dread. This is why the Ukraine war appears less as a sequence of decisive engagements than as a continuous field of irritation, degradation, and systemic pressure.

Oil refineries burn deep within Russia, not merely to destroy capacity but to disrupt flows—of capital, insurance, confidence. Soldiers are killed not only to reduce manpower but to satisfy a metric. Civilians witness fires and hear drones overhead, and their reactions become part of the feedback loop. The war is everywhere and nowhere, continuous and yet never conclusive. From this perspective, nuclear weapons occupy a peculiar and increasingly unstable position. They remain the ultimate punctual bomb, the absolute event that would terminate all temporalisation, yet their operational systems are embedded within the same distributed, digitised, and fallible networks. The question of “who holds the trigger” is no longer purely political; it is infrastructural, procedural, and psychological.

Command and control systems must be insulated against the very dynamics—speed, disaggregation, automation—that define contemporary warfare, yet they are inevitably permeated by them. The risk is not simply deliberate use, but misinterpretation, malfunction, or the erosion of clear lines of authority under conditions of constant low-level escalation. Here one is compelled to recall the figure of Vasili Arkhipov, the Soviet submarine officer during the Cuban Missile Crisis who refused to authorise the launch of a nuclear torpedo, an act that almost certainly prevented global catastrophe. In Shark I named the temporal condition that follows from this “Andropov time”: a counterfactual ontology in which our continued existence is contingent upon a decision that might easily have gone otherwise. We live, that is, in the aftermath of a non-event, a catastrophe deferred, and the system continues to operate under the shadow of that deferral.

The proliferation of drones, the gamification of killing, the erosion of boundaries between war and civilian life—all these developments intensify the underlying contradiction without resolving it. The bomb has not gone off; instead, it has dispersed itself into the fabric of everyday existence. And so the present situation in Ukraine is not an anomaly but an index. It shows us the future as it has already arrived: a world in which war determines the tempo of technological change, technology domesticates war even as it extends it, and the human mind, caught between them, oscillates between adaptation and breakdown. The question is no longer whether this system will culminate in a decisive rupture, but how long it can sustain its own indefinite deferral.

item.title: LONDON: Why I'm Voting Labour Today
item.dc:creator: Will Self

item.content:encoded:
On Lambeth Bridge stand the old Victorian personifications of civic virtue, among them local government itself: not government in the grandiose parliamentary or imperial sense, but the humbler and more difficult proposition that a dense urban population might still govern itself equitably through drains, housing, libraries, schools, social care, parks, roads, bins, repairs and the endless mediation of neighbourly conflict. Looking at the state of politics in London this week, one could be forgiven for thinking this ideal had entirely evaporated into spectacle. Yet today, trudging down to vote in the local elections in Lambeth, it is precisely that battered municipal ideal I shall be voting for. This is not because I regard Lambeth Labour as uniquely brilliant. Quite the reverse.

The borough’s housing problems are severe, its bureaucracy can appear exhausted and defensive, and its long institutional tenure has plainly produced complacencies and blind spots. But one must distinguish between a structure struggling under impossible conditions and a structure that has ceased to possess any governing DNA whatsoever. Lambeth remains an extraordinarily difficult borough to run: geographically elongated, socially fragmented, financially squeezed, dependent on a housing ecology warped by decades of financialisation, and carrying the burden of post-industrial London’s impossible contradictions. The borough attempts simultaneously to house the poor, retain fragments of mixed community, absorb global capital flows, regulate development, and survive a property market increasingly hostile to ordinary urban life. The reality is that every pressure converges here.

The trains rattle beneath the house, the aircraft pass overhead, and even in the wooded pockets of the Stockwell Conservation Area one now lives amidst the ambient roar of dromological modernity. My own backdoor neighbour, in pursuit no doubt of uplifted property value and the speculative theology of London real estate, is excavating an iceberg house beneath his garden. Meanwhile the one- and two-bedroom flat market — traditionally a stabilising layer of Lambeth’s tax base and social fabric — buckles under the service-charge crisis, cladding fears and the slow corrosion of leasehold legitimacy. The council’s housing department, for all its failures, is attempting to mediate conditions generated far beyond the borough itself. This is what irritates me so profoundly about the current spectacularisation of politics. The tail now wags the dog entirely.

Fleas crawling over the hide of the political animal become the entire object of mediated fixation while the underlying material organism disappears from view. Gaza, social-media outrage, performative radicalism, algorithmic tribalism, endless affective signalling — all of it floods the informational battlespace while the actual municipal problem remains brutally concrete: who can still run the borough with some semblance of distributive equity under conditions of systemic strain? And no, I do not say this as somebody indifferent to racism, antisemitism or historical injustice. Quite the opposite. Lambeth scarcely needs imported symbolic victimhood to understand what bureaucratic cruelty and transnational systems can do to human beings.

The borough itself contains the memory of the Windrush scandal, in which elderly African-Caribbean Londoners — many of whom had worked for London Transport and the British state for decades — suddenly found themselves treated as suspect aliens within the very society they had helped sustain. Nor does one need to look far for examples of institutionalised administrative sadism: the sub-postmasters scandal coursed through boroughs like this one too, destroying ordinary lives through bureaucratic abstraction and systematised denial. That is why the recent remarks by Green figures and fellow travellers around antisemitism have struck me as so spiritually repellent. Zack Polanski’s comments about Jewish fear and antisemitism were not merely tactless.

They were corrosive to the ethical core of environmentalism itself, because genuine environmental consciousness depends upon attentiveness to lived interdependence and vulnerability, not the ranking of historical traumas into fashionable and unfashionable categories. I am probably among the very few voters in today’s Lambeth election who literally does not fly. I live with the material consequences of aviation, extraction, overdevelopment and urban acceleration every day. Yet I cannot support a politics in which environmentalism dissolves into a species of performative anti-Western spectacle detached from municipal reality and increasingly tolerant of conspiracist or antisemitic atmospherics. So yes, Labour receives my vote today. Not because I am Jewish, despite the now inevitable attempts to drag everything through the prism of ethnically coded allegiance.

Not because Sir Keir Starmer happens to be married to somebody sharing my own heritage. And not merely because Labour has at least attempted to confront antisemitism institutionally while others have preferred equivocation. Labour receives my vote because, amid all the smoke, mirrors and mediated excitation, it remains the only formation in Lambeth that still appears to possess enough institutional memory and municipal DNA to govern a borough of this complexity with any residual sense of fairness. The Greens may function effectively as a moral weather vane for metropolitan frustration. But weather vanes do not run housing departments, adult social care systems, planning committees or temporary accommodation networks. The current wave of radicalised spectacular politics risks mistaking expressive intensity for governance itself. Lambeth cannot be governed through vibes, hashtags and symbolic alignments alone.

It requires structures capable of absorbing contradiction without collapsing into pure performative moralism. Today’s vote, then, is not really about personalities. It is about whether London retains any belief at all in municipal government as a moral form. The old figures on Lambeth Bridge still matter because they remind us that civic life is not reducible either to markets or to spectacle. The tragedy of the present moment is that both financialised capitalism and digitally accelerated politics now conspire to dissolve the middle terrain where practical solidarity once lived. I shall vote today, therefore, not with enthusiasm exactly, but with a species of bruised municipal realism. Under current conditions, that may be the closest thing left to political seriousness.

item.title: LONDON: It Would Have Been Better if Zack Polanski had been a Real Crack Head
item.dc:creator: Will Self

Zack Polanski once pretended to be a crack addict. It would probably have been better for his environmental consciousness had he actually been one. Because I have been a crack addict, and what crack teaches you very quickly is that insatiable consumption destroys the soul. Scale that pathology up from the individual to the metropolis and you have the environmental crisis in its purest contemporary form. London is a giant crack smoker. The crack it smokes is money, and the things money buys. Deliveries, flights, upgrades, streaming, speculative property, disposable commodities, data, experiences, food hauled from continents away, endless parcels moving through logistical systems powered by server farms and rare-earth extraction. The city freebases consumption itself. Any serious metropolitan environmentalism would therefore begin with demand. With appetite. With restraint.

It would begin by saying to Londoners: you cannot continue to consume at this level. Your pleasures have material consequences. Your conveniences are emissions. Your digital life has a carbon shadow. Your attention itself has become infrastructural. But this is precisely the one thing contemporary Green politics seems incapable of saying, because its own political machinery is entirely embedded within the same spectacularized consumption system it purports to oppose. So let us begin not with Zack Polanski the man but with Lambeth, where the Greens now sit as the largest party on a council they do not properly govern, inheriting a borough whose finances depend upon roughly £116 million in exceptional support arrangements, borrowing permissions, asset sales and debt management mechanisms. That money does not descend from heaven in biodegradable hemp sacks. It comes from the circulatory system of global finance capitalism.

It comes from markets animated second-by-second by high-frequency trading systems running atop colossal energy-intensive computational infrastructure. Lambeth survives because the machine survives. The machine the Greens ostensibly dislike. This is the contradiction they cannot theorize because they cannot even fully perceive it. London no longer emits primarily through factories. London emits behaviourally. Consumption emissions. The carbon cost of desire. The city’s environmental footprint emerges from mediated appetites coordinated through bidirectional digital media systems designed to intensify consumption continuously. Every smartphone is a portable appetite amplifier. Every algorithmic feed is a demand-generation engine. Every platform is a behavioural conditioning mechanism.

Amazon, Uber Eats, TikTok, Deliveroo, Airbnb, streaming saturation, perpetual retail circulation, fast fashion, instantaneity itself — this is London’s smokestack now. Which raises the devastating question: what behaviours have the Greens actually changed? Did millions vote Green because they intended to stop flying? To buy less? To consume less meat? To reduce digital dependency? To lock their phones in drawers? To stop ordering next-day deliveries from warehouses operated by precarious labour inside gigantic energy-hungry logistical systems? Of course not. There has been no metropolitan ascetic awakening. No ecology of restraint. London remains ravenous. What has happened instead is something much easier and much more contemporary: politics has become another theatre of mediated consumption. Moral spectacle. Symbolic affiliation. Identity performance. The emotionalization of distant conflicts into local status signalling.

And this is where Zack Polanski enters the frame not as villain but as symptom. The Right thinks it has discovered some enormous scandal because Polanski inflated aspects of his CV, performed role-play scenarios adjacent to the Ministry of Justice, drifted through acting, hypnotherapy and gig-economy semi-professions, and may or may not have developed an elastic relationship with bureaucratic precision. Frankly, who cares? British politics is full of puffed-up nonentities laundering proximity into authority. The more interesting question is whether this protean, performative quality reveals something deeper about the hollowness of metropolitan environmentalism itself.

Recall: this is a movement whose natural terrain is a yurt in a Welsh valley full of hairies knitting their own yoghurt: if anyone gives Zack Polanski the right to stand up openly and say he’s a gay vegan, it’s Edward Carpenter, and his radically back-to-the-land asceticism––or, closer in space and time, Peter Tatchell. How does this scale up into a conurbation of 13 million people, many of whom are prepared to riot over a low-emissions zone? Yet, as we see, the environmentalists continue maneuvering after conceptual coherence has evaporated: and this is why their manoeuvres look like night ones. Although Polanski appears less like a Machiavellian guerilla fighter than a man assembled from fragments of contemporary metropolitan precarity: actor, trainer, facilitator, diversity worker, therapeutic entrepreneur, digital-era self-curator. His politics possesses the same quality. Tactical fluency without conceptual depth.

Gesture without sacrifice. Symbolic positioning without behavioural seriousness. And because there is no conceptual seriousness, environmentalism itself becomes theatricalized. Instead of confronting Londoners with the reality that they are ecologically overconsuming at planetary scale, politics drifts toward emotionally gratifying symbolic antagonisms. The issue is not whether criticism of Israel is legitimate; plainly it is. The issue is why a municipal environmental movement became emotionally organized around the politics of another sovereign territory while remaining almost entirely silent about the behavioural metabolism of the city it sought to govern. It is easier to march against a foreign state than to tell your own electorate to consume less. Easier to perform outrage than to impose restraint. Meanwhile the actual city persists in its exhausted and deathly appetite.

Outside Stockwell Tube there is a man I think of as ‘Got Some Cash?’ because that is his perpetual croak from a nest of cardboard and dirty blankets: ‘Got some cash? Can I have some cash please?’ He lies there amid the electronic pulse of a metropolis whose currency itself is dissolving into digital abstraction. Even his mode of begging belongs to a disappearing order. The paper note bearing ‘I promise to pay the bearer’ fades… first the promisor… then the bearer… into app-payments and invisible transactions while around ‘Got some cash?’ the true metabolism of the city continues uninterrupted: screens flashing, scooters whining, parcels moving, food couriers racing, speculative capital circulating through invisible fibre-optic veins beneath the grease- and gob-spattered pavement with its distributed midden of chicken bones.

That is London now: a consumption machine whose poorest casualties still beg for analogue scraps while the real exchange mechanism has migrated into planetary computational systems consuming staggering quantities of energy merely to sustain desire at velocity: go for it: don’t just takeaway, fly chicken! And what do the Greens offer against this? Bike lanes. Slogans. Symbolic righteousness. Identity atmospherics. Tactical outrage. They don’t even pretend to knit their owwn yoghurt anymore. Instead: they have mastered the spectacularism of the very civilization they oppose. But once environmentalism itself becomes another branch of spectacle capitalism, another aesthetic performance within the feed, it ceases to possess the moral authority required to demand sacrifice from anyone: GAIA: A Voyage… to Stratford Marsh, where it can die, along with the Olympic Dream and a load of old Swedish millionaires.

Which means the contradiction tightens further. Lambeth requires balanced books. Balanced books require functioning markets. Functioning markets require consumption. Consumption produces emissions. Emissions threaten ecological stability. Ecological politics therefore requires restraint. But restraint threatens the tax base upon which borough solvency depends. The Greens inherit not power but contradiction itself: no wonder Polanski already personifies it. And underneath all this sits the deeper anxiety: London already contains a latent bellum omnium contra omnes restrained only by thinning civic legitimacy, overloaded policing, bureaucratic continuity and residual obedience to civil law. Politics organized increasingly around digitally amplified grievance and symbolic antagonism corrodes that legitimacy further. The membrane thins.

Which returns us finally to Zack Polanski in the flesh not a fleeting figuration, or a chorister on the X-Factor. The problem is not that he once pretended to smoke crack in a B-movie. The problem is that he appears never to have understood what crack actually is. Crack is the true X-Factor: appetite without limit. Consumption detached from meaning. Desire accelerated beyond human scale until personality itself fragments into tactical improvisation and spiritual exhaustion. That is also the environmental condition of London. Which is why, in the end, it might genuinely have been better for his environmental consciousness had Zack Polanski once been a real crack addict.

item.dc:creator: Will Self

item.content:encoded:
The Trump entity does not suffer from the idiot volatility of its human frontman; it metabolizes that volatility as an arbitrage surface. This is the fundamental misunderstanding still shared by much of the Anglosphere commentariat, and especially by the British political and media classes, who continue to analyse Trump as if he were a defective executive rather than the intermittently vocal organ of a distributed entity formation. His emotional vacillation, his narcissism, his impulsivity, his tendency to oscillate wildly between threat, boast, concession and incoherence, are not pathologies external to the functioning system. They are among its productive assets. The volatility itself becomes monetizable. Insurance markets price it, commodities markets hedge against it, political actors align and realign around it, media organisations amplify it, and financial actors arbitrage its fluctuations in real time.

The Wall Street Journal piece on HSBC’s exposure to the collapse of Market Financial Solutions provides a near-perfect microcosm of how such entities now function. Ostensibly, the article is about a £400 million exposure arising from allegedly fraudulent property lending routed through Apollo-linked structures involving Atlas SP, Zircon Bridging, Irish DAC entities, securitisation vehicles and layers of ‘back leverage.’ Yet what the article actually reveals is not simply fraud, but the normal operational condition of contemporary Anglo-American finance: opacity as a yield-generating mechanism. The layering is not accidental. It is the product. HSBC lends to an Apollo-linked vehicle; the vehicle lends to another vehicle; the actual property borrower disappears several membranes away behind servicing agreements, warehouse facilities, SPVs and collateral pools.

Then, when the collateral proves to have been double-pledged, everyone expresses shock that nobody possessed a direct line of sight to the underlying exposure. But of course they did not possess such sight, because the entire architecture exists to make direct sight impossible while preserving plausible deniability. This is why London remains so extraordinarily attractive to flight capital. Not because Britain is uniquely corrupt in some vulgar sense, but because the City of London still possesses the imperial infrastructure of mediation. It knows how to convert dubious capital into legally serviceable capital. It knows how to provide duration, leverage and respectability to money whose origins, security or even ownership may remain strategically opaque.

The old British Empire specialised in maritime insurance, legal arbitration, mercantile clearing and offshore administration; contemporary London performs the same function for globalised capital flows. The empire has collapsed into finance, but the techniques of abstraction remain astonishingly continuous. The British elite catastrophically misunderstands this because it continues to imagine itself as sovereign in the older parliamentary-executive sense. Hence the endless obsession with personalities, ministerial competence, constitutional theatre and ‘special relationships.’ But the special relationship now increasingly consists of Britain functioning as a servicing appendage to entity structures generated elsewhere, above all by the American financial-security-media complex that the Trump entity merely renders visible in grotesque caricature. Britain is not being conquered in any classical sense.

Rather, it is being hollowed out as an effective sovereignty while its population continues wandering about under the illusion that the institutional shell still corresponds to autonomous national power. The old neutron bomb fantasy was that the buildings would remain standing while the people disappeared. What we have instead is almost the reverse: the human inhabitants remain, the ceremonial structures remain, but sovereignty itself has been quietly vaporised. This is precisely where the British discourse fails, because it insists on analysing the Trump phenomenon psychologically or morally instead of infrastructurally. Liberal commentators still write as if the problem were merely that Trump is unstable, dishonest or authoritarian. But the deeper reality is that the Trump entity thrives on instability itself. Volatility is not an unfortunate side-effect; it is a medium of operation.

A conventional executive attempts to reduce uncertainty. The Trump entity amplifies uncertainty because uncertainty increases dependency on the very networks capable of pricing and navigating it. Every oscillation — tariffs threatened then withdrawn, military strikes floated then postponed, sanctions imposed then selectively relaxed, NATO rhetoric intensified then contradicted — produces opportunities for arbitrage, hedging and speculative repositioning. The Wall Street Journal itself inadvertently exemplifies this process. The reporting style is deliberately neutral, technocratic, managerial. One encounters ‘exposure,’ ‘counterparties,’ ‘back leverage,’ ‘warehouse facilities,’ ‘sponsor due diligence.’ The language appears antiseptic, objective and stabilising. Yet this neutrality is itself part of the Kulturkampf through which the Trump entity operates. Financial journalism now functions simultaneously as revelation and sedation.

The article discloses systemic opacity while linguistically normalising it. A scandal appears, but appears in the grammar of technical adjustment rather than existential rupture. Thus the reader is taught both to fear instability and to regard it as ultimately manageable by sufficiently sophisticated actors. This attitude derives directly from the post-2007/08 settlement. After Bear Stearns and the near-collapse of Goldman Sachs, a tacit metaphysical guarantee entered the system. The Federal Reserve would stand behind systemic liquidity under almost any conditions. The phrase ‘too big to fail’ was never merely descriptive; it became theological: but really it was the accountancy version of Fukayama’s ‘end of history’. Market actors internalised the belief that beneath every abyss lay an invisible sovereign backstop. The precise institutional mechanism scarcely mattered.

Whether the intervention took the form of emergency lending, swap lines, quantitative easing, coordinated central-bank action or implicit political guarantees was secondary. What mattered was the shared conviction that terminal collapse would not be permitted. And crucially, this metaphysical backstop now extends far beyond American banks. It suffuses the entire Western financial imaginary. One can see echoes of it even in Britain’s long trauma surrounding the Exchange Rate Mechanism crisis and Soros’s assault on sterling in 1992. There too, a fantasy persisted that sovereign systems possessed some ultimate stabilising authority capable of defeating speculative attack. Yet modern capital flows increasingly exceed the cognitive and operational capacities of nation-states themselves. The sovereign appears strongest precisely where sovereignty has already become performative. This is why the HSBC story matters.

It is not simply another banking scandal. It is a glimpse into the operational ontology of late Western capitalism: distributed entities whose executives no longer truly govern them, financial opacity treated as productive infrastructure, states increasingly reduced to confidence-maintenance operations, and publics who continue to imagine that visible institutions correspond to actual centres of control. Dromologically speaking, the decisive fact is velocity. Capital now moves faster than audit, faster than democratic comprehension, faster than jurisdictional containment, and increasingly faster even than executive cognition. By the time exposure becomes visible, the entity has already migrated elsewhere, repriced the risk, socialised the losses and resumed motion.

Everyone knows what Starmer is. Smug. Bloodless. Lawyerly. A bore. Sanctimonious. Managerial. The human embodiment of a compliance seminar. The sort of man who looks as if he’d report you to HR for making a joke about the biscuits in the office kitchen. The internet has already assembled the composite caricature: the thin smile; the prosecutorial cadence; the air of someone permanently explaining the terms and conditions. He is mocked as robotic, evasive, insincere, priggish, “North London” despite not being from North London, simultaneously too posh and too petit-bourgeois, too cautious to inspire and too ambitious to trust. Everybody knows Starmer is unbearable. And that is precisely why everybody is misunderstanding him. Because the important thing about Starmer is not that he is uniquely unpleasant, nor uniquely managerial, nor uniquely hollow.

The important thing is that he is the long historical result of a society that has proceduralized itself to the point where procedure no longer mediates trust but replaces it. Starmer is not an aberration within contemporary Britain. He is one of its purest expressions. This is why the old heuristic of the “good bloke” matters. A good bloke is not simply a nice person. The good bloke belongs to an older and thicker social world: trade union branches, pubs, regiments, chapels, bowling clubs, football terraces, local parties, old Labour wards, Masonic lodges, working men’s institutes. The good bloke may be flawed, even corrupt, but he is legible. You know where he stands. His authority arises from embeddedness. The nice person, by contrast, emerges from the lower-middle-managerial order: respectable, conscientious, emotionally literate, permanently anxious to appear decent.

The nice person follows procedure because procedure has replaced organic trust. The nice person says “I completely understand your concerns” while mentally opening a safeguarding flowchart. Starmer’s entire political personality oscillates between these two poles. He desperately wants to appear a good bloke while possessing all the sociological characteristics of the nice person. That is the hidden tension visible in every gesture, every speech rhythm, every photograph in which he attempts awkwardly to project ordinariness through rolled-up sleeves, football references or prosecutorial sternness. The King’s Speech revealed the problem perfectly. The legislative programme itself was an exercise in procedural reassurance masquerading as political fellowship. More powers, more frameworks, more protections, more authorities, more enforcement mechanisms, more administrative interventions.

The modern British state no longer knows how to produce solidarity except through compliance architecture. It can still generate procedures; it can no longer generate myth. And because Britain is now a fissiparous society — fragmented into competing legal, managerial, ethnic, algorithmic and economic jurisdictions — politics itself increasingly resembles a gigantic unresolved tort claim. Every interest group seeks recognition through procedural exceptionalism. Every grievance requires adjudication. Every identity demands managerial accommodation. The result is hypertrophic legalism and collapsing civic trust occurring simultaneously. This is where the “dog whisperer heuristic” becomes useful. A behavioural trainer once remarked of an impossible puppy: “If the puppy pisses in the house, smack yourself, not the puppy.” Exactly.

Citizens rage at Starmer because they dimly recognize in him the same procedural hypertrophy saturating their own lives. The unread contracts. The incomprehensible insurance policies. The online terms and conditions nobody reads. The HR departments. The compliance seminars. The endless documentation surrounding finance, housing, medicine, education, data protection and identity itself. People increasingly inhabit systems too complex for ordinary human intuition to grasp. And yet they themselves participate daily in reproducing those systems. The puppy heard the whistle because everybody has been blowing it. That is why Starmer attracts such visceral hostility. Not because he is secretly tyrannical or uniquely manipulative, but because he appears as the anthropomorphic embodiment of procedural Britain itself: the human face of the unread contract. Even his strengths intensify the problem.

Starmer is intelligent, disciplined and highly competent within bounded procedural environments. But contemporary governance no longer resembles a courtroom. The lawyer’s craft depends upon stable jurisdictions, interpretable precedent and rule-governed disputes. Modern politics increasingly operates instead through informational fog: algorithmic amplification, financial abstraction, fragmented publics, hostile-state influence operations and emotional contagion moving faster than institutional cognition. Which brings us to the Borodino heuristic. In Tolstoy’s War and Peace, Napoleon arrives after Borodino dimly sensing the terrifying truth that the Leviathan attributed to his will never truly obeyed him at all. The machinery of history exceeds intentionality. Starmer experiences a diminished but structurally similar revelation.

The procedural mastery that made him formidable as Director of Public Prosecutions avails less and less within a political environment where meaning itself has become unstable. Hence the strange hollowness surrounding him. The more he insists on seriousness, the more performative he appears. The more he stresses competence, the more managerial he sounds. The more he tries to seem ordinary, the more mediated and synthetic the performance becomes. He cannot recover organic authority because the social foundations that once generated it no longer exist. This is why media coverage of him becomes so obsessively physiognomic. The smirk. The voice. The spectacles. The stiffness. The forensic tone. The internet continually reduces him to mannerisms because contemporary media itself can no longer conceptualize political leadership except as personality spectacle. It pretends to psychologize while actually flattening.

Every politician becomes a GIF. And that flattening conceals the real issue. The real issue is that British politics no longer properly mediates between society and state because the old intermediary structures — parties, unions, churches, local associations, civic corporations in the Hegelian sense — have decayed into managerial shells. Executive authority therefore floats free from lived social embeddedness while still attempting to simulate it theatrically. That is why the hatred of Starmer feels oddly impersonal even when it is intensely personal. Citizens attack him as an individual while unconsciously recognizing a much larger structure behind him. So by the end of this process, “Keir Starmer” ceases to be the most useful description. The individual matters less than the phenomenon he embodies. The title dissolves into the function. The function dissolves into the system. Hence our terminology. Not Sir Keir Starmer.

Not even Keir Starmer from Surrey. But the Starmer entity.

The Jews are the people of the Book, but the problem is that many people imagine it is a book they will not lend to anyone else, written in a language only they can understand, and containing secrets about a political and economic order that has itself become illegible to ordinary citizens. That, at any rate, is the shape of the new antisemitism in London: not merely an inherited prejudice, nor simply a recrudescence of the old European hatred, but a symptom of a wider crisis of legibility in a society that increasingly cannot explain itself to itself. To understand contemporary antisemitism you first have to understand the fog of war. Not war merely in the military sense, although the American and Israeli strikes on Iran earlier this year undoubtedly intensified online hatred and conspiratorial thinking. No, the fog of war now exists reciprocally with the fog of peace.

They are matryoshka dolls of perceptual impairment nested one inside another. Citizens do not understand geopolitics; they do not understand finance; they do not understand algorithms; increasingly they do not understand the devices through which they experience the world. The smartphone is an instrument of permanent mediation whose internal functioning is opaque to almost everybody who uses it. As Nicholas Carr observed long ago, it is a tool that abolishes tools. One of the tools it abolishes is precisely the patient interrogation of symbols, words and categories. Thus words like ‘Jew’, ‘Jewish’, ‘Zionist’, ‘globalist’, or ‘elite’ become detached from stable meaning and begin to float freely through the algorithmic ecosystem, acquiring emotional charge while losing conceptual precision. The internet rewards acceleration rather than understanding. It rewards emotional recognizability rather than intellectual clarity.

Iranian propaganda, Israeli propaganda, Western propaganda, activist propaganda, influencer outrage, meme-politics: all circulate together in one gigantic symbolic slurry. In that environment the Jew once again becomes available as a universal explanatory placeholder. This is why antisemitism differs subtly from many other racisms. Anti-Black racism, for example, has historically tended toward fantasies of inferiority, disorder or threat: sovereignty is threatened––there is the enemy. Antisemitism tends toward fantasies of hidden agency: understanding is threatened––sovereignty has been supplanted. The Jew is imagined not merely as different but as secretly explanatory. The antisemitic imagination asks not simply ‘Who are these people?’ but ‘What do these people know that we do not?’ The Jew becomes attached to invisible systems: money, law, media, bureaucracy, finance, algorithms, geopolitics, lobbying, abstraction itself.

This does not mean that Jews are uniquely powerful. Quite the reverse. It means societies that cannot understand complex systems seek symbolic proxies through which to narrate their confusion. Antisemitism is therefore racism plus failed systems analysis. And because the modern world is increasingly illegible, antisemitism mutates continuously. One sees this particularly clearly in the way contemporary politics collapses distinctions between individual Jews, Jews collectively, Israel as a state, Zionism as an ideology, and the wider structures of Western power. The diaspora Jew becomes synecdochal: a portable representative of abstractions far larger than any individual could possibly embody. The Jewish Londoner is silently transformed into a local embassy for events occurring thousands of miles away.

Thus criticism of Israeli policy — perfectly legitimate within democratic discourse — can slide almost imperceptibly into ambient hostility toward Jews as such, because the signifier has already detached from any stable referent. The irony is that this process unfolds precisely in a society suffering a profound collapse of civic literacy. Previous generations at least possessed intermediary structures through which political life became legible: unions, churches, clubs, parties, local associations, even bowls clubs. Electing a secretary to a bowls club teaches procedural reality. It gives citizens an intuition for institutions. Today many people possess no such ‘starter ramp’ into politics whatsoever. Their political consciousness arrives pre-packaged through feeds, memes and outrage cycles. Politics appears not as administration or mediation but as spectacle.

Into this vacuum rushes the internet’s tendency to decouple signifiers from signifieds and repurpose them emotionally. This is why, while writing recently about Zack Polanski and the London Greens, I deliberately avoided foregrounding his Jewishness. It was irrelevant to the actual contradiction under discussion, namely the hollowness of a metropolitan environmentalism incapable of addressing consumption while thriving upon the spectacular politics generated by the very digital capitalism it ostensibly opposes. To have made the piece ‘about the Jew’ would itself have participated in the symbolic displacement I was attempting to analyze. But displacement is everywhere now. I was struck recently listening to Baroness Scotland on Michael Berkeley’s Private Passions discussing race and historical suffering.

The implication — perhaps unintended, perhaps not — was that Britain commemorates the Holocaust more fully than the atrocities of the Middle Passage. There is an understandable grievance there, certainly. Yet once suffering itself becomes implicitly ranked and compared between groups, politics begins quietly to re-racialize public life. Hierarchies of victimhood emerge. The Jew once again becomes symbolically overdetermined, not because Jews themselves demand it but because societies repeatedly place them in that role. The same mechanism explains why conspiracy thinking coheres so easily around figures like Jeffrey Epstein. Epstein became a symbolic condensation point for elite impunity, transnational networking, sexual coercion and invisible power. But if one wishes to understand whether Jewishness itself explains such phenomena, one need only place Jimmy Savile beside Epstein as a control specimen.

Savile operated openly for decades inside the heart of the British establishment, grooming vulnerable children before millions of television viewers while protected by institutions of staggering prestige. No Jewish conspiracy was required. The pathology was institutional, not ethnic. Yet because Epstein could be attached to already circulating symbolic anxieties about finance, globalization and hidden influence, conspiracy culture seized upon him differently. Again: antisemitism offers fake literacy to people trapped inside opaque systems. Kafka grasped part of this long ago. Watching Yiddish theatre performed by the Ostjuden whom assimilated Prague Jews often regarded with embarrassment, he wrote in his diary: ‘What have I in common with Jews?’ The line is often read as alienation from Jewishness. In fact it reveals something subtler and more universal.

Kafka recognized that identity itself becomes visible precisely at the moment of partial estrangement. One does not merely belong to a group; one apprehends oneself reflected through it. But the danger begins when that reflection hardens into metaphysical essentialism. That danger now surrounds all racial politics. Contemporary societies obsess endlessly over self-definition because globalization, migration, intermarriage and cultural blending have destabilized older categories. The result is frantic identity policing. People argue not only over what they are, but who possesses authority to define what they are. Yet self-definition alone cannot resolve the matter because all civic life requires reciprocal recognition between groups under shared law. If every category becomes purely self-authenticating, civic mediation collapses into competitive metaphysics.

This is why racism cannot ultimately be solved either through infinite subjective self-definition or through coercive essentialism. There are only two coherent possibilities. Either societies construct a genuinely robust civic framework of reciprocal rights and obligations applying equally to all persons irrespective of group identity; or they develop a sufficiently ‘thick’ moral and metaphysical culture capable of producing citizens who can govern themselves ethically despite profound disagreement. There is no stable middle ground composed solely of managerial language, algorithmic moderation and symbolic performance. As someone half-Jewish by birth, educated in both the Tanakh and the New Testament, shaped simultaneously by Jewish legal traditions and Christian moral philosophy, I have spent much of my life circling this problem. I do not possess thick ethnic identification in the straightforward sense.

Yet perhaps recoil from the collective ‘we’ is itself another mode of relation to it. Modern societies oscillate between tribal over-identification and radical deracination because both arise from the same anxiety: the fear that shared meaning itself may be dissolving. And perhaps it is. But if we are to avoid descending further into racialized paranoia and reciprocal hatred, then the first task is conceptual honesty. The Jew is not a mystical cipher explaining the illegibility of the modern world. Nor is Jewishness infinitely self-defining abstraction detached from all historical continuity. Jews are simply the historical people designated as such through intertwined religious, ethnic, familial and cultural inheritance, just as other peoples exist historically. Nothing metaphysically more, nothing metaphysically less.

The real problem lies elsewhere: in a civilization losing its ability to distinguish symbols from systems, signs from realities, spectacle from governance, and emotional gratification from civic understanding. Until we confront that deeper crisis of legibility, the free-floating signifier of ‘the Jew’ will continue attaching itself to every opaque structure modern societies fail to comprehend. There may well be some readers of this very article––to give an example readily to hand––who feel they haven’t understood what I’ve written, and who will ascribe that fact to another self-evident fact, as they see it: namely, that I am a Jew. And in this section exactly we can see governments themselves participating actively in destabilizing symbols rather than agreeing upon strong placeholders for necessary and long-term measures rather than expedient and politicized ones.

A good example of the government’s failure to grasp the conceptual load borne by terms such as ‘Jew’, ‘Jewish’, ‘Zionist’, and indeed ‘antisemitism’ itself may be found in the King’s Speech and the accompanying announcement of a dedicated Metropolitan Police protection team for the Jewish community. The protection of Jewish prayer sites, schools and citizens against intimidation or violence is not merely legitimate but elementary: it is already part of the Met’s remit twenty-four hours a day, seven days a week, three hundred and sixty-five days a year, just as the protection of Muslims, Hindus, Sikhs, Black Londoners, gay Londoners, and everyone else living under the civil law is part of that remit. Police liaison, intelligence and reassurance structures have long existed in relation to communities facing specific threats.

Yet the government appears astonishingly incurious about the symbolic implications of describing this as a ‘dedicated’ team when no directly analogous arrangement has previously been publicly foregrounded for another group in quite this way. The problem here is not the protection itself. The problem is legibility. Governments now communicate within a society saturated by conspiracy thinking, algorithmic amplification and collapsing civic literacy. They are not addressing rational actors gathered in an Athenian polis. They are addressing historically conditioned subjects already predisposed to suspect hidden linkages behind opaque state actions. Thus the moment the government publicly distinguishes Jewish security from general civic security, many citizens immediately begin asking themselves questions the government itself has failed clearly to answer: Why this group? Why now?

What exactly is the national-security dimension being alluded to? Does the state know something about Jewish vulnerability or foreign-state penetration that it is not disclosing? Is antisemitism now being securitized differently from racism in general? Because the government has failed to make its own reasoning sufficiently legible, the symbolic vacuum is instantly filled by speculation — precisely the condition within which antisemitism flourishes. This is particularly dangerous because one of the oldest structures within antisemitic thinking is already the fantasy of hidden coordination between Jews and state power.

If the government wished merely to reassure threatened Jewish citizens while preserving wider civic confidence, then it needed language of extreme conceptual precision explaining that the threat environment derives from a wider deterioration in public order, geopolitical spillover, online radicalization and hostile-state information operations affecting the whole polity. Instead, by foregrounding a ‘dedicated’ structure without adequately contextualizing it, the state inadvertently risks confirming the very asymmetries conspiracy-minded citizens already imagine. What this reveals, ultimately, is not malice but a catastrophic deficit in interpretive sophistication at the heart of government itself. The contemporary crisis is a crisis of signification. Words no longer remain stably attached to what they signify; they circulate memetically, emotionally and algorithmically.

Yet the British governing class, composed overwhelmingly of lawyers, policy technicians and procedural administrators, continues to treat language as though it were merely operational code: fixed terms attached to fixed functions. But political language no longer behaves like statute law. It behaves like unstable symbolic weather. What Number 10 requires is not necessarily a novelist, but certainly someone capable of reading language with enough suppleness to understand how signifiers detach themselves from their referents and acquire volatile secondary meanings within mass consciousness. Sir Keir Starmer, precisely because of his forensic and legalistic cast of mind, appears almost constitutionally incapable of conceptualizing politics at that level. And neither, one suspects, is the institution of monarchy itself equipped to compensate for that deficiency.

After all, you may well know the King’s speech––but the important question is, as it is for his Baron, Starmer: what do they read? What interests me far more than the specific books chosen by King Charles or Sir Keir Starmer is the form of mind betrayed by their reading habits. Charles gravitates toward narrative history: battles, campaigns, imperial personalities, the longue durée rendered as anecdote and procession. Starmer gravitates toward political biography, leadership studies, legal process and procedural scrutiny. Neither tendency, in itself, is contemptible. The problem lies in what both forms of reading conspicuously avoid: conceptualization. Narrative history, however elegantly written, often rests upon a hidden metaphysic it cannot interrogate. It assumes that history is fundamentally intelligible as sequence: one thing after another, rendered coherent by narrative craft.

The historian’s skill becomes the arrangement of events into legibility. But the deeper question — what history actually is, whether historical actors themselves understand the conditions under which they act, whether causation is retrospective projection rather than lived intelligibility — is usually absent. This is why narrative history appeals so strongly to constitutional monarchs. The constitutional monarch inhabits a fundamentally ornamental relation to history. His role is residual and negative: warning, advising, delaying, symbolizing. He experiences politics as procession interrupted occasionally by atmosphere and crisis. Naturally he prefers historians who render the world narratively continuous, because narrative continuity legitimizes his own symbolic continuity. Thus when Charles admires works of military or imperial narrative history, he is not merely displaying taste; he is revealing a model of temporality.

History appears as pageantry underwritten by endurance. One damn thing after another, occasionally brightened by acts of character. What disappears from view is structural opacity: the possibility that historical systems may exceed the understanding of their own participants, that institutions hollow before collapsing, or that political actors systematically misunderstand the range of options genuinely available to them. The same conceptual limitation appears in different form in Starmer’s attraction to political biography and leadership literature. Political biography flatters executives because it transforms structural outcomes into personal destiny. It tells the aspiring statesman that sufficient diligence, seriousness, moral stamina and strategic acuity may shape events decisively.

But modern governance increasingly operates within systems so mediatized, financialized and infrastructurally complex that leadership itself often becomes reactive rather than sovereign. Political biography therefore functions psychologically as compensation. It reassures the managerial class that agency still inheres primarily in disciplined individuals rather than distributed systems. This is why Starmer’s language about ‘leadership’ and ‘non-deferential scrutiny’ is revealing. It sounds intellectually rigorous, but it belongs above all to a media ecology. ‘Non-deferential scrutiny’ is precisely the ethic of the contemporary legal-political commentator, not necessarily of the practical executive confronting opaque systems whose constraints cannot simply be cross-examined into submission. The lawyer imagines that clarity emerges through interrogation.

But contemporary politics increasingly resembles navigation through fog: information overload, algorithmic distortion, infrastructural dependence, hostile-state interference, financial abstraction and emotional amplification occurring simultaneously. Under such conditions, procedural intelligence alone becomes insufficient. The problem, then, is not that Charles and Starmer are unintelligent men. It is that their intellectual habits reveal a deeper inability to conceptualize political possibility beyond inherited narrative forms. Charles reads history as continuity; Starmer reads politics as leadership. Both remain attached to nineteenth- and twentieth-century assumptions about legibility and agency while governing inside twenty-first-century systems characterized precisely by illegibility and distributed causality. And that matters because political language itself has changed.

The modern state no longer speaks into a stable civic culture capable of slowly assimilating distinctions. It speaks into an environment of detached signifiers, viral emotionality and algorithmic acceleration. Words no longer remain anchored to what they signify. ‘Security’, ‘community’, ‘antisemitism’, ‘extremism’, ‘democracy’, ‘leadership’ — all now circulate memetically before they circulate conceptually. Yet both the lawyer and the constitutional monarch remain trained in older assumptions about language. For the lawyer, words operate procedurally, attached to defined operations. For the monarch, words operate ceremonially, attached to continuity and ritual legitimacy. Neither formation adequately grasps the instability of signification under digital modernity. Which is why contemporary government so often appears conceptually unprepared for the world it inhabits.

It continues speaking as though citizens were rational participants in a shared symbolic order, when in reality they are fragmented subjects navigating mutually incompatible realities assembled algorithmically around them. The result is permanent civic illegibility. And once politics itself becomes illegible, citizens inevitably seek explanatory symbols. That is the environment in which conspiracy thinking flourishes, racial signifiers detach from stable meaning, and societies begin mistaking symbolic condensation for understanding itself. This explains, of course, why ‘everyone’ supposedly ‘knew’ that Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor was a paedophile, just as others insist that Jeffrey Epstein ‘must have been’ an intelligence asset, or attach him to ever-expanding conspiratorial systems of explanation.

Once symbolic condensation replaces evidence-based understanding, the imagination begins continuously escalating the hidden architecture supposedly lying behind events. The opaque financier becomes an intelligence operative; the operative becomes the node of a global network; the network becomes quasi-metaphysical. At that point politics passes fully into mythology, where the hunger for explanatory totality overwhelms any distinction between evidence, projection and fantasy. But then you ‘know’ that I’m a Jew, so QED: I’m also all the above. I have received a considerable amount of criticism during my career, much of it ad hominem. I have certainly been aware of it. But I have never gone looking for it, because I see little point in doing so. If my critics wished to engage me in serious discourse, I was always open to that possibility.

And if any of them felt violent towards me, I assumed that the civil law existed precisely to contain such impulses. What worries me about the present situation is that, in Kafka’s terms, I feel I have moved beyond the oscillation between estrangement from and identification with a group into something closer to compelled self-identification. The extent to which some readers encountering this essay may already imagine that the emphasis on conceptual thought, textual interpretation and symbolic analysis is itself somehow ‘inherently Jewish’ merely demonstrates how dangerous antisemitism can become. One begins to glimpse why it possesses such peculiar volatility as a racism.

It can nurture the fantasy that thought itself — interpretation itself, mediation itself, abstraction itself — belongs secretly to ‘the Jew’, and that resentment against complexity therefore becomes a revolt of instinct against interpretation, of appetite against restraint, of what Freud would have called the id against the superego. Yet Freud himself enters this discourse as another Jewish thinker. One immediately finds oneself trapped in recursive symbolic coils, Laocoön struggling against serpents that tighten precisely as one attempts to disentangle them. What has unsettled me most in recent years is not that I have suddenly ‘become more Jewish’ in any substantive sense. I am no more or less Jewish than I was before. Rather, it is that external designation intensifies internal relation.

Being identified, addressed, categorized and occasionally abused as a Jew inevitably modifies one’s consciousness of Jewishness, whether by drawing one toward identification or recoil. This is not unique to Jews. It is part of the wider phenomenology of racialization itself. The black person, the Muslim, the immigrant, the visibly marked minority — all know the peculiar psychological pressure exerted when society insists upon reading one through a signifier one may oneself inhabit only ambiguously. This is why antisemitism cannot simply be reduced to older theological or racial forms, even though it inherits from them. The Jew occupies a peculiar position within systems of colourism because Jewishness itself often appears liminal and unstable to the surrounding society. The Jew can appear assimilated and yet suddenly over-signified; indistinguishable and yet marked; white and yet not fully white; insider and outsider simultaneously.

Thus the Jew becomes a symbolic condensation not only of anxieties about power and abstraction, but of anxieties surrounding assimilation itself. Other racialized groups may begin unconsciously to project onto Jews suspicions connected to their own precarious relation to social acceptance: the fear of becoming ‘too assimilated’, ‘too acceptable’, insufficiently loyal to one’s own group, or secretly admitted into structures of legitimacy denied to others. And here we arrive finally at the deeper crisis of legibility. Human beings continuously reduce complexity into symbols because societies cannot function otherwise. Legibility itself depends upon symbolic condensation. But symbolic condensation always risks becoming racialization once the signifier detaches from lived reality and begins carrying excessive metaphysical weight. Nothing condenses symbolically more powerfully than pigmentation itself.

Skin colour becomes a visible shorthand onto which entire moral, political and civilizational narratives may be projected. But then, of course, I would say that, wouldn’t I — being, as some would now inevitably choose to phrase it, an olive-skinned Jew.

Poor old Josh Simons. Poor old Josh not simply because he has stepped aside in Makerfield so that Andy Burnham can stage what increasingly resembles a leadership coup by by-election, but because in doing so he has exposed something far larger than the crisis of the Labour Party. He has exposed the crisis of the British political imagination itself. I met Simons in the green room before Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg. He seemed pleasant enough: bright, smooth — possibly a little colourless, with the pale face that goes with too much concentration on polling rather than any more significant lodestar.

Overall, entirely what one would expect from a product of Cambridge — where he studied political theory — Harvard — where he continued to do so, eventually acting as research assistant to the eminent Amartya Sen — Meta — where he brought his ‘expertise’ on political theory to bear on the problems presented to governance in democracies by AI — and Labour Together — that gimcrack centrist machine which squared the circle for long enough, despite its obvious eccentricities, to get Starmer elected. Talking to him, the years fell away and I thought I was in the presence of Geoff Mulgan, Blair’s equivalent to Simons in the 1990s, whom I knew well. Mulgan had been full of the benefits of technology when it came to realising popular sovereignty: this was the era of stakeholders, although it was funny how many of those the Blair governments courted turned out to be holding stakes in nothing but financial capital rather than social capital.

Now comes Geoff Mulgan after the platform. The managerial meritocracy in its late-digital form. And yet when I discussed Burnham’s leadership project with Simons, who surely was a literal stakeholder in this having fallen on his sword, he seemed nonplussed. When I asked him whether Burnham understood the distinction between republican legitimacy and plebiscitary democracy, Simons paused, thought for a moment, and said: ‘I don’t know. I’ll ask him Monday.’ I emailed him yesterday to see if the popular Manchester mayor could be bothered to answer this vital question, but as yet have received no reply. Perhaps Burnham would like to phone a friend — a common desire among senior politicians. But my picayune exchange with Simons told me almost everything. Namely: that for him politics remains procedural, tactical, and therefore the polity remains governable.

This was a young, sleep-deprived father with a newborn baby, who said on the programme that his and his wife’s decision to abandon the Makerfield seat after only a few months had been difficult. Yet staring into his eyes I could sense that his mind was still full of systems management, communications calibration, governance frameworks, democratic resilience, platform accountability, institutional legitimacy. His instinct when confronted by a constitutional question was not to answer it but to defer it upwards through the managerial hierarchy. And therein lies the entire problem. The political class no longer thinks conceptually — instead it reacts purely tactically. Not even strategically: the battlespace is too constricted, too overflown by the drones of social media for strategic intelligence to emerge. Which is why what intellectuals remain in British politics are little more than policy wonks.

Simons has written a thesis on AI governance and democracy, worked with Amartya Sen, passed through Meta’s ‘responsible AI’ ecosystem, emerging with caveats but no real ideas on how to control AI in a way his electorate understand. Then he went into Westminster seemingly convinced that the legitimacy crisis of liberal democracy can be managed through better systems cognitio! Duh! So what struck me when we went live in the studio was not that he was stupid — quite the opposite. It was that he had no felt relation whatsoever to the cultural-symbolic terrain upon which Burnham is attempting to fight. This was shown in his response to my intervention concerning the well-known Wigan delicacy, the smack barm: in fact a buttered roll served with scraps of fried chips scraped from the bottom of the basket together with an optional serving of pea wet — namely the liquor from mushy peas.

My reference to this occurred because I know Wigan fairly well. Well enough that I evoked this signature snack of the urban poor in the post-industrial North knowing that the Makerfield seat is in fact no longer full of people who depend on smack barms, but rather of those who are nostalgic for the industrial past out of which the necessity for this food emerged. It is of course this industrial heritage that continues to form the bedrock of what passes for communitarianism. These older white people, experiencing their own form of precarity, reach back towards a time that never was in support of their politics: a uchronia, not a utopia. I shouldn’t imagine any of the Makerfield electorate really want to live in the Wigan portrayed by George Orwell in his celebrated account of the area during the Depression of the early 1930s.

Nor indeed in the Wigan described by Stephen Armstrong in Wigan Pier Revisited a decade ago: a Wigan of gig workers, very little money, and black and brown faces unlike the Makerfield constituency itself. If Burnham does win Makerfield on his nostalgic agenda and subsequently becomes Prime Minister, he will be leading the entire country implicitly back towards a future that is quite simply inconceivable in terms of modern Britain. Because Burnham’s politics are not really procedural. They are nostalgic, while his potential electorate have moved on more than him… into the past. They now read the Daily Mail, not the Mirror, and they don’t belong to unions or work in factories, neither do they live — for the most part — in council housing. Much of the emotional economy of the Mail consists in othering one undeserving group or another.

How is Burnham going to convince such voters he shares their anxieties without dog-whistling the same bigotries? Ones that, far from being exhausted, are noow reearing their heads like XL Bullies fed on… smack barms. At first I described Makerfield as a smack barm floating in a sea of pea wet moored to Daily Mail Hate Island. But that’s not quite right. Makerfield is not the smack barm itself. It is the nostalgia for the smack barm. The Instagram feed of the smack barm. The memory-image of industrial solidarity translated into trad-food photography, pints in pubs, municipal sentimentality and emotionally reassuring localism. The references to pubs and pints come thick and fact from the Burnham camp: these are, its implied, their true symbols of comity, rather than the Oxbridge common rooms that really formed them.

The actual constituency is not composed primarily of heroic industrial workers waiting to resume collective labour in giant foundries. Large sections are older voters, retirees, economically inactive people, households dependent on combinations of private pensions, property equity, public transfers and low-growth service-sector remnants. Puffer people. Puffed-up with resentment, anxiety, nostalgia and the fear of downward mobility. Burnham therefore finds himself in the extraordinary position of having to recreate the social conditions that once produced Labourism in order to revive Labourism itself. This is the contradiction at the heart of his project. Social democracy emerged from socialised production.

Labour’s republicanism — and I don’t mean by this anti-monarchism — rested on labour corporations in the older sense: unions, municipal structures, collective workplaces, industrial identities, mass institutions capable of mediating between private life and the state. The House of Commons functioned as part of a wider constitutional organism in which organised blocs confronted one another, sublated one another, and gradually produced consensus. This was the old British republican settlement. Britain conceived of itself as republican in spirit even while remaining monarchical in form. Sovereignty was not plebiscitary. It was mediated. Crown-in-Parliament. Two parties. Two great constitutional lobes. The Commons and Lords functioning dialectically: a thesis from one side of the House, an antithesis from the other, sublation––eventually––via the House of Lords and the monarch’s assent.

By the 1970s this had become so stable that political scientists developed the theory of ‘Butskellism’: the notion that Labour and Conservative governments had effectively converged around a common administrative understanding of Britain itself. Then came Brexit. The real constitutional significance of Brexit was never simply whether Britain should or should not have left the European Union. It was that the referendum introduced plebiscitary sovereignty directly into a constitutional order historically built around mediated parliamentary sovereignty. And once that happened the old consensus cracked open. This is why, when asked by Kuensburg whether I though the question of rejoining the EU should now be back on the political agenda, I demuured: beefore we can even get to that, we need to deal with the constitutional problem the plebiscite revealed.

The political class is still unable to grasp the necessity for this: they’re too focussed on the back of each others’ suit jackets, looking for the best place to insert a dagger. The referendum was won narrowly. The demos spoke, yes, but precisely because the margin was so narrow the result exposed the problem the Athenians themselves feared in democracy: that majoritarian voting alone does not necessarily generate legitimacy. It may instead intensify division and demagoguery. The old British republican settlement had depended upon gradual mediation through institutions, parties, parliamentary process and constitutional ambiguity. Brexit replaced this with direct democratic instruction and then expected the old system simply to digest it. It could not.

The result has been a terrible case of societal indigestion ever since, and much in the way of mephitic afflatus — of which the appointment of Peter Mandelson is only the latest –– initially silent but eventually deadly –– emission. This is why Kemi Badenoch’s remark on the programme that Britain now exists as a multi-party political system was so important. In one sentence she quietly acknowledged the exhaustion of the old constitutional machinery. The bipolar structure no longer coheres. And yet Burnham’s answer is effectively to pretend that the industrial republic of the twentieth century can be emotionally restarted through municipal affect: Pints. Pubs. Railways. Public ownership. Lowry paintings of figures as crudely, naively-drawn and stick-like as his vision. Council housing. Reindustrialisation. But where are the labour corporations that once sustained Labour’s republican grammar? Where are the mass industrial workplaces?

Where are the trade-unionised productive communities capable of underwriting the moral economy Burnham invokes? He must recreate them before he can politically represent them: the Hacienda must be rebuilt before anyone in Manchester and its environs can rave again.. This is why his project feels not just spectral like a ghost –– but wavery in the white light of the screen: a mirage, in fact. Because in lockstep, Simons and his technocratic generation propose not nostalgia but systems management. AI governance. Algorithmic fairness. Platform regulation. Digital accountability. This reassures no one: the electorate already experiences the existing state as opaque, illegible and procedurally hostile –– that’s why they’d like to hang the mild-mannered lawyer who’s currently at its helm.

And now comes the latest ratcheting-up of the Mandelson affair — behind which, it must be emphasised, lie all the other governmental malfeasances of the past decade, including those that took place under the Johnson, Truss and May premierships and which have yet to be fully investigated. Those responsible for the malappropriation of government money and the erosion of political transparency have yet to be held accountable. But at least with the Mandelson affair the effluent has floated sufficiently to the surface for us to observe carefully what is actually happening there. The issue is not simply Peter Mandelson’s vetting file or Jeffrey Epstein or redactions or security clearances. The real issue is the emergence of government-by-thread, which is why the move to recover WhatsApp messages involves the procedural state being caught in its underwear — if not exactly guilty of sending dick pics.

Government now increasingly operates through attention flows, encrypted chats, rapid tactical signalling, screenshots, deniable informality and permanent low-level factional management. Ministers and advisers imagine themselves merely chatting — not even communicating in a definable sense, let alone engaging in anything with the conceptual weight of productive discourse. It’s all he-said then-she-said so-we-must-say. And in reality, far from being some Oz-like digital puppet-master, the state itself is acting through these feedback systems. And once Parliament demands disclosure, the supposedly ephemeral medium becomes constitutional evidence: we chowed down on this, the scrag-end of sovereignty. But here’s the rub: the emoji appended to the scrag-end becomes archive, just as much as all the “likes” I got on my X feed after I sang the praises of the smack barm.

This is the truly dangerous intersection between the Burnham nostalgia project and the Simons technocratic project. One seeks to revive the moral imagery of the industrial republic. The other assumes that digital governance can simply be layered on top of a collapsing constitutional settlement — thereby making an ass out of you and me, quite possibly forever. The discussions the government have already been having with the FANG companies concerning the introduction of a new AI-dedicated superweb tied to the state do nothing to reassure an electorate who, while digitally literate in the sense that they know how to use the device in their pocket to access consumer goods and services, are nonetheless profoundly suspicious of machines that now regularly demonstrate conceptual capacities they themselves no longer share.

No longer share because it’s this very technology, in its already mal-absorbed state that’s responsiblle for an effective decline in literacy of 50% within barely a decade, it is no surprise that neither nostalgia nor technocracy can address the deeper legitimacy crisis. A crisis being accelerated by the bidirectional electronic media systems which people like Simons regard primarily as governance challenges rather than anthropological transformations. The public senses this instinctively ––even as it reaches for its phone to stop itself thinking about it, and instead look at an image of a tasty smack barm. They may not understand AI governance conceptually, but they understand perfectly well that the existing state already feels remote, procedural, unreadable and manipulative. Why would they welcome another layer of algorithmic mediation administered by policy intellectuals from Harvard and Meta?

Hence the impossible position Labour now occupies. Burnham must convert an ageing nostalgic electorate into the social-democratic industrial citizenry of the past without possessing the industrial base that once produced such citizens. He must reassure puffer people — and I use the term advisedly: this clothing is cheap, warm, synthetic, protective, and entirely oil-derived — whose lives are structured less by productive labour than by asset anxiety, media saturation, welfare dependence and demographic fear. Hence the puffers. And all the while the unspoken issue of race hovers over the entire landscape. Because the welfare economy, immigration system and demographic transformation of neighbouring constituencies remain structurally present in the political imagination even when unstated in Burnham’s rhetoric. Makerfield may be an island — but it’s still part of the main. Poor old Josh Simons.

He thought he was handing Andy Burnham a constituency, what he he may actually have passed him is a phone, the screen of which displays a thread detailing a great deal of useless careerist chit-chat; guff, that in the end amounts to a constitutional decomposition: the barm, saturated with gruel, disintegrates, and the smack floats downstream into the polluted canal beside the pierhead. Farewell Wigan and Makerfield –– we’ll see you down the pub for a pint with Nige.
