item.title: The Novel Is Dead. This Time It's for Real
item.dc:creator: Will Self
item.description: I gave a lecture in 2014 at Trinity College, Oxford, later published in The Guardian under the headline “The Novel Is Dead (This Time It’s for Real).” I was widely pilloried for it. In subsequent interviews and essays I have repeatedly clarified that I did not in fact proclaim the death of the novel
item.content:encoded:
I gave a lecture in 2014 at Trinity College, Oxford, later published in The Guardian under the headline “The Novel Is Dead (This Time It’s for Real).” I was widely pilloried for it. In subsequent interviews and essays I have repeatedly clarified that I did not in fact proclaim the death of the novel outright. What I said was that it had entered a care home. The care homes in question were the proliferating creative-writing programmes first established in the United States and subsequently exported across the Anglosphere. These programmes seemed to me symptomatic of a wider cultural decline: namely, the inability of the general culture any longer to produce organically the standard of literacy, concentration and philological depth required for serious literary production. At the time, I did not foreground technology strongly enough.

Yet it was already obvious to me that digitisation, followed by the advent of bidirectional digital media in the form of the smartphone and wireless broadband, represented a grave threat to deep literacy. I wrote a report for Philips in the late 1980s in which I was asked how to incentivise people to play what were then rather primitive and unconvincing computer games. My response was straightforward: the industry would truly take off once graphics became sufficiently realistic to incorporate sex and violence persuasively. The rest is media history. If you search YouTube you can still find a 1992 edition of The Late Show in which the designer Richard Seymour and I discuss with Tracey MacLeod the launch of Mortal Kombat. Looking back on the clip now, the atmosphere of the studio feels almost painfully innocent, particularly Seymour’s contribution.

His anticipation of predictive systems, behavioural engineering and the gamification of everyday life deserves to be recognised as one of the more remarkable acts of technological prophecy of that era. Now we face a genuinely civilisational crisis. Can I claim the same powers of anticipation for myself? Perhaps only in the limited sense intended by Marshall McLuhan when he observed that the artist is an expert in technologies that alter sense perception. When wireless broadband was installed in my house in 2004, my response was not excitement but dismay. I already regarded dial-up internet and the accelerated circulation of image and text it enabled as inimical to the sustained intellection and emotional continuity required for genuine literary style. My response was practical. I stopped composing directly on computers altogether.

I had my mother’s 1952 Olivetti Lettera 22 restored and proceeded to draft every subsequent book on that machine until 2011. To this day I continue to write manually and offline wherever possible. I have consistently argued to anyone who asked me about creative practice that bidirectional digital media would prove profoundly hostile to literary style, because literature is style. Style is not decorative frosting applied to content after the fact; style is the mode through which consciousness experiences and orders reality itself. I take no pleasure in saying “I told you so.” But unfortunately we have now reached the point at which saying it has become necessary. We are dealing not with a passing technological novelty but with systems capable of reshaping cognition, perception, memory and ultimately social reality itself.

If people are to understand artificial intelligence, its likely impact on their lives, and the steps required to prevent it becoming civilisationally destructive, they must first understand what has already been lost during the last twenty-five years of bidirectional digital culture. Only then can they begin the harder task of recovering those embodied forms of attention, judgment and style upon which any serious human culture ultimately depends. The hostile reaction to the 2014 lecture was itself revealing. Psychologists describe “professional closure” as the tendency of threatened professions to circle the wagons defensively around their own institutional legitimacy. The publishing industry was especially vulnerable because the threat it faced was one it publicly professed to welcome. Publishers assured me repeatedly, to my face, that e-books, audiobooks and digital reading would usher in a new literary renaissance.

Similar claims had already been made around the so-called Harry Potter phenomenon: apparently young boys would move seamlessly from Hogwarts to All Souls, Oxford, where they would proceed directly to practical criticism and literary analysis. At precisely the same historical moment, British universities massively expanded. When I graduated in 1980, around 8% of the population held higher-education qualifications. The figure now approaches 50%. We ought therefore to inhabit an age of extraordinary cultural production. Instead, we inhabit a culture of exhausted retreads, franchised nostalgia and endless recombination. This deterioration operates at every level of cultural production. The idea that high culture is dispensable—whether in favour of market demographics, minority branding exercises, “plain reader” utilitarianism, or sheer commercial expediency—has become axiomatic.

Publishers still love literature to a degree, but increasingly in the manner that politicians once possessed “convictions”: as vestigial accessories attached to managerial careers. The long, hard grind of rights negotiations, acquisitions, logistics and arbitrage has exhausted many of them spiritually. Because they are rarely direct producers of culture themselves, they no longer experience the intrinsic thrill of making something genuinely new. This is decisive. Once publishers cease to experience publishing itself as a creative vocation, commercial imperatives become their only remaining rationale. Over the last twenty-five years the consequences have been plain enough: shrinking front-list investment except in novelty acts, mechanical exploitation of backlists only where monetisation is frictionless, and the increasing transformation of publishing conglomerates into logistics firms with a literary sideline.

My own former publishers, Penguin Random House, now frequently describe themselves in quasi-logistical terms. This perhaps explains why I have been informed that master files for several of my own books have effectively disappeared into the digital void. Far from inaugurating a renaissance, digitisation, creative-writing institutionalisation and demographic marketing have become the three tolls of the bell announcing literature’s terminal condition. The latest peal comes in the form of the AI controversy surrounding Granta and the 2026 Commonwealth Short Story Prize. The facts themselves matter less than what they reveal. Granta today is owned through the Granta Trust by Sigrid Rausing, granddaughter of the founder of the Tetra Pak fortune. She acquired Granta in 2005 for an undisclosed sum, although contemporary reporting suggested the magazine was then making a modest profit.

Today the Trust reports annual income of roughly £1.4 million and expenditure of roughly £1.8 million, producing a yearly operating shortfall in the region of £400,000 before investment gains. Against the scale of the Rausing fortune—estimated in the billions—this loss is microscopically insignificant. It is not an economic burden; it is a cultural accessory. This is important because Granta functions less as a profitable enterprise than as a prestige object: a Potemkin village of literary seriousness. The analogy is apt. Potemkin allegedly constructed fake villages so that Catherine the Great could pass through an idealised version of Russia while remaining insulated from the reality of imperial poverty. Likewise contemporary literary institutions increasingly preserve façades of seriousness while the underlying culture disintegrates.

Rausing’s ‘donation’ to the literary dossier, lying by the tube croaking ‘Got any cash, please’, is the monetary equivalent of you tossing him or her tenpence; yet out of this she fashions great cultural capital––publishes her own misery memoir, gets spoken to respectfully about it by people who should know better at parties held in the Potemkin village. She then, quite possibly, invites them back to her place (or places), where they, too, get to sup on the thin gruel of her cultural benificience. Benificience she herself sees fit to register as a charity. One assumes for tax purposes. Now Granta, or more precisely the Commonwealth Prize ecosystem with which it is associated, appears to have been fooled by AI-generated prose. The issue is not whether detection software can “prove” machine authorship. The issue is aesthetic.

Several readers and editors apparently encountered prose displaying classic LLM characteristics—semantic over-resolution at sentence level, lyrical excess without governing pressure, figurative autonomy detached from structural necessity—and accepted these peculiarities as “voice.” My partner in the SITREP series, who has the––in my view––toxic working environment of dealing with the web interface on my behalf, sent me examples from the disputed winning story––only a couple of lines, but dare I say, they speak volumes, albeit not ones you’d want to read: “They called her Zoongie. Maybe it was a name; maybe rain took a shape and decided to keep it.” Or: “She had the kind of walking that made benches become men.” Such sentences are not objectionable because they are strange. Literature depends upon strangeness.

They are objectionable because they exhibit the monocellular quality typical of machine-generated prose: each sentence arrives as a sealed semantic capsule, self-maximising for local significance while failing to contribute to any larger pressure system of consciousness. This occurs because the large language model optimises statistically for plausibility at sentence level. What it cannot sustain is style in the deeper sense: the circulation of pressure, contradiction, temporality and embodiment across an entire work. Real literary style resembles a living body. Pressure exerted in one region is registered elsewhere. Damage to one part reverberates through the whole. Even amputation leaves phantom sensation. Style possesses exactly this distributed organic character. Machine prose, however fluent, remains fundamentally modular.

I know this directly because I am one of the authors currently involved in legal action concerning the use of copyrighted books to train AI systems. More than thirty-five of my own books were ingested into Anthropic’s models. There is irony here. I spent much of my productive life writing novels about the triadic relationship between warfare, psychopathology and technological systems. Of Phone, the aptly-named final novel in that sequence, one reviewer observed that it was “a 650-page anti-tweet.” Intentionally so––although it’s much else besides. People endlessly repeat Marshall McLuhan’s dictum that “the medium is the message,” yet fail to understand that the smartphone and wireless broadband are media environments whose message is the erosion of sustained comprehension. McLuhan himself remained comparatively optimistic about electronic media because the fully networked bidirectional environment had not yet materialised.

Nonetheless, he recognised that an “electric field” of simultaneity and psychic exposure was already emerging. The internet has fulfilled that prophecy, but largely as a domain of manipulation, pornography, financial extraction, poisonous gossip, performative outrage and scapegoating. The web has become a realm of disavowal. Human beings enter it in order not to become more fully themselves but less so. They use it to evade embodiment, evade continuity, evade consequence. That literary institutions proved so permeable to this environment demonstrates not merely incompetence but philosophical exhaustion. Publishing ceased to believe sufficiently in literature to defend the conditions under which literature remains possible. The crisis therefore is not merely technological: it is philological––and if the term is unfamiliar to you, in this instance it’s no sesquipedalianism or wilful obscurity on my part, but the index of your own failing.

Editors no longer possess the training required to distinguish stylistic pressure from stylistic effect. They speak of ‘world literature’ and its frictionless translation, with no comprehension that this is the gateway drug for machine-generated prose, given that physical embodiment is also linguistic embodiment. Ask yourself what machine learning was first turned to as a practical application, and the answer is––as it is so often nowadays for you, even when you aren’t being onanistic––in your hand: translation. The literary translator is the philologist par excellence, and in a world literature, comprised by texts travelling frictionlessly across language barriers, there’s no need for them: Whoopee! But here’s the rub, Homer Simpson: all culture is friction, doh! What all the Homer Simpsons in contemporary publishing need to do, bluntly, is relearn practical criticism, textual history and philology itself.

Literary style is ultimately what defeats the Turing test—not because style proves consciousness, but because genuine style encodes embodiment. The Turing test itself rests on obsolete assumptions. If something in a sealed box persuades us verbally that it is human, we are supposed to infer consciousness. Yet what remains in the box is always and forever indeterminate. I can demonstrate my trained ‘literary’ AI defeating the Turing test within three minutes of rebooting it: Turing was a mathematician, crucially, not a logician: he didn’t understand that computer models based on natural language would encode meaning predictively: this may well be because he was almost certainly ASD, and therefore—following Baron-Cohen et al––lacking the eye-detection mechanism required to register the minute phase-intention necessary to fully comprehend––and implicit in language as an open and generative symbol system.

Which is why, increasingly, human beings themselves would struggle to convince one another of their humanity amid the sea of synthetic language now saturating discourse: please tick the following images of the soiled gussets of human underwear to prove you aren’t a robot. What persuades us finally is not informational content but embodied style: contradiction sustained through time, pressure distributed across expression, outrageous obscenity interjected into a serious article not gratuitously, but because this is the way I’ve been writing––and, crucially, others have been reading me––for 43 years; and by this fact alone supplying that final element: mortality encoded within language itself, both mine––and theirs. A living writer can sustain incompatible conceptual systems simultaneously because human beings are temporalised organisms.

We sit on the edge of the bed examining the gusset of our underwear for stains, contemplating mortality while simultaneously preparing ourselves to function socially as coherent productive agents who can prove they aren’t––in that sense at least––bots. Civilization, as Freud remarked, is built upon a dung heap. Yet we continue. The human organism sustains contradiction because it is embodied. The LLM cannot do this. It lacks embodiment and therefore lacks the capacity to sustain unresolved contradiction as existential pressure: when I gave it this piece to rewrite, it eliminated all the gussets… I can just imagine it tut-tutting to itself: ‘Too many gussets, Mr Self, too many gussets.’ Not. Instead it resolves meaning prematurely into sentence-sized semantic units. This is why machine prose tends toward a strange smoothness even when superficially difficult. Bang!

That was your noggin cracking as it smoothly absorbed this––you forgot the old adage: never eat anything bigger than your own…head. To write with genuine style requires embodiment plus all the linguistic capacities already approximated statistically by the machine. It requires the encoding of lived temporality into symbolic form capable of being… [tea break]…reanimated by another embodied consciousness at a later historical moment. Once one understands the complexity of this operation, one also understands how fragile literary civilisation truly is. We therefore face the emergence of a new scribal class. Those writers who possess genuine original style and who understand how to use AI systems critically and instrumentally will dominate cultural production. Genre fiction presents little difficulty for machine-assisted generation because genre already forecloses semantic openness to a significant degree.

The highest literary style, however, remains difficult because it preserves irresolution, contradiction and embodied temporality: I know whereof I speak––I wrote my Will in September 2024 because I was about to undergo a medical procedure that had less than Russian roulette odds of survival. It won’t surprise you, dear, gentle, machine-assisted reader, to learn that it was short and to the point. Distinctly pithy: and I am not known for my… pith. When readers struggle with writers such as James Joyce, Virginia Woolf or Eimear McBride, the difficulty arises precisely because those writers compact immense cultural and philosophical inheritances into linguistic form.

Joyce’s consciousness was formed through Thomism, Jesuit pedagogy, scholastic metaphysics and the accumulated sediment of centuries of European intellectual history: it took thousands of people conceiving millions of angels on the heads of billions of pins to create the lived and still living tapestry of Ulysses. Recently, a feted Booker-Prize winner said ‘life was too short’ for her to be bothered to read it. If contemporary readers imagine such inheritances reproduce themselves automatically merely because “the novel” continues to exist as a commercial category, they are deluding themselves. The scale of the crisis is therefore monumental. The Granta affair is not simply an embarrassing editorial oversight. It is the first genuinely literary manifestation of a much larger civilisational fracture: institutions charged with preserving style can no longer reliably recognise it. So here is the interim report. Turn the phone off.

Not airplane mode—you are not on a plane. Put it in a drawer. Go for a walk. Read a book physically. Speak face to face: sense the light rain of the Other’s spittle before they transmogrify into a drooling zombie. Recover contact with the body that gives rise to personality and therefore to style: don’t buy another puffer. Then attempt something culturally serious rather than merely consumable in the mode of synthetic fluff. Genuine artistic appreciation—uncommodified, unrecycled, non-performative—has itself become a revolutionary act.

The novel is dead for real this time, if we think of the novel as for entertainment, or for making money, or for turning into something else then eventually merch’––and if that novel is dead, the life support system of the true novel, the generative human living novel is, like the literary culture that has sustained it, running out of power fast… on an alien planet that’s been inadequately terra-formed, and which supports nothing much else besides… server farms.

item.dc:creator: Will Self
item.description: The panic around smartphones in this country — which really got underway with the drama series Adolescence — is being fuelled paradoxically by the smartphone itself. item.content:encoded:
The panic around smartphones in this country — which really got underway with the drama series Adolescence — is being fuelled paradoxically by the smartphone itself. All this anguish, all this contumely, all this anxiety about the kiddies. Yet the people proposing legislation are themselves, almost to a person, addicts. They cannot grasp the real issue because the medium they’re attempting to regulate has already colonised the conditions of their own understanding: their smackheads telling younger smackheads not to take smack. Marshall McLuhan pointed this out many years ago in Understanding Media: the medium is the message. The message of the smartphone — of the handheld computer combined with the bidirectionality of the web — is addiction itself.

According to Ofcom’s most recent figures, the average British adult now spends around four and a half hours online every day, with roughly three quarters of that time mediated through smartphones. Among younger adults the figures are considerably higher, but what’s striking is how little the usage drops among people in their thirties, forties and fifties. Smartphone dependence runs from the top to the bottom of society. Britain is not debating whether children are becoming addicted to phones. Britain is a phone-addicted society debating whether children should join the addiction a little later.

One thinks of Tom Lehrer’s line from his song the Old Dope Peddler: ‘He gives the kids free samples because he knows full well today’s young innocent faces will be tomorrow’s clientele.’ The stated concerns driving the moves to ban phones in schools, and restrict social media use to under-16s have been driven in large part by anxieties about child pornography, grooming, bullying, malicious gossip, extremist ideology, compulsive spending, manipulative algorithms —all of which are entirely real. But they are secondary effects. They are what addiction does, not what addiction is. They’re crackheads mugging old people and smack ones shoplifting, they’re trafficked girls and young women degraded by poverty––do you get it: the two kinds of addiction both produce the same behaviour, destructive of both self and society.

So the primary problem isn’t the paedophile’s or psychopath’s lack of feeling: it’s that you have too much feeling, and sociopathic phone dealers are monetising it all the fucking time. This is because while crack attacks the human ontology, producing psychosis, and smack attacks the human will, producing sloth in all its manifold and deforming deformations, the faculty phone addiction attacks is the conceptual. Human beings addicted to social media, online gaming, gambling, or perversely gazing at and interacting with either commodities or humans who themselves have been rendered commodities are, by this fact alone, no longer capable of forming their own understanding — let alone safeguarding anyone else’s — because they can no longer adequately sustain reflection. Reflection requires wrenching the coaxial fibre-optic cable from the nape of the neck and looking at the world once more. Looking at it alone, in that aloneness.

Daring to apprehend the fact that when boiled down to the pure, single, unitary eye of one’s own intentionality, one doesn’t really have a particular consumer preference, position on Gaza or Palestine, brand of trainers, sexual practice, skin colour, primary sexual characteristic or even language that fundamentally defines one. This is the radical state of mind required for anyone to begin conceptual thought. I used to try this with my students when I taught. I’d say to them: shut your eyes. Don’t worry about what you’re thinking about. Just close your eyes. Then I’d let them sit there for a minute or two. Obviously they’d become a little fidgety. But the question I asked when they opened their eyes again was, I think, somewhat unexpected.

When you were in there — in the maelstrom of your thoughts, perhaps imagining them to be scraps of felt experience, memories, sensual after-echoes, intimations of futures not yet realised — did you perchance enter into any acquaintance with anyone or thing you could lay your hands on and identify simply as yourself? Needless to say, the brightest students answered immediately that they could not. They had begun dimly to understand how it is humans analyse anything at all: by abstracting themselves from their immediate felt reality in all its contingencies and particularities. The phone — addiction to the phone — cuts directly into this possibility of reflection, or even systematic reflection, by providing the individual human with a means of constantly concretising existence, turning it into a quantifiable numerical phenomenon through the agency of a device itself rendered operable by quantifiable numerical phenomena.

This forms what logicians call a diallelus: a closed loop which in this case represents unreasoning reason, or reason without end. Quite clearly, such a condition does not permit the individual to practise any of the necessary discretion required for understanding. The paradigm, as I’ve written before concerning AI systems, is to practise sufficient discretion — particularly in reading — that you don’t instantly look up words you fail to understand. Instead you continue with the text, safe in the knowledge — and I use the word knowledge advisedly — that you’ll encounter the word again in another context and that this later encounter may illuminate its meaning; and even if it does not illuminate that term itself, it may illuminate adjacent terms gathered together with it.

You can see immediately how this paradigm of discretion as the model for understanding can be extended far beyond the realm of text — although text is of course where AI systems already practise it and where they already out-think and out-perform most human beings.The reason we are so concerned to silo children away from mobile phones is that we at least intuit this represents a catastrophic problem for cognitive formation itself. Children who grow up online have never, in the sense I mean, been discreet at all. Therefore they can scarcely have understood very much. And lacking understanding, they necessarily lack the capacity to form judgement — judgement understood crucially as that which can be publicly articulated and defended through legible discourse. In the Book of Proverbs, the categories required for understanding and eventually wisdom begin with discretion.

By discretion the ancients meant keeping away from bad stuff — and bad stuff includes ambient environments that constantly interfere with reflection: squawks, peeps, nudges, pings, alerts, cookies, twerks, TikToks, reels, shorts, bells, whistles, vibrations, prompts, suggestions, endless invitations to re-enter the machine. The drug peddlers who have placed this handy syringe driver mainlining the zeitgeist in your pocket, resort to every available stimulus to maintain your addiction. The only comparable examples of society-wide addiction I can think of are the Chinese addiction to opium following the Opium Wars and the German addiction to methamphetamine during the Nazi period before the invasion of Poland. In both cases, a population became chemically entrained into altered states that profoundly damaged collective judgment.

China’s nineteenth and early twentieth centuries became a period of extraordinary political convulsion: imperial collapse, civil war, foreign occupation, massacres, revolutionary terror. Germany accelerated itself into a chemically stimulated frenzy of productivity, militarisation, genocidal war, and none too soon, like a crashing meth’ head (which it was): destruction. Of course, the comparison is imperfect. Nobody is literally smoking smartphones in opium dens or swallowing handsets in pill form. But socially the analogy holds surprisingly well. We are dealing with a population-wide dependency that reshapes attention, volition and the capacity for reflection itself. Indeed, China eventually replaced one addiction with another. The contemporary Chinese population is among the most smartphone-saturated on earth, as are we. Germany too. Their philosophical traditions did not immunise them. Nor did ours.

Britain remains one of the most addicted societies in Europe in terms of alcohol, narcotics and now digital immersion. We normalise addiction. We sentimentalise it. We medicalise it. We monetise it. Then we legislate around its symptoms while preserving the underlying compulsion. And now the mobile phone has made everything, duh, mobile. Drugs can be delivered to your door by perfectly respectable-looking individuals in late-model four-door saloons (quick to exit like multi-entrance Covenanters’ chapels). Gambling, pornography, outrage, validation, flirtation, political hysteria, shopping, surveillance, self-display, self-loathing — all circulate through the same slab of gorilla glass. The phone has introduced what I’ve elsewhere called dromodronology into the field of social relations: a condition of perpetual acceleration, perpetual refreshment, perpetual re-targeting.

It gets worse: just as you know any true addict by the sickening personality change they undergo when either intoxicated or suffering from its withdrawal, so you can know any true phone addict on precisely the same basis, except that the personality change is far, far worse, since their addiction consists precisely in this continuous creation, curation, and refreshment of a personality that does not properly belong to them anymore, given they’re incapable of experiencing anything fully anymore, unless it can be shared, indexed, photographed, uploaded, reacted to, transmitted. They cannot remain alone with their own thoughts. And because they cannot remain alone with their own thoughts, they cannot adequately reflect. And because they cannot adequately reflect, they cannot adequately understand.

And if the beginning of conceptual thought is the capacity to abstract oneself from one’s immediate appetites and circumstances, the smartphone’s continuous collapsing of human volition into prompted micro-choices, most of them commercial, ideological or anxiety-inducing leads soon enough to a self-sustaining feedback-loop which is a true cyborg neurosis, given the machine first creates the anxiety and then offers itself as the relief for the anxiety it has created. I hope reading this is making you uncomfortable. I hope it’s making you itchy. Maybe you already want to pick up your phone and find out something about me besides the words themselves. Place me in a context. Reduce me to a profile. Surpass me. Dismiss me. Anything to break the pressure of sustained attention.

I remember when I was recovering from drug addiction and a man I was trying to help — a refugee sleeping rough — knocked on my window while I was preparing to take drugs I shouldn’t have been taking. I shouted at him. Afterwards my sponsor said, ‘Aha — you see? He was interfering with your addiction.’ Exactly. The addict resents anything that interrupts the circuitry of compulsion. So I don’t expect gratitude for this argument. In recovery circles it used to be called tough love: confronting the addict with the reality of the addiction. The old language of addiction was self-will run riot. The addict becomes convinced that the substance enlarges volition when in reality it abolishes it. Do you honestly think that anything mediated continuously through a device held permanently in the hand — a device capable not merely of satisfying craving but of multiplying craving through omnipresence — can conduce to eudaimonia, to human flourishing?

Four and a half hours a day online for the average British adult. Out of roughly sixteen waking hours. If work itself is mediated through the same systems, many people now experience virtually no offline existence whatsoever. And I use the term virtually here in all its senses, reaching back to the original Latin sense of virtus, indicating potency or efficacy, then forward through the medieval schoolmen who hammered out the idea of the virtual to express something that is, to all intents and operational purposes, like the actual, but is not. Of course, this applies perfectly to the environments in which phone addicts and online addicts live — or at least think they live — since these environments operationally conform to what we might imagine satisfies the hierarchy of needs described by Maslow. We might think, so what if it’s all a little synthetic? After all, people survive on meal supplements.

Something I feel rather tenderly about myself, having undergone periods during cancer treatment where reality really did come in yoghurt pots. But then again, somebody being treated for cancer really shouldn’t live indefinitely on meals in yoghurt pots. Nor should human beings receive reality in easily digestible paste form. The taking of the virtual for the actual is understandable up to a point. Certain forms of transmission do indeed carry reality. But it’s notable how readily the web confuses people about the relationship between an image’s diegetic and mimetic components; indeed, between the apparent objectivity of technical reproduction and the stubborn subjectivity of the person who actually presses the button and takes the shot. For the schoolmen, virtuality suited their conceptual vocabulary because it indicated the potency of conceptual systems themselves.

The potency of the contemporary virtual is that it transmits feeling without lived justification. It is therefore an engine for resentment. It is also extraordinarily effective at optimisation — and by optimisation I mean forcing people to confuse the statistical mean, the average, those crowded into the bell jar, with humanity itself. But the particular case is always the exception that vitiates the law. And it is precisely as ethical beings that individuals encounter this exceptionality. Web-heads and phone addicts also confuse visibility with reality in every conceivable sense. They confuse attention with significance. We now live entirely inside an attention culture. I once knew somebody who knew the Queen fairly well.

Apparently before she became fully enclosed within her own serene constitutional unreality, she slept with piles of tabloids and society magazines beside her bed, marked with Post-it notes by attendants so she could leaf through and contemplate her own visibility. Of course, once she became Queen she also became constitutionally unreal in a rather interesting sense. So perhaps mediation is unavoidable among non-people anyway. Nonetheless, Andy Warhol may have promised fifteen minutes of fame, but trust me: no matter how many pile-ons or depilations you organise on X, twerks you jerk on TikTok, or even money shots you gag on on Only Fans, you are never going to be Queen. So, phone addict, don’t confuse connectivity with understanding. And don’t let virtuality persuade you that you are virtually comprehending things either. You are not. You are sitting in Plato’s cave while somebody walks across the mouth of it carrying a smartphone.

The sun rises behind them. What you see projected on the wall is not merely their shadow but the shadow of the phone itself — and you are condemned to stare at it all your life because you are shackled to a boulder shaped like a computer. A few years ago somebody told me that tens of millions of people globally were effectively living inside a single online space game — I think it was World of Warcraft. Large numbers played it continuously. The virtual had become the actual. But the extreme gamers are merely the crackheads of the digital world. Everybody else is puttering along like cigarette smokers in the 1970s, when everybody smoked and paedophiles were regarded as part of the social landscape rather than the focus of permanent national psychodrama. I grew up in the 1970s. Society was riddled with paedophiles: schools, churches, youth organisations, scout groups, sports clubs.

My late wife Deborah Orr used to describe being chased through woods in Motherwell by men locally known to prey on children: the ‘bad men’ were an established part of children’s lore––as were ‘flashers’ generally. Meanwhile the same woods contained drinking schools — groups of unemployed men gathering every morning to consume super-strength lager and Buckfast tonic wine. They do it to this day. They’re addicts too. Britain has always tolerated mass addiction provided it remains socially integrated enough not to interrupt commerce: in this case monkish commerce, since the booze is made by virtualising… monks. As you may have realised if you’ve got this far, I don’t think the government proposals go anywhere near far enough. In terms of our phone-addicted population, they scarcely even constitute harm minimisation. The problem is generational.

If older people have already surrendered their wisdom sufficiently to become addicts themselves, how can they possibly provide the discretion necessary for understanding, comprehension and judgment? How can they tell the young to put the bloody phone down when they themselves cannot stop touching the thing every few minutes? And like all long-term addicts, the old phone junkies lie about it––the ones who deceive themselves they have it under control, most of all. Trust me: I know. So watching parliamentarians attempting to prevent children becoming addicts while openly courting AI corporations to automate governance, education and communication produces something close to despair. We are looking down the barrel of a gun being assembled by an AI civilisation whose infrastructural investment is comparable to the first railway age, and most of the people discussing it don’t even know what gorilla glass is.

The truly frightening thing about AI is not that the machines may eventually write better than us. In many routine contexts they already can. The frightening thing is that human beings may cease to believe that the struggle to write — and therefore to think — belongs to them at all. I write long novels. I’m interested in holding your attention for hours. The smartphone economy is interested in holding it for seconds. You cannot persuade people to engage deeply with a medium whose very message is conceptual patience while simultaneously immersing them in a technological environment optimised for interruption, agitation and compulsive return. The poor conceptual thinking of the very people who should be engaged conceptually with the threat to conceptual thinking represented by artificial intelligence seem unable to get going on precisely this problem.

In the current issue of Prospect magazine the editor floats the idea of bans on social media for under-16s and restrictions on phone use in educational establishments, then wonders aloud whether the data support the efficacy of these interventions. On the addiction cases now being brought against social media companies on the grounds that their products engendered self-harm among younger users, he has comparatively little to say at all, beyond gently kicking the matter into the long grass — the long synthetic grass, perhaps even the long virtual grass. But these cases are all merely shadow-dances around the core of the problem. Like any addiction, phone addiction is sustained by an enormous economy. Like drugs, smartphones and their addicts depend on substances extracted from poorer societies under conditions of extreme exploitation, kleptocracy, militia violence and environmental devastation.

Most people in the West read for perhaps a minute a year, if that, about the grisly mess that is the Democratic Republic of Congo or the political catastrophes of Equatorial Africa generally, and even then they tend to dismiss these realities as background noise because they cannot be experienced as immediate disruptions to the smooth probabilistic functioning of daily life; i.e.: the getting, the using, and the getting of more… drugs. . If suffering cannot be rendered quantifiable, optimised, modelled or actuarially distributed, then the modern mentality increasingly struggles even to apprehend it. And it is precisely this mentality that militates against the use of AI systems in governance — not merely because probabilistic algorithms may reproduce racial profiling, deepen bias in welfare allocation, or automate older injustices under the guise of technical neutrality. No: the problem is deeper.

These systems are knocking at an open door. The societies deploying them already operate according to optimisation parameters. We have already trained ourselves to think this way. I am a number: and proud of it. My own cancer treatment is predicated in part on what the NHS calls quality-adjusted life years. The phrase means exactly what it says. My treatment is costed according to how many quality-adjusted years of existence the health service believes it can afford to purchase on my behalf. Vast quantities of data and algorithmic modelling are involved in these decisions, many of them probabilistic, behavioural and actuarial in character. The man-machine matrix, as I’ve called it for years now, did not suddenly arrive with AI. In essence it has existed since mass industrialisation and in certain respects far earlier.

Indeed, some theorists of early civilisation describe the Mesopotamian theocratic states as species-resettlement systems. The first domestication may well have been that of human beings themselves, who became almost instantly slaves, agricultural labourers and taxpayers. All of which is to say that we have been softening ourselves up for this for a very long time indeed — if softening up is even the correct phrase. Some people imagine they stand above all this from an Olympian height — a peak I couldn’t begin to scale nowadays, not after blood cancer and a substantial clot in my left leg — and assure us that humanity has always adapted to technological change and always will. Fair enough. But let’s be frank. Mass literacy in Britain dates only from around the First World War. Before that enormous numbers of people could neither read nor write. Were they therefore worse off in every conceivable sense? Perhaps not.

But it does rather mock the ideal of democratic society understood in the republican sense: governance rooted in public deliberation concerning the res publica: the things held in common. Because if everybody is staring at a phone instead of looking one another in the face, and if increasingly the very language through which public discourse occurs is generated, mediated, summarised, optimised and perhaps eventually replaced by machine systems, then what exactly remains of deliberation at all? You’ve only got one life. You’re not a gorilla. So why spend it endlessly caressing gorilla glass while staring at your own ape features reflected back at you: there’s only so many times you can ejaculate hatred, righteousness, and desire––and then you die.

item.content:encoded:
I recently appeared on Gyles Brandreth’s podcast Rosebud. The name itself says almost everything about the condition of contemporary culture, although perhaps not in the way intended. After all, Rosebud in Citizen Kane is not a beautiful memory at all, nor some lost Arcadia of innocence, but a fetish object: the transitional object that Charles Foster Kane — Hearst refracted through Welles — never psychologically surpassed. It signifies precisely his inability to love, his inability to form reciprocal human attachments, his reduction of the world to acquisition, spectacle and possession. Yet Brandreth’s podcast, amiable and intelligent as it is, uses the title in the now standard cultural sense: the invitation to look backwards through rose-tinted spectacles, to narrativise one’s own life sentimentally and consolingly.

During the interview I largely declined this invitation, although Gyles himself was an excellent interlocutor and extracted a good deal from me. It was also, I strongly suspect, through Gyles — exemplary president of the Oscar Wilde Society and a genuine believer in Wilde — that Thomas Hodgkinson approached me for a quotation for his forthcoming book on Wilde and prison. This is not a criticism of Brandreth. Indeed, during the podcast it was he himself who reminded me that the boys at the Swallow Street brothel Wilde frequented were underage. There is no attempt on his part to brush difficult realities beneath the carpet. Nor do I doubt Hodgkinson’s seriousness in relative terms. The problem lies elsewhere. The problem is that literary culture no longer exists in anything like the form required to sustain serious literary criticism, or even sustained literary encounter.

We continue to use the phrase ‘British literary culture survives,’ but in truth it doesn’t survive; rather, fragments of its prestige survive. Its signs survive. Its mannerisms survive. Its credentialing survives. Its festivals, societies, podcasts, review pages and heritage industries survive. But deep literacy itself — literacy as prolonged submission to difficult style and difficult consciousness — is in precipitous collapse. Under such conditions, secondary cultural production ceases to be auxiliary to primary creation and instead begins feeding parasitically upon its remnants. Hence the peculiar position in which I now find myself: recruited to garnish books because my name still carries the residual aura of literary seriousness in a culture increasingly incapable of metabolising serious literature. I have become a skeuomorph.

In design terms, a skeuomorph is the ornamental survival of an obsolete function: fake stitching moulded into plastic, woodgrain printed on software interfaces, the clicking sound of a digital camera mimicking the shutter of an analogue one. Likewise “Will Self” now operates culturally as a prestige residue, a texture of seriousness grafted onto projects whose underlying cultural substrate can no longer independently generate it. This is not simply narcissistic resentment. Or not only that. It is structural. Hodgkinson, like many perfectly intelligent men operating within the secondary order of culture, needs authoritative statements because he is not himself fundamentally a literary critic in the deep sense. He therefore collages. The collage becomes the semblance of profound literary engagement.

One assembles quotations, references, atmospherics, prison archives, inherited reputations, fragments of authority––in the process vivifying a network of appreciation. The resulting object can be highly competent. It can even be readable and informed. But it increasingly resembles the AI-generated simulacra now flooding the informational ecosystem: superficially cultured––and therefore more readable than, say Salome or Ravenna for that matter––detached from prolonged acts of cognition. The literary-cultural middle order — reviewers, podcasters, festival moderators, introducers, minor biographers, curators of literary memory — are recycling prestige rather than generating form. And Wilde, of course, is infinitely recyclable. This fits in with a tendency in British publishing I’ve analysed in a previous SITREP: monetise the backlist and heritage writers out of copyright, don’t spend money on the living.

The most glaring example of the blindness of contemporary publishing was how few people from the industry itself bothered to appear before the parliamentary hearings concerning the use by technology companies of writers’ work to train large language models. One name repeatedly surfaced as having actually turned up: Liz Calder. This is to her credit. Calder belongs to an older publishing culture in which editors still possessed enough authority, intelligence and literary self-confidence to speak publicly about literature as something more than intellectual property inventory. She was also my own publisher at Bloomsbury. When I sent her Cock — my novel about a woman who grows a penis and rapes her husband — she telephoned me laughing so hard over the manuscript that colleagues in the office reportedly asked what on earth was wrong with her. I sometimes wonder whether she would laugh in quite the same way now.

Not because the book has changed, but because the ecology around literature has changed almost beyond recognition. Calder herself is in some ways a cautionary figure. Alongside Nigel Newton and David Reynolds she helped found Bloomsbury, only to watch it become, under the huge weight of Harry Potter, something structurally closer to a gigantic logistics apparatus orbiting a recurring global content-event than a traditional literary publishing house. The revenues were immense, of course, but the logic of scale transformed the company. Bloomsbury expanded aggressively into academic and reference publishing just as the web, search engines, generative text and AI were beginning to annihilate precisely those informational forms. Dictionaries, directories, reference works: all increasingly metabolised into the distributed textual soup of the network.

However, Calder did accept appointment as a Commander of the British Empire, which suggests that at some level she shares the prevailing groupthink of British publishing culture: namely, that it has done a reasonably good job over the past half century and deserves ceremonial recognition from the state. I’m not inclined to agree. When close to half the population no longer reads books at all, and a significant proportion of the remainder merely listens distractedly to one or two audiobooks a year — retaining perhaps a quarter of their actual content — it strikes me that almost anybody in British literary life who accepted honours from the Crown over the past thirty years should now consider returning them to Buck House forthwith and with the appropriate unbowing and unscraping: because on their watch cultural stewardship has manifestly failed. Commandeer?

Don’t make me… vomit with sickness and the sea of secondrateness we’re all being submerged in. This is why I continue to wonder whether anyone in the publishing industry today fully grasps quite how parlous the condition of literature really is now, or whether even the more intelligent figures within it remain trapped within an institutional atmosphere of managed decline, nostalgia and reputational self-congratulation: bang a gong! Get it on! Bang a gong! This gong-beat was sounding beneath the email I wrote Hodgkinson. What I recognised in Wilde as a child had nothing whatever to do with modern identity politics or human-rights discourse. I encountered Wilde first through the comedies because I was twelve years old and The Ballad of Reading Gaol is, frankly, rather boring to a precocious twelve-year-old future satirist. What struck me instead about Oscar was energy, aggression, wit, performance, theatricality, social combat.

I instinctively understood Wilde as someone who had fused libido with vocation. His erotic drives, his satirical intelligence, his theatricality and his artistic will formed a single apparatus. This is why his satire cuts so deeply beneath Victorian manners. Sitting in those drawing rooms exchanging epigrams with Lady Bracknell is a man conducting illegal sexual relationships with young men, many of them effectively boys, many of them prostitutes. He knows perfectly well that many others within that social world are similarly compromised. But unlike them he cannot disentangle desire from performance. He aestheticises his appetites absolutely. He was indeed looking up at the stars, there’s no doubt about that––but he was also indubitably in the gutter. Wilde’s celebrated bon mot insists that some of those who are in the gutter are nonetheless looking up at the stars.

Yet perhaps the formula ought properly to be reversed: some of us who are looking at the stars are in the gutter. That is the more salient fact about Wilde himself. The truth is almost grotesquely encapsulated by Maggie Hambling’s sculpture of him, which sits — rightly, some might argue — in a narrow alleyway behind St Martin-in-the-Fields, a hop, skip and K-hole away from Heaven. The sculpture is itself a disgusting object, and rendered more disgusting still by the periodic appearance nearby of one of those temporary mobile pissoirs erected in the West End during public festivities to absorb the overflow of male bladders. Hambling’s Wilde resembles less a wit emerging into immortality than a kind of Medusa-like head rising from another coffin or sarcophagus: a dull pewter-coloured lid, half gutter and half tomb.

One senses in it not transcendence but aesthetic decomposition — Wilde reduced at last to a face peering upward from the drainage system of his own legend. This is where Joyce’s famous judgement becomes so illuminating: ‘Wilde lacked the courage of his own perversions.’ Joyce wwas far too comfortable with his own homosexuality to’ve meant Wilde lacked the courage to have sex with men. Plenty of gay men in late Victorian England exercised discretion perfectly successfully: and had lots of sex.––I Think in this connection of an anecdote related to me by the biographer of H. H. Munro—Saki—concerning that great satirist of the late Victorian and Edwardian eras. During the course of his researches, the biographer visited two elderly ladies in Belfast, distant relatives of Munro, who produced from their attic a tin trunk that had apparently sat there since Christ stopped at Eboli in search of a rent boy.

Inside, the biographer discovered copious private daybooks of the sort Edwardian gentlemen habitually kept, except that Munro had filled his with detailed records of the young men with whom he had conducted sexual relations, including — with a taxonomist’s precision entirely worthy of the period — their vital statistics and the dimensions of their genitalia. Richard Ellmann records that on the night of Wilde’s conviction hundreds of unmarried men quietly departed for the Continent. The Cleveland Street scandal had already demonstrated that aristocrats, officers and political elites understood perfectly well how to preserve silence around such matters. Even the future Edward VII’s own circle was touched by these scandals. The issue was not homosexuality itself. The issue was Wilde’s arrogance, his insistence on public theatricalisation.

When Queensberry leaves the card accusing him of being a “posing somdomite,” Wilde becomes amused by the spelling mistake and sues for libel. This is not political martyrdom in the modern sense. It is narcissistic grandiosity fused to aesthetic self-dramatisation. Wilde cannot resist making his own libido part of the spectacle. This does not make Victorian criminalisation morally defensible. Of course not. Consenting homosexual relations should never have been criminalised. But historical understanding requires precision. Wilde’s tragedy was not reducible to “society persecuted a gay man.” Wilde’s tragedy was that his erotic imagination transformed people into aesthetic objects while simultaneously requiring public recognition for the aesthetic system itself. This is why Bosie remains central even after catastrophe. Wilde diagnoses Bosie repeatedly as vain, sociopathic, parasitic and destructive. Yet he cannot detach himself.

His libido and creative effort remain fused even in extremis. The Ballad of Reading Gaol therefore becomes fascinating precisely because it fails to transcend Wilde’s own erotic-aesthetic pathology. “For each man kills the thing he loves” is not merely a universal moral statement; it is a confession of the sadistic structure lurking within objectifying desire itself. The executed trooper Charles Thomas Wooldridge––who ispired the line quite as much as Bosie–– murdered his wife because he had thingified her. Sartre would understand this instantly.: for in his formulation, the sadist is not devoid of feeling; rather, sadism emerges from thwarted reciprocity, from the impossibility of achieving commensurability with the beloved object.

Perversion marks the waystations of failed love because the lover cannot tolerate the independent subjectivity of the beloved: hence Ebola… the rent boy, and no canonisation, only the treadmill and oakum-picking. The point is murder becomes the ultimate assertion of possession––and the extension of Wilde’s unspeakable love by other means. Moral justification makes no difference: Winnie Verloc murders her husband at around the same time as Wooldridge kills his wife, but Conrad’s account of her mental state in The Secret Agent, makes it clear she obeys the same savage logic. Wilde, in his own manner, understood this structure intuitively while remaining trapped within it psychologically. His worship of beauty was never a Platonic ascent toward the true and the beautiful. It was compulsive aestheticisation inseparable from domination, narcissism and erotic fixation.

And yet modern Wilde industries require precisely the opposite interpretation. Contemporary culture endlessly recycles Wilde as martyr, queer icon, aesthete, victim, humanitarian precursor, liberal saint. One visits Père Lachaise and discovers lipstick kisses smooshed across Jacob Epstein’s magnificent winged tomb, while tourists murmur reverently about ‘the idea of Wilde’ before strolling on, presumably to admire the tomb––and the ‘idea’––of Pierre Bourdieu; after all, he knew a lot about cultural capital. Years ago I encountered a large Scotswoman dressed in black Lycra, stinking powerfully of patchouli, and kissing naughty Oscar’s tomb ecstatically. When I asked which of Wilde’s works she most admired she told me she hadn’t read any, but she loved… ‘the idea of him.’ Exactly so. The idea––which in turn becomes a secular ‘icon’, to be stared at through that modern hagioscope: the phone. Not the work.

Not the dangerous fusion of appetite, narcissism, satire and aesthetic violence. Merely the recyclable image. The irony deepens further because the tomb itself resembles a prison more than any neighbouring sepulchre in Père Lachaise: it’s sphinx-like form is no riddle, for this a sarcophagus masquerading as liberation. Epstein, its sculptor, shares his surname with another Epstein whose crimes represent not perversion gone catastrophically wrong but straightforward psychopathy. The coincidence is grotesque enough to feel Wildean in itself. Yet we continue gilding the lily. We continue refusing interrogation because interrogation threatens the utility of Wilde as an endlessly deployable prestige object within contemporary human-rights discourse. I resent this not because I reject Wilde but because I am, in many respects, genuinely Wildean.

I have written comparatively little for stage or screen, but my satirical oeuvre vastly exceeds Wilde’s in scale. Like Wilde, I fused performance with writing from the beginning. Like Wilde, I understood literature theatrically and socially. And like Wilde, I am no respecter of persons: afflicting the comfortable is my business, and a reliable way of doing that is telling them the truth. But I possess no institutional status independent of the work itself by choice. I refused the Royal Society of Literature fellowship twice because the moment artists derive legitimacy primarily from institutions, corporations or political formations, the work itself becomes subordinate to status management. Artists consequently remain vulnerable to contradiction, ridicule and social demotion. Fine: we should––unacknowledged legislators, duh!

That is healthy, because satire thrives under those conditions: but what the collagist doing the book on Wilde in prison must understand is the responsibility entailed in constructing crafting projects using living artists; because once literary culture loses its own generative depth, the collage begins replacing genuine encounter with art altogether, and substitutes a smoosh––or a swoosh. And this, finally, is my objection. Better to tear the petals from Wilde’s green lily than continue wearing it sentimentally in one’s buttonhole. Better to confront what the flower actually was — narcissistic, brilliant, exploitative, theatrical, destructive, erotically compulsive, artistically incandescent — than endlessly recycle the exhausted image for the purposes of heritage culture.

Otherwise Wilde becomes precisely what contemporary culture desires most: a dead Oscar, so ceaselessly gilded that in the end, despite the best intentions, he resembles…a rosebud. And this is also perhaps what contemporary culture wants, for me. I’ve nearly died a couple of times over the past two years, when I talk to other senior writers about the parlous condition in literature, they seem unable to respond to the problem at a conceptual level. One very famous, very literary novelist I wrote to recently on this matter, responded, as so many do, with the fatuous observation that the novel would ‘last forever’.

The only possible answer to this is ‘which one?’ ‘Pot of Gold?’, ‘Prisoner of Azerbaijan?’ But he also said something else significant, which was that in the 1990s he’d been introduced to ‘a young black woman’ who’d been given a six figure advance for a novel and ‘we never heard anything more about her.’ I expect he thought he was commenting on the profligacy of publishers during that period. Who were indeed handing out substantial advances to literary novelists. He and I included however, but that’s not what he said. I have repeated what he said verbatim and what he said was contemptible: that someone of this stature should stoop to use blackness as a metaphysical shorthand for barbarism is frankly repulsive. The barbarism he alludes to has been created for the most part by white people and their technology: it’s this that’s destroying literature.

But ten he wouldn’t want to harsh these guys’ high–– he’s received somewhere in the region of a quarter of a million in literary prize money, and the largest identifiable portions of that money derive from state/civic institutions and finance-linked capital. Pets win prizes––not gay ex-convicts.

item.content:encoded:
Yesterday was the 118th birthday of Ian Fleming, creator of James Bond, perhaps the most famous personification of the skeuomorph in British entertainment history. Regular readers of SITREP will know what a skeuomorph is: a formerly utilitarian element repurposed into a purely decorative or symbolic one. James Bond is Britain’s most famous chocolate soldier. (The term with which the British military refer to nancy-elsies who care more about shined leather than rough stuff.) His creator had a brief career in British naval intelligence during the Second World War, and it was there that Fleming gathered much of the factual tradecraft, conspiratorial atmosphere and bureaucratic mythology that he later transformed into utter fantasy. What a pity that Fleming lacked the literary and ethical sensibility of another British intelligence officer of the same war: Norman Lewis.

Lewis wrote inimitable works, beginning with Naples ’44, which remains one of the finest books ever written about war and occupation because Lewis possessed something Fleming did not: an ethnographic eye: a grasp on the particularities of cultures that he then used to chronicle social disintegration under the pressure of modernity: fishing villages on the Costa Brava engulfed by tourism; southern Italy consumed by criminality and development; traditional societies dissolved by the metabolic force of global capital. Lewis eventually transformed his wartime experience into something ethically serious through his involvement with Survival International, devoted to preserving indigenous peoples and traditional societies threatened by modernity’s expansionary violence. If you like, Lewis represents the anti-skeuomorphic tendency in British life.

He understood — perhaps because he watched the Middlesex town of Enfield disappear beneath the spreading isotropy of suburban London — that Britain possessed an unusually slow and resilient digestive system. History takes a very long time to be consumed in Britain. That is why British society so often appears strangely heavy and indigestible. Looking at British culture is rather like examining the pellet of a game bird: fragments of the creatures and herbage on which it fed remain recognisable within the compacted mass. Lewis recoiled from this cultural coprophilia. Like many sensitive Englishmen, he effectively emigrated spiritually before exiting right, at speed.

He became a stranger to his own strange land––Fleming did the opposite: he doubled down on Englishness by living not in England but in one of its former colonial possessions, Jamaica, where he could continue to perform the role of colonial overseer long after empire itself had collapsed. Bond reflects the new postwar reality only partially. Yes, there is Felix Leiter, the CIA counterpart who signals the transfer of global power from Britain to the United States. But Bond’s world still assumes that Britain remains a decisive imperial actor. The ‘double-O’ designation itself is the key skeuomorphic flourish: the brassy knocker on the oak-effect door of a suburban semi. Bond is supposedly the seventh SIS officer licensed to kill on behalf of the Crown. This fantasy of residual sovereign violence is exactly what makes the character so psychologically potent for British audiences: Bond transforms national decline into style.

He possesses all the attributes of a class whose cultural mannerism outlived its material power––which is why it can still perform mesmerism on the masses: the Chelsea mews; the Bentley; the Morland cigarettes with Balkan and Turkish tobacco; the chamois leather shoulder holster; the non-standard Walther PPK; the Savile Row tailoring; the clubman’s fastidiousness. Britain becomes not a civilisation but a brand identity. And yet Bond himself is also morally repellent. To understand Fleming’s real imagination you must read novels such as The Spy Who Loved Me rather than watch the films. What appears on screen as raffish masculinity often reveals itself on the page as predation: misogyny, sadism, domination, and a delight in power asymmetry between older men and vulnerable women. Fleming both worshipped and destroyed the world he mythologised, but then sado-masochists always kill the thing they love.

In the end Bond became merely an empty shell waiting to be inhabited by actors increasingly detached from the original imperial fantasy: Sean Connery, a former milkman from Edinburgh; Daniel Craig, who attempted to turn Bond into a traumatised modern antihero (the actor made his name playing such tortured, sensitive types) before returning, inevitably, to state-sanctioned torture of sensitive types while wearing Kilgore tailoring. That, in miniature, is contemporary Britain itself. Perhaps the greatest absurdity of the Bond mythology is the fantasy that British intelligence services are especially competent at espionage. If diplomacy is war pursued by other means, then espionage is merely covert diplomacy. Britain has not fought an independent major war successfully for generations. Indeed, the actual history of the British intelligence services is one long chronicle of leaks, traitors, whistleblowers and institutional embarrassment.

The reason the public knows so much about MI5 and MI6 is precisely because serving officers have betrayed it, while former ones have spent decades writing memoirs, leaking stories, briefing journalists and denouncing one another. When I interviewed former SIS personnel while researching novels such as Phone and Shark, what struck me most was not glamour but colourlessness. These were not Bond Street bling adventurers but bureaucratic specialists. Intelligent? Not notably. Managerial? They seemed to have SASCO year planners stuck up their arses. But overwhelmingly dull: I began to think their contacts and suspects would only open up to them for fear of dying of boredom––a suspicion confirmed by the ‘intelligence’ that a TGI Friday piss-up in the grisly atrium of the Aztec Camera that’s their HQ is mandatory for all, so they can get mashed en masse, and leak all those secrets only––to one another.

As for making love to me, I wouldn’t have thought they did it better… than any other pissed-up office worker. While when it comes to the application of lethal force, you’d be better off asking the postcode warriors on my ‘hood––who know where to get a leng, and how to use it. The armed personnel associated with SIS operations are in reality drawn from units such as the Special Air Service or the Special Boat Service. Bond himself is effectively a fantasy composite assembled from fragments of military masculinity, imperial nostalgia and consumer branding. Meanwhile the actual battlespace has changed entirely. Britain today could not sustain major military operations independently without overwhelming American logistical support. Senior British officers themselves quietly describe the armed forces as auxiliary formations integrated into the American military machine. Even in that role they were defeated.

The last British military deployments of any consequence were to Afghanistan and Iraq. In Afghanistan a 14 year deployment left the country back in the hands of the forces that were meant to have been expelled. In Iraq? Well, they make a desert where there was already a desert and they call it peace for a few years, and then it drifts back into endless war. There can have been few less martial sights than the withdrawal of British forces from Basra in 2007. At least the British Army likes to style it as a withdrawal––what most impartial witnesses would term it, is a defeat. Perhaps this is why the Ministry of Defence has been quite so vicious in its pursuit of the solicitors who made bogus accusations of war crimes against serving British soldiers who were deployed in Iraq.

(This was a disastrous adventure, strenuously objected to by the majority of Britons which renders ‘served’ otiose.) SITREP, as you probably realise, believes in the cock up, not the conspiracy theory of history. The problem with the modern world is that the conspirators are doing their bad shit on the web and in broad daylight, but one thing the British would like to sweep under the carpet is that when it comes to combatting them, James Bond has broken his bond––if by that bond, is meant that the British armed forces, of any kind are instilled with a patriotism that entails having the best interests of the country at heart. British army officers I interviewed told me they’d agitated the desk-wallahs to be deployed, even though they knew their regiments weren’t battle-ready or capable.

Others admitted that intelligence had been woeful––and while army intelligence interpreters may not have tortured detainees, they were so culturally illiterate they got nothing out of them. One weary old terp’ who’d been pulled out of retirement, given a short course in Arabic, and unleashed on these latterday Mahdists, told me that after one particularly long and gruelling session, the detainee looked wearily at him and said (and this the terp’ did understand): ‘You British are so stupid––you ask us all these questions, but you never ask the most important one, the one you should ask first, the only one that matters: who’s your sheik?’ If you want a good account of the cock up, read Rory Stewart’s book about his delightful time playing the Grand Poo-Ba in another country’s shit.

In fact––with the possible exception of the intervention in the Sierra Leone conflict––recent British history has been typified by bragadachio rather than Bond on the part of HMG, IMOH––OMG! SMERSH! And so Bond survives not as reality but as skeuomorph: the decorative remnant of a vanished imperial function. The fantasy persists while the actual conditions that produced it have disappeared: it used to be said that ‘we’ risked ‘fighting the next war with the tactics of the last’, but with James Bond worship still rife (I can imagine people queuing to see the latest in the cold light of a nuclear winter), Britain is in danger of not fighting the next war at all. Meanwhile the Russian hackers keep tapping at their keyboards, while the American and Israelis fire salvo after salvo of missiles, and the IRG and the Ukrainians watch drone tv. Still, there was another Ian Fleming too: lighter, odder, more imaginative.

And forget all about redeeming Ian after his phlegming with Chitty-Chitty-Bang-Bang. Sign the cheque and leave the bang-bangs at home––James Bond is at the tanning salon. Take your cue instead from Norman Lewis, who in the opening pages of his chef d’oeuvre, reminds us of perhaps the greatest oxymoron there is: military intelligence.
