item.content:encoded:
One of the assumptions about the war currently being waged by Ukraine in its eastern provinces of Donetsk and Luhansk is that while deaths and destruction are now increasingly effected by drones, their operators somehow no longer partake in the traditional psychology of young men charged with killing others in the name of an abstraction — which is what Ukrainian independence was always going to become in a terminally fissiparous world. I recently read a long and very informative article by a French journalist in Le Monde, later syndicated by Prospect magazine, that gave a compelling picture of what Ukraine’s drone war is actually like. Young men, for the most part, crouched in bunkers before screens, wrapped in protective gear, effectively playing computer games. Except that unlike the games my own computer-addicted son once played, in this case the Nazi zombies are real, while the first-person shooters were very recently just that.

There are perhaps as many as fifty million people worldwide who did little outside working hours except play World of Warcraft: their principal craft consisting in waging a war with employers, relatives, and reality itself so they might return to Azeroth as quickly as possible. As for several million others, they scarcely exist outside the game world at all except to perform the basic necessities of life. Which means that long before the current conflicts in Donetsk and Luhansk, there already existed a vast population voluntarily inhabiting conditions remarkably similar to those now endured by drone operators. I suspect both gamers and operators both love killing Nazi zombies.

Much has been made––and rightly so––of the manner in which the battlespace in eastern Ukraine has now been comprehensively gridded, so that square-by-square drone operators can eliminate ‘targets’—a useful euphemism for living, breathing, sensing, morally capable human beings—according to quotas. Given that the overwhelming majority of those being killed are themselves young conscripts, often ethnically and culturally adjacent to those killing them, commentators have searched for new language adequate to this condition. It is not genocide in the classical sense, but something colder and more procedural: dronocide. The target is no longer merely dehumanized: it is factored into data alone. In a word: processed. Some years ago I was invited by the executor of T.S. Eliot’s estate to introduce the annual Eliot lecturer in Dublin. The fee was generous and the lecturer himself intriguing: Steven Pinker.

His book The Better Angels of Our Nature had recently appeared, and during the lecture Pinker bounded about the stage displaying graphs purporting to demonstrate that everything in this, the best of all possible worlds, was steadily improving, above all in the sense that the world was becoming less violent. I was not especially minded to dispute his statistics, but rather question his sanity. Because regardless of whether fewer people were technically dying in wars at that moment, the world was already saturated with young men killing on an industrial scale, albeit only Nazi zombies. But that was precisely the problem. My fourteen-year-old son, addicted to Call of Duty, is now thirty. Fortunately, he will probably get to a lucky number, and escape conscription.

Yet knowing his game scores, and the enormous number of views accumulated by videos of his competitive gaming, I have little doubt that he would have made an extraordinarily efficient killer. We are indebted to Nicholas Carr for two important books: The Shallows that did an excellent job of warning people about the precipitate downside of bi-directional digital media’s rise to supremacy; and The Glass Cage, which was similarly percipient when it comes to the internet of things and automation. In the latter he describes virtualization has become the vector for what we might term the gamification of everyday life. However, the notion that somebody can press a button in one part of the world and kill somebody elsewhere is by no means new: the fantasy of instantaneous remote destruction entered the collective imaginarium with the V-2 rocket attacks on London during the closing stages of the Second World War.

It was these raids, together with another technological innovation—the Sperry ball turret—that activated the imagination of Thomas Pynchon in Gravity's Rainbow. The novel features an American lieutenant wandering through wartime London, whose imagination is, um, activated by the arrival of incoming V-2 rockets, in the form of involuntary tumescence. This is, after Mary Shelley’s Frankenstein, one of literature’s earliest intuitions of the emergent cyborg. The Sperry ball turret itself was another proto-cyborg assemblage: inner and outer shells mounted gyroscopically, responding to primitive targeting systems while the human operator swivelled helplessly through the sky inside a bomber, machine and flesh fused into a single weapons platform.

Randall Jarrell captured the horror of this man/machine matrix perfectly in The Death of the Ball Turret Gunner, which concludes: ‘When I died they washed me out of the turret with a hose.’ It is difficult to imagine a more concise anticipation of the future relationship between wetware and hardware: first the human is coddled within the machine, then finally scrubbed from it. During the Cold War the assemblage of intercontinental ballistic missiles and the DEW early-warning system intended to shield North America from thermonuclear annihilation represented another stage in this same fusion between human beings and machine systems.

But now, with this latest war—the war that never ends, whose fronts currently extend through South Kordofan, Darfur, the eastern Congo, Donetsk, Luhansk, Gaza, South Lebanon, the Strait of Hormuz, and half a dozen other killing fields—the drone, once the plaything of children, has at last come fully of age and become once again the plaything of children. My youngest’s girlfriend was a champion drone operator when she was young––but then that was also when she was a boy. She told me the the sense she had when flying even a tiny four rotor drone around the cramped flat she shared with her extensive immigrant family, was extraordinary; that it was as if she was the drone, while the feeling of power and control was phenomenal. Why wouldn’t it be? This, after all, is every child’s fantasy: to be able to fly around the place dealing out arbitrary punishment.

That’s why we all used to awake from troubled sleep to realise that during the night we had turned into sublunary things. I must’ve watched my fourteen-year-old kill tens of thousands of Nazi zombies, but there were always more: I would observe his REMs: flicking between the heads-up display and those spectral figures leaping through the ruins of this or that imaginary city. No matter how many he killed, they sprang back to life as if sown dragon’s teeth. Many people at the time, myself included, hoped that this obsession with killing things through computer games might somehow ‘harmlessly’ channel the aggression of young men. It was a ridiculous notion, of course. Masculinity, like femininity, is largely performative. As Simone de Beauvoir observed, one is not born but becomes. All those young men killing Nazi zombies were performing being soldiers.

Well, now it appears as if the curtain, having first twitched aside, may slowly and inexorably rise higher in the years to come. These bashful bedroom warriors, these hikikomori of a new H-bomber, who have been waiting for so very long to do their bit, rather than eat another Welsh rare one, may creep from their fetid, cheesy rooms and resume what young men have always done in large numbers: kill one another. Except that this is not entirely true either. During the Second World War American military psychiatrists sent to Normandy shortly after D-Day, encountered thousands of young men suffering from what was then termed battle fatigue. These were boys from Poughkeepsie or the Okefenokee Swamp suddenly confronted by Wehrmacht veterans who had been fighting continuously for six years. Many collapsed psychologically within days. Later studies suggested that only a minority of infantrymen consistently fired directly at the enemy.

Human beings, it turns out, are not naturally efficient killers. Nor is this surprising. Anybody who has fired a .303 rifle or a .44 handgun knows what bullets do. Even if they have never seen ballistic trauma inflicted upon a human body, they have seen what rounds do to timber, brick, stone, or flesh. Violence possesses weight, recoil, consequence. A rifle kicks. A body bleeds. Retreating from Moscow with your toes dropping from frostbite is not the same thing as toggling a pair of plastic levers on a games controller. But what of the young man whose entire experience of killing consists of clicking buttons and manipulating avatars? Carr’s The Glass Cage gives a disturbing account of a future in which the causal connection between humans and the world is increasingly obscured by automation.

Airline pilots cocooned within digital systems lose the bodily sensation of flight itself––some aviation disasters may even stem from this loss of tactile intimacy with the machine. I once flew in the cockpit of an old DC-10 the last aircraft and commercial service to have mechanical servo mechanisms and the pilot let me take the plane’s handbrake off, it was quite difficult. Now, the operator no longer feels the aircraft moving through the air; he merely supervises interfaces. To read the Le Monde report on the drone war in Donetsk and Luhansk is to encounter precisely this condition militarised. Drone commanders speak as calmly of quotas as sales managers: first there are prospects––then you convert them using the coldest calls of all. The business of killing has become exactly that: a business.

Which means, in turn, that Ukraine is currently the world leader in dromodronology and, ipso facto, although there are Nazi zombies on both sides, killing more of the Russians’ ones. Why? Because the young men conducting these operations are extraordinarily good at them. Volodymyr Zelensky, the former comedian turned wartime president, has effectively mobilised an entire generation of former gamers. Operation Dynamo called upon South Coast yachtsmen to rescue the British Expeditionary Force from Dunkirk––Ukraine has called upon adolescents raised inside first-person shooters: the model-yacht enthusiasts de nos jours. That is why they are so adept at target acquisition, navigation, tracking, and destruction: they already possess the reflexes, having spent twenty years training inside virtual killing fields.

Like my son fifteen years ago, their barely-moving bodies, thumbs twitching as if those of spasming corpses, can be seen staring into heads-up displays. Meanwhile their spirits hover above soon-to-be-destroyed individuals and objects at immense remove: here, they maintain quotas. Reading the Le Monde piece I sensed the unmistakably clammy and sebaceous atmosphere of bureaucratic extermination––of killing transformed into throughput. And carried out by trahison des clercs. One thinks not merely of mechanised slaughter in the twentieth century, but of the First World War’s assembly line of death stretching across Flanders. The killing zone of Babi Yar, where tens of thousands of Kyiv’s Jews were murdered over two days, was physically tiny compared with the planetary battlespace now opened by drones, satellites, fibre optics, and gaming interfaces. Yet dromodronology shrinks the globe to the dimensions of a compulsive gamer’s bedroom.

We comfort ourselves with the illusion that the world has become a more welcoming and apprehensible place because we can open laptops and glide virtually over the Taklamakan Desert or the Weddell Sea. In reality what has shrunk is not geography but ethical distance. What is occurring now is quite simply the gamification of war. I first noticed it during the invasion of Iraq. BBC television footage showed troops sprawled in the backs of Hercules transport aircraft on their way to combat. In earlier wars they might have smoked cigarettes or played cards, but these happy squaddies were playing war games on laptops while travelling towards actual war. That was just before the inception of bidirectional digital media––since then nearly a quarter of a century has elapsed for them, their younger brothers, and now perhaps even their children, to prepare cognitively for remote violence.

Millions upon millions of young men throughout the world have spent decades digging virtual trenches for themselves. They progressed from Snake to Space Invaders, from Mortal Kombat to Call of Duty, rehearsing warfare as entertainment while waiting unknowingly for warfare itself to absorb the grammar of entertainment. These adipose and pimpled warriors, lit by the pale blue glow of their screens, may prove every bit as efficient at dispatching their fellow human beings as their forefathers who once marched into the Somme or Stalingrad. The difference is that the modern war machine no longer needs to brutalise civilians into soldiers––it merely recruits from populations already zombified by interfaces, abstractions, reward loops, and simulated death. All of which means the drone operator does not necessarily experience himself as killing in the old sense. He experiences himself as succeeding.

And that may be the most terrifying development of all––until that is, we’re all compelled to keep the three-minute silence, and the sombre face during that most important ceremony of national coming together, namely: laying the wreath at the tomb of the Unknown Gamer. (Or should it be Nazi Zombie?)

item.title: USA: Bill Gate's Mannequin wasn't on the Epstein List
item.dc:creator: Will Self
item.description: The Wall Street Journal piece on Bill Gates and Epstein looks, at first glance, like another plutocrat-reputation story: sex, secrecy, staff-managed image, foundation panic, congressional questioning, the usual midden of sullied private conduct and wipe-clean public contrition. item.content:encoded:
The Wall Street Journal piece on Bill Gates and Epstein looks, at first glance, like another plutocrat-reputation story: sex, secrecy, staff-managed image, foundation panic, congressional questioning, the usual midden of sullied private conduct and wipe-clean public contrition. But the real subject is larger, stranger, and frankly, murkier. The article is not principally about Epstein, nor even about Gates’s affairs: it’s about what we might call ‘the moral operating system of American hypercapitalism’—and the point at which its own agents can no longer believe WYSIWYG. The most revealing detail is not the Epstein connection but the mannequin utilised by the Midas of Chips. Gates’s staff, we are told, keep a custom-size mannequin to test his clothes: crew and V-neck sweaters in neutral tones, soft shirts for soft emollient skin, and carefully managed, carbon-framed glasses (implying that what he sees he gets in a numinous way).

Overall, the aim (which is, of course, his own) was to depict him as ‘calm and approachable, like Mister Rogers.’ The reference being to the persona of a responsible neighbourhood elder: who, gulp, keeps a benignant eye on the kids, not eye-detection surveillance software aimed at its employees. In Gates’s image-making resides the real iconostasis of late pseudo-philanthropic capitalism: the monopolist, who definitionally made money by excluding the intentionality (and hence the moral being) of others, must become the nice old guy next door. The anti-trust defendant must be reborn as the global health benefactor––and the man who won the software wars, must reappear not remotely disheveled, rather: in the soft-knit glow of measurable and quantifiable compassion. This is why the sex scandal can be embiggered far more than Gates or any one of his corporate organs.

A powerful man using that asymetry, in part, to conduct affairs with women in or near his professional orbit is not unusual. A billionaire moving through zones of sexual and social impunity is, franchement, passé; nor is it proved, on the facts available, that Epstein was Gates’s procurer. That remains guilt by association, or, at most, a plausible suspicion generated by the murk of Epstein’s network. (And ‘network’ is the operative word here: the networks facilitated by bi-directional media naturally foment conspiracist feverishness, as the medium operates on the human individual to privilege associative meanings over conceptual reasoning.) The more defensible charge is simpler: Gates behaved like a powerful man who gets what he wants, then panicked because his entire late-life identity depended on being seen as giving what he wants away. The key here is that Gates is not merely fabulously and unimaginably rich.

(It’s worth considering again how anyone with tastes that mundane could possibly spend all that money. Faced with Gates’s duff philanthropy, one almost longs for him to be some Hannibal Lecter, who would at least build a Topaki Palace-sized torture chamber with all that dosh, rather than just torment us with normcore.) No, Gates is the poster boy for the proposition that making money can be made not only an acceptable necessity, the deforming effects of which on the human soul needs must be ameliorated, but, gulp: morally good. The Gates persona exists to incarnate the redeemed capitalist: first the ruthless acquisition, then the global amelioration; first the monopoly rents, then the polio campaign; first the operating system, then the foundation; first the coercive platform––then the saving of children. It is as Hume says: there is nothing much to human causal reasoning beyond the habitual empirical association of cause and effect.

Understood this way, the soft sweater is not a simple garment but sort of ephod: the mantic garment worn by the ancient Hebrew priests, with jewels set in its fabric that lit up and so transmitted Divine revelation. That is why Warren Buffett matters not mundanely––but cosmically. Buffett is the John the Baptist in this gospel of American moneyed utopia. He goes before Gates in the wilderness of accumulation, a leviathan full of moms and pops proclaiming the older creed: thrift, patience, compounding interest, hominy gritted teeth, folksy plain dealing, the billionaire as dry Midwestern custodian: ‘I made it all out of grain hoppers, I tellya.’ Then comes Gates, the Jesus of the computer revolution, translating the primitive message of money-making into global neoliberal salvation. Buffett baptises money in the wilderness––Gates redeems it.

So when Buffett begins to withhold full sanction — when he waits to see what more the Epstein files reveal before deciding on his annual gift to Jesus’s foundation—the whole structure trembles. The elder witness has not denounced the messiah; worse, he has suspended belief. The weeping of Gates’s employees, and the gnashing of their teeth, and the rending of their own garments (normcore by necessity, not choice) are the heart of the matter. They were not merely crying because Bill Gates had behaved badly, or because Epstein’s poisonous name had entered the corporate bloodstream––they were crying because God’s image––and with it their own moral universe––had fractured. TerraPower and Breakthrough Energy––the Gates Foundation itself, with its supposed ‘initiatives’ to supposedly ‘end’ disease and poverty, while supplying ‘clean’ energy: these institutions offered their superficially (i.e.

technically not conceptually) intelligent, liberal, highly-trained employees a way of believing that capitalism can cure the very injuries capitalism produces. All the US philanthropists seem to desire this bizarre inversion of the Midas myth: that every bit of exploitatively gained and non-renewable wealth they touch, is somehow by that act rendered pure, ethical gold. That they themselves should fall for it is unsurprising––that those lower on the corporate food-chain do as well is evidenced by the copious tears which come when that belief-system begins to fail. For there is no clean energy in a moral sense: there are less dirty technologies to be developed, and necessary transitions to them to be made––there could be better grids, improved storage systems, and offset carbon jiggery-pokery subject to venture-capital bets.

But when all the hullabaloo dies down, there is no innocent energy regime compatible with permanently rising consumption, anymore than there’s a magic money tree, or a perpetual motion machine its leaves can be used to fuel. We cannot ameliorate the climate emergency with the same exploitative economic model that produced it in the first place. We cannot, above all, ameliorate it by actually intensifying extraction as a result of accelerating throughput––which makes of all the philanthropy cadres and the PR flaks, merely the rubber-booted abattoir workers, cleaning the blood off the floor. These employees were crying because they’d slipped after falling for the bullshit––and now realised the real sanguinous nature of the enterprise. The so-called ‘maxmin’ or ‘difference’ principle is often supposed to justify economic equalities in freemarket capitalist economies.

Developed by John Rawls in his ‘Theory of Justice’ it states that inequalities of wealth, income, status and even power are not inherently unjust so long as institutions can arrange them to the benefit of the least advantaged and preserve the fair value of rights. But hypercapitalism produces inequalities that deform the very field in which rights are exercised. It does not merely distribute more to some and less to others; it reorganises attention, law, media, governance, science, philanthropy and even conscience around its own continuance, not Gaia’s. Once billionaires become quasi-sovereign providers of global health, climate research and technological futurity, justice is no longer a distributive correction to capitalism. Justice has been made dependent on capitalism’s victors. Edmund Burke saw one part of the problem from the opposite ideological shore.

Once the separate arms and estates of government fall into conflict, they cannot mediate sectional interests evenly––then the rich and powerful divvy-up the res publica between themselves. In America now, the branches of government do not merely check and balance one another; they increasingly act as rival corporate embodiments––each captured by antagonistic sectional energies. The heritability of the Constitution—its transmission as a living compact between generations — has been disrupted. The result is not republican order but corporate civil war by procedural means. The barons fight each other: the King eats cheeseburgers and surfs channels. In that context, Gates’s conscience becomes synecdochic. It is not guilt over accumulation itself––but rather terror that the image of benevolent accumulation might collapse, and the villeins will quit the demesne.

The question is not whether Gates has done good through his foundation; plainly, in many measurable respects, he has. The question is whether measurable good can redeem the system of power that made such private sovereignty possible. The Gates Foundation’s achievements in global health are real; that is precisely why the moral problem is so acute. Hypercapitalism does not fail because it does no good. It fails because the good it does becomes dependent on the continued legitimacy of the structures that caused, intensified or monetised the harm it also conspicuously does: harm to the environment overall, but even more: harm to the capacity people have to believe in the good at all when it’s parachuted from above by a cargo cult headed by a John Frum who shops at Costco. This is why the sight of a 70-year-old man in a grey crew neck reassuring employees that he is good, and therefore the world he embodies is good, no longer cuts it.

The sweater has lost its sacramental force because it wasn’t an ephod to begin with: just another item of fast fashion, which is why the staff can see it’s a walking, talking mannequin that’s wearing it: an accountant––not even an entrepreneur, let alone a true philanthropist, which definitionally means a lover of humankind. The pseudo-philanthropic machine can still operate, the funds can still be disbursed, the malaria programmes can still run, the nuclear pitches can still be made, the documentaries can still be edited––then reedited; but it’s too late––the conscience began to split when the Gates’ squeaky-clean screen of a marriage cracked from side to side. Gates is not an aberration: he is the avatar of American hypercapitalism as it wished to appear to itself: brilliant, empirical, secular, generous, emotionally understated, technically competent, morally serious, and finally harmless.

In a nutshell: Graham Greene’s eponymous ‘quiet American’ shat out on demand to fuck up another whole era. The scandal matters because it reintroduces not just harm into the image––but moral tragedy, and possibly napalm. It says: behind the neutral sweater stands power; behind the foundation stands accumulation; behind the clean-energy prospectus stands dirty and oleaginous extraction; behind global benevolence stands private impunity; behind the philanthropy stands the unresolved question of whether making money was ever good in the first place. That is the gravamen: not Epstein as psychopathic turbercle––but Gates as moral symptom. Not one man’s hypocrisy, but the collapse of a civilisational alibi.

item.content:encoded:
Pope Leo XIV’s encyclical on artificial intelligence is a significant intervention, and should be welcomed as such. We need this kind of intervention from the major religions. We need institutions with memory, moral ballast and anthropological seriousness to enter a debate otherwise dominated by engineers, speculators, policy technicians and a clerisy of corporate ethicists whose moral vocabulary rarely rises above the language of risk mitigation. The Pope builds, intelligently and often movingly, on Catholic Social Doctrine. This matters. Catholic Social Doctrine, at its best, has helped create the conditions for viable civic society: solidaristic, associative, anti-monopolistic, wary of both state absolutism and market idolatry.

For all its patriarchal and generative assumptions — assumptions many of us find deeply problematic — Catholicism has often retained in contemporary societies a capacity for cohesion, mutual obligation and moral seriousness that liberal individualism has largely squandered. The encyclical’s strongest sections are those in which the Pope identifies AI not simply as a tool, but as a concentration of power: data, platforms, infrastructure, compute, capital and political influence converging in the hands of a few transnational actors. His call to "disarm AI" is valuable precisely because it sees the arms race as military, economic and cognitive. The race for larger models, greater compute, deeper integration and wider capture is not neutral innovation. It is domination under the sign of inevitability. Here the Pope comes close to a genuinely socialistic critique.

He understands that technology cannot be evaluated apart from ownership, access, labour, exploitation, surveillance and the common good. He sees that the human being is being reduced to a functional unit within an optimisation system. He understands, rightly, that the danger is not chiefly that machines become human, but that humans become machine-like. But this is also where the encyclical falters. Christian anthropology cannot quite shake off its refusal to accept the full implications of evolution. It continues to propose the human individual as exemplary, as though the visible phenotype were the final moral unit, rather than a temporary synecdoche of the genotype and of the longer biological, historical and social processes through which human beings become what they are. The human being is not an already completed essence accidentally threatened by technology. Human societies are temporally mediated. They exist in becoming.

Any serious account of technology must therefore have a Hegelian sense of mediation, contradiction and historical formation. The Pope sees the danger of dehumanisation, but he still treats humanity as something to be safeguarded from outside assault. The deeper problem is that humanity itself is being reconstituted through the very systems it has built. The machine is not merely attacking the human. It is training the human, habituating the human, formatting the human, recoding attention, memory, desire and social relation. And this brings us to the great omission. The Pope will not attack baseline consumption. This is the failure of almost all contemporary thinking. It sees the catastrophe, names the structures, deplores the inequalities, calls for regulation, education, transparency, accountability, oversight and dialogue — and then refuses the simple negative command: Stop. Stop doing it. Stop scrolling. Stop posting.

Stop refreshing. Stop answering. Stop consuming the machine. Stop feeding your consciousness into an attention economy designed to capture, fragment and monetise it. The root problem is not that we need to start doing something new. It is that we need to stop doing things we are already doing compulsively. The addiction issue is massive. We are not dealing with a marginal habit or an unfortunate side effect. We are dealing with mass cognitive impairment and affective derangement on an industrial scale. Four hours a day on a smartphone is not a lifestyle choice. It is closer, in moral and cognitive terms, to smoking crack for four hours a day: a patterned derangement of attention, reward, memory, anxiety and selfhood. It produces populations that are distracted, neurotic, suggestible, volatile and, at the edges, psychotic in their relation to reality. Catholicism has the language for this. It has always had it. Spiritual hygiene.

Fasting. Abstinence. Custody of the eyes. Examination of conscience. Mortification. Restraint. The discipline of desire. The refusal of temptation. The struggle against bondage of the will. So why does the Pope not say it? Why does he not say to Catholics, and to all people of goodwill: restrict your time online. Put the phone down. Keep one day a week substantially free from digital media. Do not give your children smartphones. Do not take the machine to bed. Do not allow your first and last act of the day to be submission to the glowing rectangle: the hagioscope in which you worship yourself. Limit your use to an hour. Recover silence. Recover boredom. Recover prayer. Recover reading. Recover the face of another human being. That would be a true pastoral intervention, and a truly Catholic move. Instead, the encyclical remains partly trapped in the managerial language of the age it seeks to challenge.

It calls for responsible innovation, ethical design and improved governance. All of that is necessary, but insufficient. The machine is not only out there in the corporations. It is in the hand, the bed, the pocket, the nervous system, the twitching thumb, the interrupted sentence, the uncompleted thought. The Pope says: rebuild Jerusalem––yes, but first stop building Babel. Stop laying bricks. Stop supplying the mortar. Stop confusing connection with communion, information with wisdom, stimulation with life, and availability with love. The most urgent moral act in the age of artificial intelligence may not be innovation, regulation or education. It may be refusal.

item.content:encoded:
Martin Amis’s war against cliché was never merely a war against bad writing—as if there were writing on the one hand, and the world on the other, while nary the twane shall meet. I mean, you may well consider the felicities of literary style to be infra dig so far as you’re concerned: you have your eye on more important things… really. The very essential things the things that matter in this world, not words—things. And the fact that words are used to describe things is merely a technical matter— much like the way, say, a computer programme can be designed so as to provide doctors with unified patient information across the National Health Service.

No doubt Amis—although he died in Florida, so not under the aegis of the NHS—would nonetheless have taken some interest in the prospect of Wes Streeting, the former Health Secretary becoming leader of the Labour Party, and—such is the nature of the British constitution—by that fact alone, the prime minister, and hence the most powerful individual in the realm. The realm Amis became a knight of shortly before his surcease—the realm that was, for all his philo-Americanism, the omphalos of his own literary style; one so very resistant to cliché, almost to the end. Which was unsurprising: death being a sort of cosmic cliché in Amis’s own terms: death, unless apprehended authentically, results in the malformed awareness we see in all those cliches of the deathbed scene: the loving relatives, the serene acceptance, the tearful embrace.

The phrases used to describe it represent not simply laziness, but a failure of perception; not merely the long-since worn out verbal gadget that comes too readily to hand, but the mental hack that enables a writer—or a politician—not to think at all. Amis’s famous triad, the clichés of the pen, the mind and the heart, needs now to be extended. All governing, like all writing, should be a campaign against cliché—against the inherited verbal, emotional and institutional mistakes by which societies repeat themselves into decline, death, and, once that death—having been memorialised only in cliches, is forgotten—utter oblivion, whether they’re former health secretaries or knights of the realm. Wes Streeting’s memoir, ‘One Boy, Two Bills and a Fry Up’, is an almost exemplary deposition when it comes to building the case against the cliché-ridden contemporary British political class.

True, politicians aren’t ever conspicuously good writers—but that doesn’t mean they have to be execrable ones. If Streeting’s credentialled by his class mobility, why doesn’t he care to demonstrate its most obvious cause and effect: education. As a Cambridge graduate in History, he cannot—one would imagine—have avoided being exposed to writing that aims, ipso facto, to convey how political actors think and feel about the societies they inhabit, and upon which they hope to act. Just as the writer needs to make it new, so does the politician—especially one operating in a political system that has lost the ability, through public debate, to speak to itself.

There’s a marvellous book by Julian Jaynes called ‘The Origin of Consciousness and the Breakdown of the Bicameral Mind.’ In it, Jaynes proposes that the origin of our reflective self-consciousness lies in the severing, within historical time, of the corpus callosum: the thick hank of neural tissue which unites the right and left sides of the human brain. Jaynes places this bio-historical event in the Bronze Age of Greek society, somewhere between the composition of the Odyssey and that of the Iliad. His reasoning is that the former text displays a schizophrenic style: the gods speak in lieu of human interiority; whereas, by the time the Iliad was composed the gods have become only semi-detached from the psyche.

I only reflect on this because it’s worth considering, by analogy, that the problem with contemporary British political debate is the corpus callosum has grown back; reuniting not just the two sides of the House of Commons, but the two sides of society they represent as well. Moreover, the two houses of Parliament itself are now conjoined in the same contumely—because this isn’t a unity born of consensus, but a febrile and an utter diversity of opinion; one mediated solely by a doom-scrolling feedback loop of affective signalling: a Streeting-level pseudo-discourse of utter and superficial cliché mongering. As I say, politicians as a rule aren’t the greatest of writers—while Churchill famously won the Nobel Prize, having recently sat down to enjoy a gentle hour or two with his ‘History of the Second World War,’ I can tell you there are few more effective sedatives available through the National Health Service.

However, Churchill’s works at least have the virtue of providing the reader with vital empirical information—the same cannot be said for Streeting’s memoir of his battle royale of an upbringing. Its first chapter alone is so saturated with cliché that one begins to feel the prose itself has been assembled out of prefabricated verbal units: ‘all hell broke loose’, which then ‘spread like wildfire’, ovewhelming the ‘life and soul of the party’ to ‘earth-shattering proportions’, such that they were ‘over the moon’; unsurprisingly, given they were riding an ‘emotional roller coaster’. Even so, they would have to ‘face the music’, prove they were ‘a tough cookie’, and, like little Wes, capable of ‘a new lease of life’, one effected by ‘pull(ing) myself together’, ‘putting a brave face on’, and of course ‘work(ing) well to take my mind off my own problems’.

When it comes to the mise-en-scene, there are clichés of East End matriarchy, clichés of adversity, clichés of medical ordeal, clichés of political redemption, clichés of family trauma, clichés of uplift. The cliché-mongering is not occasional—it’s structural. On these meagre pages, bedizened with type, one finds several such otiose formulae per page—and more importantly, one finds a prose that continually converts felt inner experience into highly-visible social currency before experience has had time to become thought. Rachel Cooke, reviewing the book in The Guardian, noticed the clichés but gave them a light ride, not so much by misinterpreting, but by using Amis’s notion of the just war against cliché as a mere placeholder in lieu of any sustained criticism of them.

This is a well-worn, de-haut-en-bas manoeuvre in liberal literary culture, one Guardian journalists (many of whom are Oxbridge educated themselves) deploy with consummate legerdemain. Yes, a lousy style in a leftist’s political memoir is, in theory, regrettable, but it doesn’t really matter, given the story is both ‘inspiriting’ (whatever that means in an avowedly Godless society), as well as being ‘compelling’ (this we do understand, given we live in a society comprised mostly by addicts); the prose is thin gruel, but one’s life is nonetheless ruled straight and firm, which is good enough for us. Why? Because the piss-poor writing paradoxically confirms the steepness of the ascent up the social pyramid, and hence—one presumes—the steely grip Streeting has maintained on the greasy pole.

None of the lucubrations bestowed on Streeting’s sentimental rise too powerlessness represented generosity: it was all condescension—the return of the repressed English class system manifesting yet again inside the supposedly ‘progressive’ consciousness. The middle-class critic grants the working-class politician absolution from style because she believes his content is socially useful. The right, meanwhile, welcomes the same book for opposite reasons: here is a man who pulled himself up by his bootstraps, accepted discipline, aspiration, faith, family and institutional advancement. Both sides patronise him. Both sides excuse the writing because it serves a prior political fantasy—one, they themselves no longer possess the integrity, intellect, and crucially style to interrogate.

How, pity please Rachel Cooke, is a man who deals in clichés so egregiously going to come up with policies that don’t themselves betray the same, um, clichéd turn of mind? In particular, the hoary old myth that ‘class mobility’ alone will result in… well what precisely? To hear politicians and commentators of all stripes (and increasingly, none) discuss this vital issue, is to enter into a wonderland not even Karl Marx envisioned, one in which an entire class of society somehow magically ascends into that empyrean of moneyed privilege, while mysteriously leaving no one behind to clean the toilets except, in the case of the right, psychotic asylum seekers; or well-paid and unionised effluent removers educated to degree-level, in the case of the left.

Dear, gentle, Harry-Potter-educated reader, style is not separable from personality: style is personality, which is why I take my lead on gender rights from Simone de Beauvoir, not JK Rowling, who’s prose is so bedizened with adverbs reading it you do feel there are dark forces at play in the world… menacingly… creepingly… phallically... If contemporary society—and by extension, politics—insists on personality, authenticity and lived experience, then prose becomes evidence. Streeting’s prose reveals not a mind struggling toward form, but a mind as intensely comfortable with banality as another Banalmeister, Peter Mandelson, once was with people becoming filthy rich. This is not to say that a bad sentence disqualifies a politician sans parse; it is to assert for the record that a settled dependence on ready-made language suggests a settled dependence on ready-made feeling.

The cliché is not only a literary defect: it’s an ethical symptom: the blazoning of psyche evading the expression of authentic emotions. Either because it’s not advantageous, or because its incapable, or, worse still, because it doesn’t have any at all, having already transmogrified all that subtle interiority into crass—and yes, clichéd—exteriority. This becomes most striking in Streeting’s account of cancer. One might expect such an experience to force metaphysical pressure on, and then through the page—especially given his reader, in this instance, was actually ill with cancer as he was reading, and remains so. Not just pressure, either—sympathy. Illness, after all, is a greater leveller than progressive taxation: because unlike the latter, it strips away the administrative fiction that ‘life’, in all it marvellous multifariousness, is a sequence of manageable tasks.

It confronts the sufferer, in Heidegger’s phrase, with ‘the ownmost possibility of death.’ Yet Streeting’s account repeatedly moves away from authentic inwardness toward it’s diametric opposite: publicity, procedure and response. The diagnosis becomes a media event, a campaigning inconvenience, a story managed through phone, video, broadcast and social-media feedback. One of his most revealing moments is his relief at a Twitter troll becoming kind to him when cancer is announced. Here, surely, is the affective core: the self-sustained by the crowd summoned from the pocket, rather than any heartfelt conviction, let alone, gulp, love. This is why Streeting is not merely phoney in the old sense: he is phone-y—his emotional life, at least as represented in the memoir, is mediated by bidirectional digital attention.

He does not so much suffer privately and then communicate publicly; he appears to discover the meaning of suffering through its circulation, while, not being apprised of difference, he cannot understand that each retweet attenuates rather than reinforces it. The cancer passage thus moves strangely between the statistical and the pseudo-personal: cancer as diagnosis, cancer as public statement, cancer as response management, cancer as proof of resilience. The old truism is that no patient feels himself to be a statistic. Streeting’s book suggests something odder: a patient who can barely stop seeing himself as one, given his ‘feelings’ are being titrated, in real time, through the emotional testbed of a multitude’s response.

This phoneyness carries directly into his politics: the one phrase for which he will remembered as Health Secretary is especially damning: the ‘NHS in your pocket’ formula, which, while it might be a little light relief for those suffering from ovarian or testicular cancer, is not an incidental slogan, but the entire Streeting anthropology: the patient becomes a user, the service becomes an interface, care becomes access, community becomes connectivity. It is not that digital technology has no place in healthcare, it’s that Streeting’s imagination—in common with those of so many of our wannabe ‘leaders’—seems unable to distinguish between a society and a platform, between a community and a feedback loop, between public trust and an app.

The same frictionless personality that writes in clichés imagines the NHS as a frictionless device—but just as I said in a recent post that culture was friction, so is medical treatment: I cannot even estimate how many hours I’ve spent in consultation with doctors over the past four years of cancer treatment, but it’s hundreds. And thank Christ all-fucking-mighty, Cockney Wes, they weren’t in my pocket, either physically, or—more to the point—financially. The same problem appears in his constitutional imagination. Streeting studied history at Cambridge, yet he talks about Britain and Europe like a man devoid of historical sense. The question of rejoining the European Union cannot be treated as a mere policy preference, still less as a gesture of managerial sanity after Brexit’s damage.

Britain entered in the early 1970s, what was presented, under Heath, as a common market: a customs union, a tariff-free zone, a sphere of economic cooperation. Over the subsequent decades, quantity became quality: incremental legal and political adjustments, each defensible in its own terms, cumulatively altered the relation between Parliament, sovereignty and inherited constitutional practice. The change was not experienced as revolution because the English constitution is precisely arranged to absorb change without announcing rupture. Nonetheless, the violent diremption of Brexit is what happens when, in the words of Isaiah (not a prophet given to good tidings) ‘precept is piled upon precept.’ That is the conundrum contemporary politicians cannot unknot because they’re too entangled in… cliché.

England is a profoundly non-ideological country: one of empiricists and pragmatists sans pareil, ones whose ideology consists in pretending not to have one at all: genius! Its constitution is not the product of rational design—it is a temporalised inheritance: Crown, Parliament, common law, custom, Protestant suspicion, popular sovereignty mediated through representation, and the reciprocal powerlessness—the negative capability—of monarch and bicameral legislature. The dictatorship in Parliament does not usually become tyranny because it is held within a duopolistic and historically sedimented arrangement: something socialists in particular are wont to ignore—one thinks of Kafka’s aphorism in this context: ‘The decisive moment of human development is continually at hand.

This is why those movements of revolutionary thought that declare everything preceding to be an irrelevance are correct—because as yet nothing has happened.’ At least according to them! And under the English constitutional dispensation it becomes even easier to comprehend why their hope springs eternal—it’s by reason of these immemorial arrangements themselves. The sovereign, who’s own majesty is itself a coefficient of its supposed antiquity, is powerful solely by being powerless: Chucky II very definitely remembers what happened to Chucky I, and he doesn’t want to be a sequel in the franchise. Burke, with characteristic elegance, observes that the reason we shouldn’t indulge in lèse-majesté is that it’s rude to remind our servants that this is the case. Mutatis mutandis, Parliament is also absolute precisely by being embedded in what it has not made: no making horses consuls here, thank you very much!

One of the most wearying effects of a long life of observing British politics is the spectacle of now generation after generation of the political class who, uncomprehending of the constitution in its essence, constantly propose policies altogether inimical to the settled English predisposition. So persistently has this been done, that in conjunction with phenomena such as… oh, I dunno, modernity—and the globalisation that has danced attendance on it—that this usually bovine nation has now become rather uselessly frisky. Like a bullock—not John Bull. The European question, like devolution, exposed the fragility of the English/British constitutional arrangement.

The problem was not simply that Britain joined Europe, nor simply that it left—the problem, in point of fact, wasn’t a problem: it was a disaster: Britain, together with its crew and passengers, none of whom possessed adequate orientation, drifted into ever-closer union without a serious constitutional reckoning, and then tore itself out by referendum without one either. Both entry and exit were constitutional deformations. Both were badly understood. Both were treated as policy questions by politicians who no longer understood the vessel they were steering. So when Streeting or any other Labour leadership hopeful starts opining about Europe as though Britain can simply tack back toward Brussels, they show the same underlying defect visible in the prose: a belief that inherited forms can be handled like slogans written on the contemporary equivalent of billowing sails: the gossamer and tacky filaments of the web.

So it is, that wrought by the digi-hands of Streeting et al., the constitution becomes a cliché, sovereignty becomes a cliché, Europe—together with its extraordinary literary heritage—becomes a cliché; and yes, that ownmost reality of the scoundrelly politician, patriotism— that, too, becomes a cliché. And one should always mistrust patriotism when it is expressed by a person whose language is full of clichés of the heart, because as I believe we’ve already established such an individual doesn’t know their own heart, let alone our heart of oak. The Labour Party’s current manoeuvring around Europe therefore reveals more than tactical confusion: it reveals the rotten hollowness of the political class—no heart of oak here, move on please ladies and gentlemen. Brexit was, as I and everyone else right-minded now agree.

(The rest are busy ‘taking back control’.) It hasn’t just injured Britain’s social fabric, economic structure and geostrategic position—it’s spindled and mutilated it. But the remedy cannot be another constitutional mend conducted by politicians who have not understood the pattern, let alone how to cut fabric on the bias—fast fashion will do that: jog on in your jeggings, my son, if you aren’t too puffed-out in that puffer. To repair Britain’s relation with Europe requires first an account of what was constitutionally altered by membership, what was violently torn by departure, and what form of sovereignty can exist in a post-imperial, post-Brexit, digitally saturated polity. Without that, ‘rejoin’ is—you guessed it—nothing save the liberal equivalent of ‘take back control’. In other words, a slogan for people who cannot think historically. A cliché of the mind, if you will.

And so this is where the jollily entitled memoir and the monitorly banal politics converge: Streeting writes—so reads—like a tweet, because he thinks like one: he even looks and sounds like one, with his compressed affect (one part Gay to two of Estuarine), his instant recognisability twerking out policies on TikTok, which itself represents the desired high engagement, while manifesting very low depth indeed. His life story may be compelling material; but why write it in prose that turns it into emotivist bubblewrap: pop one while you’re bored—you’ll feel better. The very apoptosis of his metastasizing cancer cells becomes “pop-pop-pop!” content. His childhood becomes content. His politics becomes content. The human being is flattened into transmissible personality, then wound on to a roll and shipped next day; or, praise be to Tim Berners-Lee, even more expeditiously.

This is why the cliché matters so much, because it isn’t just a dead phrase, it’s an act of avoidance—or, at least reaching for a cliché feels that way: ‘Mm, how should I express this important personal feeling…? I know: “you could’ve knocked me down with a feather”.’ But reached for again and again? That’s many, many little acts of avoidance, each one sparing its ‘author’ the risk of perception, either of himself, or the other. It spares the politician the burden of thought. And there’s an unforced serendipity in this capitulation to the cliché, rather than warring with it: for thereby it also spares the reader the shock of reality, leaving them, too, to sleep the sleep of Merrie England’s immemorial unreasoning. In literature, this produces bad prose—and in Streeting’s execrable—in politics, it produces bad government, which, in the fullness of a time no longer immemorial (although Farage et al.

treat is as if it were) in constitutional affairs it leads to catastrophe. Gird up your lexicons! Re-pinion your split infinitives! Go boldly up to the war against cliché! Martin Amis once vouchsafed to me that he thought it a cosmic solecism that Shakespeare had been a mere dramatist, but given he also once avowed ‘we’re all Labour now’, I feel his shade by my side, as, like King Henry before me, I call upon all true Britons to join the fray. Yes! We few, we happy few, we band of non-gender specific affiliates; for whoever today that sheds their ink with me to write stylish prose, shall be my brother or sister; be he or she ne’er so compulsive a pusher of the cliché button, this day shall gentle his condition, such that instead of pretending he can factor taverning in Eastcheap into the highest office in the land, he brushes up on his constitutional history.

Cambridge University would be an excellent place to start, since the faculty places particular emphasis on just this subject, with readings from such percipient stylists as Burke, Bagehot and Oakeshott prominent on the syllabus to this day. I recommend this national service for the war against cliché not just to Streeting, but the political class in general, who have become so addicted to the cliché that one wonders whether they would be able to say anything of real profundity on any occasion whatsoever I struggle to see Kemi Badenock, let alone Nigel, producing the right words, say, at their beloved’s funeral but really they should get some practise in because the war against cliché is no longer simply literary: it is political, constitutional and moral—therefore, Streeting: civilisational. A country governed by people who speak in clichés will eventually be governed by people who think in clichés.

And a country whose politicians think in clichés will mistake its deepest inheritances for adjustable settings on a phone. Streeting as a devout Christian—something he manages, along with many other contemporary Christians, by skating round a great deal of its doctrine—would have been in sympathy with the Anglican priest I spoke to recently, who, when I suggested that some of the ills of our polity could be ameliorated if people simply stayed off social media, told me ‘My life is on my phone so you won’t get me to do that!’ But of all people, the idea that those whose faith is in the intangible and eternal, should have to hang on so conspicuously to the material and the external, is surely a savage indictment of both that faith and by extension Christianity’s ethical fitness for our era itself. Come the hour: ecce homo!

And that is the danger Streeting represents—not that he’s uniquely bad, nor puddle-shallow, nor unique in his insane ambition. Quite the opposite: he is a cliche. He is the ersatz, POD politician of 2026: educated but unformed, fluent but thin, personal but impersonal, confessional but unauthentic, digital to the pixelated marrow of his cancer-free (we hope) bones. The clichéd twitterings of the human tweet are not a private literary failing: they are the dawning chorus of the governing class discovering that it has nothing inward left to say. No wonder you feel like closing the curtains. A decade ago, in her review of Streeting’s memoir, Cooke posited three explanations for the lack of any interior life on display in this story of a human conscience who wishes to wield power. They were, one: he was a sociopath; two, he found it too painful to write authentically about his difficult upbringing; and three, he was a little ‘robotic’.

Presumably, in the ensuing ten years of doom-scrolling his own opinion ratings, dear little Wes has become even more of a cyborg. It’ll take more than a fry up to relieve this condition.

item.content:encoded:
Westminster sees a cabinet rupture, a Starmer crisis, a tremor before the Makerfield by-election, another twitch in the cadaver of Labour managerialism. This is the Gilbert and Sullivan reading: ministers entering and exiting through the wrong doors while the chorus explains that nothing fundamental has altered. But something fundamental has altered, and it is not Healey. The resignation is the symptom, not the event. The event is the collapse of Britain's old defence settlement and the substitution of an Americanised software-sovereignty model in its place. For forty years, Britain imagined that its defence-industrial position was underwritten by BAE, the Gulf, Saudi Arabia, oil money, aircraft, service contracts and the long afterlife of Al-Yamamah – the biggest sale of anything by anyone to anybody, or close enough for the myth to matter.

That arrangement gave the British state a fantasy of autonomy: Atlantic enough for Washington, European enough for NATO, mercantile enough for Riyadh, and corrupt enough, in the old imperial style, to be called pragmatism. Hormuz has blown that settlement apart. The Gulf is no longer the cashbox of British strategic continuity but the exposed circuit through which war, energy, insurance, shipping, drones, missiles and American power now pass at terrifying speed. The British political class cannot name this because it is still cognitively arranged around the Cold War: Europe, Russia, NATO, tanks, budgets, deterrence, posture. It has not understood thermodronology: the movement of war through heat, fuel, data, shipping lanes, swarm systems, insurance rates and automated perception. Into that failure steps Palantir. Not as an ideology, not even as a conspiracy, but as the operating system of an abdication.

The Starmer entity, unable to think defence or governance except as procurement, abrogates itself to the Trump entity: not Trump the man alone, but the American sovereign stack of money, war, platform, cloud, contractor and command system. The fog of war moves into Britain's own London particular of peace. Healey's resignation matters only because it reveals the argument has already shifted from whether Britain should enter this architecture to how fast it can afford to wire itself into it. The Met pause and the NHS break clause are visible scratches on the glass. The MoD is the screen itself.

item.content:encoded:
An occasional publication evangelising Jehovah’s Witnesses ‘God is present when the eyes of those who give and those who receive meet’ Simone Weil I respect your tradition of refusing to do military service on the grounds of conscience. Doctrinally, I’ve no objection to your anti-Trinitarianism, personally, I’d be dead without regular blood transfusions, and yet I accept your right to object to them – but your millenarian eschatology blinds you to the ways you abandon Christian ethics. You are close to gnostic heretics who, finding the world entirely sinful and ruled over by a demiurge or devil, argue that doing what they want is the whole of the law. You’re doing what you want right now, which is to conduce people not to salvation – since you offer this only conditionally and belatedly – but your own organisation.

Inasmuch as you are free in terms of conscience and belief, you abrogate that freedom by refusing to accept any differences of opinion among you on either theological or political grounds. Monstrous pride! Simone Weil, the great Christian thinker glosses the Parable of the Good Samaritan (Luke 10.25) thus: ‘Christ taught us that the supernatural love of our neighbour is the exchange of compassion and gratitude which happens in a flash between two beings, one possessing and the other deprived of human personality. One of the two is only a little piece of flesh, naked, inert, and bleeding beside a ditch; he is nameless, no one knows anything about him. Those who pass by this thing scarcely notice it, and a few minutes afterward do not even know they saw it. Only one stops and turns his attention towards it.

The actions that follow are just the automatic effect of this moment of attention.’ The bold italics are mine, because week after week I pass you by and here you stand: completely inattentive to the suffering around you. You are the priest and the Levite of who Jesus speaks – you ignore the traveller who was stripped and beaten and robbed and left for dead in a ditch. You’re ignoring him right now: he’s lying within a few feet of you, in a dirty sleeping bag, his soul wracked with distress, his body with pain. Remember what the Good Samaritan did for the ‘little piece of flesh’ you disdain: ‘when he saw him, he had compassion on him, And went to him, and bound up his wounds, pouring in oil and wine, and set him on his own beast, and brought him to an inn, and took care of him.

And on the morrow when he departed, he took out two pence, and gave them to the host, and said unto him, Take care of him; and whatsoever thou spendest more, when I come again, I will repay thee.’ That’s what you should be doing right now, instead of standing here chatting with your friends. What you’re doing isn’t evangelism, it’s a recruitment drive. I wrote the above two or three years ago, when I was still attending psychotherapy with an existential therapist whose consulting room occupied a drab office block inserted into one of the masonry crevices opposite Liverpool Street Station. The therapy proved utterly fruitless: a man who claimed his therapeutic method conformed to an authentic awareness of death was utterly unable to assist me in confronting my own finitude.

Eventually I terminated the therapy myself, concluding our final session by charging the therapist with an ethical failure and reporting him to his professional body. What finally repelled me most, besides his intellectual and emotional dishonesty, was the realisation that he responded to my distress with a kind of procedural automaticity rather than genuine attention. His interventions felt less like the response of one human being to another than the execution of a protocol. In retrospect, the auto-therapist’s practice seemed oddly analogous to the activity of the religious evangelists who assembled every lunchtime on the pavement outside the station. You find them in cities throughout the developed world.

Their eschatological claims are curiously addressed to societies that have largely been emptied of any serious sense of an ending, while offering little comfort to those whose endings are already pressing upon them: the diseased, the damaged, the starving, the homeless, or anyone confronting an overwhelming coefficient of adversity. Such people cannot meaningfully be consoled by the doctrine that the elect have already been chosen before birth. Whenever I pass Jehovah's Witnesses standing beside their display of The Watchtower and their neatly arranged pamphlets, I am struck by their extraordinary stasis. Very often—not merely nearby but almost at their feet—lies someone damaged, diseased or destitute, precisely the sort of person any compassionate Christian should first attend to. Yet their attention is directed elsewhere: towards the prospective recruit rather than the immediate neighbour.

It was this paradox that first suggested to me the project I have come to call The Will Tower. My concern is not merely with the decline of reading, but with the decline of attention itself. Deep literacy is only one expression of a more fundamental ethical capacity: the willingness to stop, to notice, and to respond. Watch this space.
