item.content:encoded:
Sleepless on Saturday night, in the humid heat of a London summer increasingly rendered oppressive by the climate emergency, I found myself once again listening to football. Not watching it—listening to it. Before we get to the beautiful game, it’s worth considering the sticky heat. There’s a tension now around heatwaves in London, as there is elsewhere in the world. People are faced each summer with a dreadful paradox: the conventional idea of repose and relaxation is, for people in the Northern Hemisphere at least, so formed by centuries now of cultural perception and evaluation, concluding in a mass obsession with ‘going somewhere hot’ that renders the experience of suffering under a heatwave is almost unassimilable. This, despite the fact that the English physically dislike the heat so much, that they endlessly complain about it.

Yet more bizarre still, is the fact that members of London's burgeoning ethnic minority population—at least several with whom I am in daily contact—also describe the close weather as somehow unbearable. Surely this is because it represents something uncanny and disturbing. There’s a dreadful cognitive dissonance here: it’s early July, the schools will be breaking up soon—people are going to go on holidays they must perforce feel ‘entitled to’; moreover, they’re going on holiday to all the same places they normally go on holiday, thereby flying from heat, into heat—out of the frying pan of technologised hyper-accelerating capitalism, into the burning fat it’s engendered, and thereby making it all sizzle still more. Yet they must simultaneously construct this as the most relaxing transition of the year—‘chilling’, I believe they call it.

For the past fortnight they have also been engaged in another act of mental diplopia, holding in their minds simultaneously the world of football—which, in a certain sense that I shall presently reveal, now constitutes the arena within which human history, conceived as the temporalisation of the intentions of human actors, still appears to take place—and another world: a world in which people are dying, infrastructure is being destroyed, and a war that has never truly been declared—yet is continually being waged and endlessly litigated as being on the point of ending—never actually ends. The always-already endless war of what I have come to call dromodronology has been repressed so that the world can take a holiday—but take a holiday in the only place where it still believes it can act.

The England match had finished hours before, yet the city was still speaking: from my bedroom in Stockwell I could distinguish two quite separate acoustic fields. One reached me from the pubs and streets around Vauxhall to the north-east, the other from Brixton to the south. They overlapped, interfered and dissolved into one another until the atmosphere of inner south London itself seemed to have become their medium: there were cheers, groans, shouts and even howls; car engines revved; I could hear motorcyclists pulling wheelies along the long, straight stretch of Brixton Road—I could picture them passing the turning into the road where Cherry Croce, the woman whose death at the hands of the Met led to the 1983 riots which convulsed the neighbourhood: I can remember seeing burning barricades there, and a different sort of petroleum heat: Molotov cocktails.

After many years of living here, I have become aware that the signals that come from Vauxhall and those from Brixton are not identical. They possess different textures, different rhythms, even different social compositions. As the World Cup has progressed, and successive teams from Africa, the Caribbean and the wider Global South have disappeared from the tournament, I have had the distinct impression that the Brixton signal has grown louder. Allegiances have shifted. The distributed emotional body through which the city metabolises the tournament has reorganised its alimentary track in real time. Ali, in the corner shop, put the matter to me with characteristic directness: as a second-generation British Asian in his fifties, he’s spent much of his life supporting other national sides in international tournaments. ‘When I was younger,’ he told me ‘my attitude was: why should I support England?

This wasn’t a country that was good to me.’ Now, however, his own children are adolescents and think of themselves simply and uncomplicatedly as English and support the England team without hesitation. In response, Ali’s own allegiance has become fluid: once those teams with which he feels a stronger religious or cultural affinity have been eliminated, he finds himself quite content to support England. His loyalty is neither fixed nor cynical: it oscillates. Much the same process is occurring across many of London’s communities. A young Black friend who lives in north London told me yesterday that she had gone to Hackney to watch the match. She too remarked upon the noticeably increased support for England in this phase of the tournament, once sides with which first- and second-generation members of the African diaspora often feel a more immediate affiliation had been eliminated.

Nonetheless, she and I agreed that however tumultuous the scenes in Hackney had become, they were probably not as tumultuous as those in Brixton, for the reason that the residual post-colonial identification remains latently strong among the African-Caribbean community. I confirmed this empirically this morning, by tottering along to the local scrap of parched park, where I often chew the fat with a gang of other alter kockers, although not demi-Yiddisher ones like me. In the group this morning were three kockers of my own age: two Jamaicans and one Ghanaian, and the Jamaican guys were definitely keener on an England win against Argentina than the Ghanaian. Lying awake in my bedroom on Saturday night, I could hear a general atmosphere of almost ecstatic revelry—nothing comparable had accompanied any of England’s previous victories in the tournament.

Something had shifted, and whatever it was had become audible before it became intelligible. This was not the first time I had noticed the phenomenon. Indeed, I suspect it belongs distinctively to the modern era. Just as football itself was once concentrated within local communities, with players and supporters alike drawn from them and held in tight territorial allegiance, so too the signal system associated with the game was communicated through hierarchical media that allowed the significance of individual matches—their meaning, their interpretation and their influence within the wider population—to remain largely localised. I was a four-year-old child when England won the World Cup in 1966. I owned a World Cup Willie, the little lion who served as the tournament's mascot; mine was perched atop a miniature plinth containing a concealed ball-bearing.

I flicked my World Cup Willie about the place rather more than was probably good for me and, generally speaking, the English population has been flicking its World Cup Willie ever since. The joke is no joke at all. For all that flicking really is a spasmodic attempt at priapism: namely, the recurrent fantasy of a return to footballing pre-eminence that continues to haunt post-imperial English identity. The dream is not simply of victory but of restored potency. Every tournament promises, once again, that history might briefly begin to run in the right direction: the direction confirmed—despite concurrent imperial decline—by three signal victories: the one concluded at Versailles in 1919; at Ludendorff Heath in 1944; and at Wembley in 1966. The fantastical character of this hope—eliding once more, the pitch and the battlespace—is confirmed by the extraordinary oscillation of the national mood during every major tournament.

Support for England has become one of the principal occasions upon which the so-called cricket test of political loyalty is enacted. Fidelity to the national side is no longer an uncomplicated patriotic reflex; it has itself become politically negotiated. This wasn’t always primarily a question of multicultural Britain. During the 1980s and well into the 1990s, contested sovereignty remained, to a significant degree, a function of class. It is here that Nick Hornby enters the story—not merely as a successful author, but as the exemplary chronicler of the proletarianisation of the English middle class that accompanied both the dissolution of the old industrial working class and the attenuation of football as the privileged expression of proletarian sovereignty.

Few people realised that Fever Pitch was written by a Cambridge graduate from an affluent professional family whose father, Sir Derek Hornby, occupied the commanding heights of British corporate life. Hornby presents himself instead as emotionally adrift rather than socially privileged: the child of divorce who discovers in football not merely belonging but masculinity itself. The displacement is significant. Class quietly recedes behind psychology. What had once been understood as a question of material position becomes a question of identity, affect and self-fashioning. This was no accident: Fever Pitch, published in 1992, appeared at precisely the historical moment when English football was undergoing one of the most remarkable transformations in its history. Hillsborough had exposed the lethal consequences of treating working-class supporters as a public order problem rather than as citizens.

The publication of the Taylor Report, the creation of the Premier League, the arrival of satellite broadcasting, the rebuilding of stadiums and the commodification of fandom together constituted nothing less than the logistical re-engineering of the game: the beautiful game ceased to be primarily a territorial institution and became an informational one. Hornby’s typically understated English middle-class genius was to narrate precisely this transition without ever quite naming it. He appeared to be writing a memoir of obsession, but in retrospect he was documenting the migration of football from the factory gate to the media network. The terraces became audiences; supporters became consumers; local institutions became globally circulating brands. The sovereign crowd dissolved into a distributed public.

This also explains why Fever Pitch became such an emblematic text for New Labour Britain: it appeared to democratise football just as football itself was ceasing to be democratic in any straightforward sense. The old industrial working class, which had supplied the game with its social foundation, was itself dissolving under the pressures of deindustrialisation and financialisation. In its place emerged a newly anxious—and newly manufactured—middle class, eager to inherit the emotional authenticity once attributed to labour while quietly forgetting the economic conditions that had produced it. Football therefore survived not because its social function remained unchanged but because it acquired another. It became one of the last theatres in which history still appeared to be made by identifiable human actors. Eleven men faced another eleven men; a referee blew a whistle; victories and defeats could still be narrated in moral language.

Meanwhile, outside the stadium, wars, financial markets, climate systems and algorithmic infrastructures increasingly escaped the temporal horizon of individual intention. Human beings retained sovereignty on the pitch at precisely the moment they were losing it almost everywhere else. Thus, Hornby, gave literary expression to a new historical settlement—thereby making Britons (those identifying as ‘men’ in particular), happy to live in a country that, in terms of force projection in the geopolitical arena, had become Hornby size. Middle-class men who no longer possessed any direct relation to the means of production, nor any convincing public role in the making of history, rediscovered solidarity through the ritual contemplation of working-class men playing football. The stadium became a substitute polity. Spectatorship itself became a mode of political affect.

Football, in this sense, is a synecdoche for the diminution of sovereignty itself. Increasingly unable to act historically, the English middle classes found themselves investing emotionally in a domain where history still appeared to possess recognisable protagonists, decisive moments and unequivocal outcomes. That tendency has now become so pronounced that Britain may yet produce a Prime Minister whose strongest claim to popular legitimacy rests not upon the exercise of sovereignty in government but upon the exercise of sovereignty in football’s political afterlife. Andy Burnham’s championship of the Hillsborough families came comparatively late in his career. It was only after the commemoration service in 2009, when relatives of those who had died angrily challenged him to do more, that he fully embraced their cause.

Yet it is difficult to imagine his subsequent political authority in places such as Merseyside without that identification. Football had become the arena through which a wider claim to justice, solidarity and political legitimacy could once again be made. On the evening of 26 June 1996, I went for a drink in a pub in Maida Vale, only vaguely aware of the significance of the occasion. It was, in fact, the semi-final of the European Championship between England and Germany, and the match had gone to a penalty shoot-out. The atmosphere inside the pub was almost unbearably charged. I had no particular interest in football, yet found myself caught inside an emotional field so intense that I decided to leave. As has often happened during major tournaments, London’s streets were almost deserted. Taking advantage of the empty roads, I drove rapidly across the city towards Hampstead Heath and climbed to the summit of Parliament Hill.

My intention was perfectly straightforward. I wanted to escape the football. Instead, I discovered something altogether stranger. Standing above the city, I realised that I could hear the penalty shoot-out—not the commentary; not the crowd inside Wembley—London itself. There was first the suspension: not silence exactly, but a strange collective holding of breath, as though the city had momentarily forgotten to inhale. Then came the strike—a fraction of a second later the wave arrived; a roar… then again… suspension… Strike: roar… suspension… Strike: roar. Each penalty announced itself not visually but rhythmically. Without seeing a single image, I could reconstruct the progress of the shoot-out from the successive waves propagating across the capital. Then, finally, the rhythm broke—the pause seemed longer than before.

The kick must have been taken, but this time instead of release there came an immense, effortful groan, millions of bodies apparently contracting in involuntary sympathy with Gareth Southgate as Andreas Köpke saved his penalty. The sound did not resemble disappointment so much as physical pain. It travelled across London like one of the great orchestral swells in Debussy’s La Mer, gathering and dispersing as though the metropolis itself possessed lungs, muscles and a nervous system. Shortly before, a man had arrived, climbing up the hill from Gospel Oak towards me, breathless, a cigar clutched in one hand: ‘I came up here to get away from it,’ he said. ‘I got this,’ he showed me the cigar ‘to celebrate, but now… I dunno… I dunno… I can’t stand the tension.’ And so we stood together: me intrigued, him, gutted, as intelligence of the shoot-out became available on this eminence. Only much later did I understand what I had witnessed.

Claude Lévi-Strauss (who lived and thought until he was over a hundred years old, so, in common with James Lovelock, he probably knew a thing… or two) remarked that understanding frequently proceeds by what he called sacrifices of scale: abandoning the immediately sensible in favour of the intelligible. Standing on Parliament Hill that evening, I had unknowingly performed precisely such a sacrifice. At street level there were simply thousands of football supporters, each responding individually to the unfolding match; however, from the summit of the hill those countless separate experiences resolved themselves into something quite different: a single informational waveform propagating across an entire metropolis. Millions of individual nervous systems, television broadcasts, electricity networks, architecture, roads and atmospheric conditions combined to produce a phenomenon that no individual intended and no individual controlled.

The city itself had become a communications medium. Years later, searching for an adequate vocabulary with which to describe the distributed forms of causation emerging in the twenty-first century, I eventually found one. I now call them Brocken spectres, after the uncanny optical effect produced in Alpine regions, whereby a solitary individual witnesses themselves rendered gigantic in the mists. The modern Brocken spectres are thus these apparent centres of intentionality generated by the recursive interaction of countless smaller agencies, each entirely real, none individually sovereign. Montaigne observed that one should mistrust the man who takes games too seriously because he does not take life seriously enough. For centuries that seemed an unexceptionable judgment, but let’s suppose the converse has become true.

Suppose football now bears such extraordinary emotional weight precisely because it has become one of the very few arenas in which large numbers of ordinary people still experience themselves as participating directly in history. On the football pitch decisions still appear decisive, referees still possess authority, victory and defeat remain intelligible. There are identifiable protagonists, recognisable climaxes and final results. Outside the stadium, matters have become considerably stranger. While London surrendered itself once again to the rhythms of the World Cup, another contest was unfolding around the Strait of Hormuz. It too was described in the language of sovereign actors, executive decisions, victories, ceasefires and retaliation.

This language might as well be football commentary, because beneath those familiar words now lies an entirely different structure of causation—one that football, paradoxically, now helps us to perceive more clearly than politics itself. During precisely the same weeks in which England’s progress through the tournament reorganised the emotional metabolism of cities such as London, another drama unfolded in the Persian Gulf. Here too commentators spoke confidently of sovereign actors making sovereign decisions. There were strikes and counter-strikes; threats, ultimatums and retaliations; declarations that the conflict had entered a new phase, followed almost immediately by declarations that it had ended. Within a matter of days the war had apparently begun several times and concluded several times, without ever quite succeeding in becoming either war or peace. What oscillated was not merely military activity but language itself.

This continual switching-on and switching-off of hostilities is not simply diplomatic confusion, it is now symptomatic of a deeper transformation in historical causation. Classical warfare possessed recognisable temporal boundaries—wars were declared, fought and concluded; treaties ratified what armies had already achieved. The contemporary battlespace increasingly resists such periodisation: instead it resembles an electrical circuit whose current continually fluctuates without ever being fully interrupted. Sovereign actors announce decisive interventions, yet those interventions almost immediately dissolve back into the logistical systems that generated them. If one wishes to understand whether a war has truly begun, it is increasingly less useful to listen to presidents, generals or foreign ministries than to observe the behaviour of marine insurers.

Insurance premiums possess no ideological commitments, being little else than—as Schopenhauer observed—a public sacrifice on the altar of anxiety. This is because they do not applaud military victories, celebrate national honour or participate in the theatre of sovereign will, they merely calculate distributed risk. Precisely because they are indifferent to political rhetoric, they have become among the most sensitive instruments for detecting the actual structure of geopolitical reality. Hull insurance functions, in effect, as an epistemological instrument. It registers not what governments say is happening but what globally distributed logistical systems believe is happening. When underwriters abruptly increase premiums for vessels entering the Strait of Hormuz, they are not expressing an opinion. They are measuring the changing probability that the circulation of commodities may be interrupted. Risk itself has become informational.

The distinction becomes clearer if we compare the present crisis with the last occasion upon which the Strait of Hormuz genuinely ceased to function as an ordinary commercial waterway. During the so-called Tanker War, the maritime phase of the Iran-Iraq conflict between 1984 and 1988, both belligerents deliberately attacked oil tankers and merchant shipping in an effort to disrupt each other's exports and to internationalise the conflict. Hundreds of commercial vessels were damaged. Insurance premiums rose dramatically, but the decisive point came when commercial insurers increasingly found themselves unable to price the risk at all. The problem had ceased to be actuarial. It had become geopolitical. The response was correspondingly sovereign: Kuwait sought external protection for its shipping, and the United States responded by reflagging Kuwaiti tankers and escorting them through the Gulf under Operation Earnest Will.

The market had reached its limits—at precisely the point where distributed commercial risk became uninsurable, sovereign power stepped in and assumed responsibility for maintaining the circulation of oil. The distinction mattered because the war itself was recognisable. There were identifiable belligerents, declared strategic objectives, geographically bounded theatres of operation and an intelligible progression from escalation towards ceasefire. The present situation is altogether stranger: during the confrontation between Israel, Iran and the United States in June 2026, public discourse repeatedly announced that war had either begun or ended. Missiles were exchanged; American aircraft struck Iranian nuclear facilities; Iran retaliated; ceasefires were announced almost before the smoke had cleared, only for further exchanges to follow.

Commentators continually reached for the vocabulary of classical warfare, yet the events themselves stubbornly refused to conform to it. The shipping market reflected this ambiguity: hull premiums for vessels entering the Gulf rose sharply, while the cost of war-risk insurance increased still more dramatically. Yet commercial shipping did not cease, while so far the Strait of Hormuz has never formally closed. Oil, the lifeblood of accelerationist hyper-capitalism has continued to move, albeit under conditions of heightened uncertainty. What the insurance market was registering was therefore not war in the classical sense, but something more elusive: the increasing difficulty of assigning calculable probabilities within a battlespace whose boundaries, participants and temporal limits had themselves become unstable.

That distinction is more than technical: hull insurance has become one of the most sensitive instruments through which contemporary history may be observed. Politicians continue to describe events in the language of sovereignty: decisions, deterrence, retaliation, victory. Underwriters ask a different question entirely: can the circulation of commodities continue? They possess no interest in prestige, honour or national myth. They ask only whether risk remains sufficiently bounded to be priced. It is therefore often the insurance market, rather than the diplomatic communiqué, that tells us whether the underlying logistical system remains intact. This also explains why so many recent crises seem simultaneously to be wars and not wars. The sovereign drama continues to occupy the foreground, but behind it lies an infrastructural reality whose overriding imperative is continuity: oil must continue to flow.

Container ships must continue to sail. Financial settlements must continue to clear. The extraordinary achievement of the contemporary logistical order is not that it prevents conflict, but that it increasingly absorbs conflict into itself without allowing conflict to interrupt circulation for very long. We are no longer witnessing the suspension of commerce by war so much as the management of war within commerce. Mutatis mutandis, the same applies to football.

Guy Debord, the Marxist theoretician and founder of the revolutionary groupuscule, the Situationist International, argued that sports tournaments were, under late capitalism, the equivalent for the working class—who, not having achieved revolutionary class consciousness, were as yet not historic actors themselves—the illusion that they were: the year’s sporting calendar was their equivalent of the old church festivals—harvest suppers, Rogationtide etc—a zeitgeist determined for them; and, given the divinity stood outside time, a necessarily unchanging one.

It’s this that now so uncannily synchronises with the doublethink of conventional politics: Donald J Trump, the organic component of the Trump entity: the oscillator that effects hull repricing and allows for the mondial churn that keeps the Brocken spectres in play, capriciously overrules a decision in one battlespace—the football pitch—precisely because his will is ineffectual geopolitically. Under such conditions it becomes difficult to see the match, because to do so is witness the peculiar totalitarianism of our age in action. Not a totalitarianism that’s a function of sovereign will—a Hobbesian leviathan—but one made of many, many little purchasing decisions: one made of millions of tiny decisions to turn on, tune in, and drop out of history.

It’s precisely because of the existence of the distributed intentionality that in a peculiar sense I, who care not one jot or tittle for the beautiful game, can hear not only the fate of the English football team being played out as I lie awake on a hot night, but the fate of England as well.

A self-annihilating interview in today’s Telegraph shows that the bloviating entity formerly known as Toby Young is still, futilely, attempting to style himself as some sort of noble soul. But what is the spiritual realm of this lord temporal—and, one would hope, temporary? Why, only the half-lit, crepuscular realm of the web and its volatile economy of attention. This pixellated demesne is no surprise: after all, attention is what Young has always craved above all else: the title of his most famous—one hesitates to say ‘literary’—oeuvre being not only a theft of another author’s title, but an inversion of his own steely, decades long resolve precisely to win friends and influence people. Although not me, clearly.

For, as to the identity of those Lord X of Acton wishes to secure in amity, or guide in adversity, the interview provides the answer: people just like him: rich, entitled (and quite possibly titled themselves) ones, who see nothing wrong in decking themselves in the motheaten finery of a constitutional order they’re busily engaged in dismantling—not, I hasten to add, through any conscious effort on their part: I’ve known the organic element of Lord X closely enough to also become aware that he possesses the emotional intelligence, political vision, social understanding and economic grasp of the small-minded opportunist he was, is, and always will be. No: Lord X of Acton, like so many of the extreme right’s fellow travellers is a useful idiot entirely for forces that his organic component—which hides, coddled inside its screen-mediated ermine shell like a peeled egg—cannot comprehend at all.

Yes, I remember Toby Young perfectly well from the early 1990s, when he and Julie Burchill—another TERFsycorian termagant, spun by the winds of change into a dizzy incomprehension of unfolding realities—were partners in that crime against culture, The Modern Review. This was perhaps one of postmodernism’s most piffling little productions: a magazine dedicated to the proposition that if highbrows affected sufficient enthusiasm for low culture, something amusingly transgressive must be happening, when in fact all that was going on was the liquidation of critical discrimination by the market, with Toby Young and Julie Burchill bobbing about delightedly among the cultural jetsam, mistaking their own intoxicated buoyancy for navigation.

Some years ago when profiling that other useful idiot of the extreme right, I inverted Burchill’s apercu concerning Stephen Fry (namely, that he was ‘a stupid person’s idea of what an intelligent person was like’) to describe its coiner: Burchill was, I averred, what an intelligent person would be like if they spent a lifetime actively rendering themselves more stupid. I’m afraid Lord X’s organic component cannot even lay claim to this bizarre inversion of Hegelian Bildung—he’s simply a pretentious person who, with great effort, has made himself into a preposterous one; by which I mean Lord X: a puppet whose strings are manipulated by the algorithm calculating the coefficient between the mob’s regard and Toby Young’s ego—which, for him and his true believers, numinously constitutes ‘free speech’.

Now comes a reverential Telegraph interview, staged in the sun-scorched garden of his west London home, with the Cavapoochon nestled against his firm and manly thigh. Let’s hope the breed’s absurd name is a semantic prolepsis. We have another shot of Lord X standing in front of the serried volumes that index his own intellectual preeminence—at least in the eyes of his interior decorator, and the former Torygraph’s photographer. (Although the hoary old nickname will hardly do, now that the title regularly boosts the likes of Lord X, and the other fellow travellers who cluster under Nige’s capacious, if holey skirts.) Meanwhile, his rental hagiographer breathlessly… admiringly… describes his wife, a luxury travel publicist, who they can see conducting a Zoom meeting through the French windows.

As for the philoprogenitive and pedagogic Lord X’s children, they and their descendants must, we imagine, constitute an ever-burgeoning mutant piglet army, sworn to defend all that is good and true. But what’s this? Our only sighting of this emergent political formation is an exiguous figure; the interviewer tells us this is one of Young’s four children sloping home after ‘a heavy night out’: and so the entire softly-upholstered logistical integument of contemporary bourgeois life is presented to readers one presumes must be equally self-satisfied; for only such as they could accept all this ghastliness as though it were merely incidental scenery surrounding a pocket colossus in a pinstripe shirt: the Embattled Defender of an Older England. Better get that conservatory castellated, Tobes.

Lord X presumably believes that the interview will in some sense define him for those googling grandchildren whom he sees—a little mutant piglet army of his own, waiting in the woods to assail whatever glassy empyreans of insubstantiality have accreted to his name after the mediatised death that lies in store for him. It’s this that is now the proximate agon for all his grandstanding: the social media cancellation visited on him when he lost his position on the board of the Office for Students in 2018. But the whiny self-exculpation and attendant pseudo-moral elevation extends far beyond Lord X’s otiose twittering: it encompasses everyone who imagines that the attention economy constitutes some kind of posterity, rather than the endless algorithmic redistribution of a permanently receding present: a present in which they do nothing much but twitter and preen.

For Lord X’s original trauma was not simply that he lost positions and income after the excavation of his noisome Twitter archive, but that his grandchildren might Google him and encounter the caricature he claims was constructed by his enemies—but in fact was there for all right-minded people to see. Google is thus his tribunal of posterity, the search return his Last Judgment; and the Free Speech Union, which he founded in the aftermath, is the apparatus through which he continuously manufactures fresh material for that judgment—cases, controversies, enemies, victories, interviews, headlines, interventions—feeding the very web whose distortions he imagines himself to be resisting. He has mistaken the struggle to optimise his searchable identity for the defence of Western liberty. Ha-bloody-ha! It’s wonderfully postmodern!

Meanwhile, of course, the facts remain the facts—while, as the teachers in his traditionalist free school doubtless remind their pupils, good proverbialists as they are: handsome is as handsome does; and what Toby Young did was what so many people who aren’t at all handsome do: vent online, thereby revealing himself to be a misogynist and a homophobe. His self-exculpation consists in asserting—as if it were beyond dispute—that having been a journalist for thirty years, he couldn’t be expected not to have made such remarks; purely, as it were, by way of lending a little, shall we say, colour to his otherwise insipid prose. But here’s the rub of time, Toby-baby, some of your colleagues didn’t hearken to the seductive sirens of bigoted populism as sedulously as you. Moreover, some of your peers had genuine convictions which they genuinely revised; not merely adventitious postures they’ve contorted themselves into.

I wouldn’t want to look into the funhouse mirror in which you contemplate yourself—and I never have: this account is only for influencing people intellectually, Toby, not receiving the slings and arrows of what overall, in your case, has been outrageously good fortune. The Free Speech Union may perform useful work in particular cases: institutions are quite capable of behaving vindictively and disproportionately towards their employees, and the multiplication of vaguely drafted speech codes has undoubtedly provided timid managers with new instruments of coercion. But Lord X has no reasoned analysis of the machinery producing these conflicts.

This prince of the pen describes cancel culture as a ‘religion without forgiveness’, thereby converting an apparatus of accelerated accusation, counteraccusation, reputational panic and platform-mediated identity formation into a heresy conducted by uniquely wicked people who remain conveniently shadowy, so they too, in the course of time, can also be persecuted. Christianity, he claims, distinguishes the sin from the sinner; his own counter-church distinguishes only the cancelled from the cancellers, then offers the former salvation in return for an annual subscription: every little principle helps, eh. Indeed, Young describes his method with an unconscious candour bordering on the sublime: employers retreat, he says, if they believe there is going to be ‘an even scarier mob on the other side’. This is the whole man (and I use the term in this respect, advisedly) in a sentence.

The answer to the twitchy digital mob is another mob; in this instance, one professionally constituted, furnished with lawyers and regulators, flanked by Telegraph columnists and backed by 45,000 paying members. This is not an alternative to cancellation but its reversal of polarity: cancellation with professional indemnity insurance. Lord X does not, of course, do anything as reckless and foolhardy as, duh, opposethe web’s punitive dynamics; he has incorporated them, branded them and installed a direct debit. His educational project displays precisely the same intellectual poverty—which, in common with his title, he has not inherited: ‘Traditional subjects taught in a traditional way’ —this, together with his mobile phone, is his vade mecum: more kings and queens, greater teacher authority.

These are in point of fact—and I should know, having spent fourteen years up the necrotic back passage of British higher education—perfectly possible pedagogical preferences, but they constitute no account whatsoever of what digital mediation has done to attention, memory, literacy, childhood or knowledge. Lord X’s free schools are attempts to erect miniaturised real-time monastic communities within digital and logistical reality, enclaves whose apparent cultural autonomy remains financed, supplied and administered by the system they notionally exclude. He wants the classroom of 1955 while preserving the consumption, communications and property arrangements of 2026. The traditional community is staged; the Zoom call for the luxury travel company pays for—we may speculate—the electricity bill. This is why the agon with his father, which Lord X bravely recounts to his media confessor matters.

Michael Young was a socialist activator not unlike my own father, the political scientist Peter Self. But Toby Young’s dad was obviously more illustrious: he wrote the Labour Party’s historic 1945 Election Manifesto—Dad limned the urban and regional plans that would hopefully ensue. Nevertheless, both men were formed by those institutions that arose from the postwar settlement—in particular from Butskellism, that conflation of left and right within the transcendent English constitutional arrangement which Toby now affects to despise, although he owes to it not merely his education and opportunities but his very intelligibility as a public person. Yes: the father attempted to construct institutions such as the Open University, ones capable of extending participation in a common culture; the son constructs defensive enclaves within its ruins.

Michael Young coined ‘meritocracy’ as a warning about a society in which successful people would redescribe inherited and structural advantage as personal desert. Young fils’s career has fulfilled the satire with almost indecent exactitude: the privileged son who performed failure, converted failure into celebrity, converted disgrace into victimhood, converted victimhood into an organisation, and converted that organisation into a peerage—while continuing to present himself as a dissident beyond the perimeter fence. Then there is the transgender fixation, without which no contemporary Dick-o-graph profile can apparently attain tumescence.

The article identifies a university employee as transgender although her gender has no bearing upon the alleged offence, before moving rapidly through Graham Linehan (another furious social media-addict), female-only spaces, LGBT education and the remarkable claim that 37 per cent of the FSU’s caseload concerns sex and gender. Transgender people must perform—if you’ll forgive the figuration—the double office allotted to every culture-war scapegoat: they are numerically infinitesimal but civilisationally omnipotent, a minuscule minority somehow capable of occupying an enormous proportion of Young’s political imagination; an imagination that must, indeed, be the same size as the changing room these male transphobics, together with their embattled womenfolk, are forever cowering in.

If only they’d look in the real mirrors on the walls of this imaginary changing room they’d see what contemprary women really fear: them—cis-men, the historic and perenduring rapists par excellence. So, Lord X’s statistics establish far less than he thinks—which, as we’ve observed, isn’t much. An organisation publicly identified with gender-critical cases naturally attracts people involved in gender-critical disputes; its self-selected caseload cannot be treated as a disinterested survey of national persecution. We are given no coding method, no independent verification, no account of the cases rejected and no explanation of how Young knows that the women concerned ‘mostly identify as Left-wing’. Their presumed leftism then becomes evidence of his neutrality, as though the presence of defectors from the opposing army proved that no war was being fought.

The passing declaration that Young has been a Zionist since he was seventeen is more revealing for the absence it creates than for the allegiance itself. It enters the interview only as evidence of his magnanimity: despite being a Zionist and disapproving of Palestine Action, he will defend someone prosecuted for displaying support for it. Yet the interviewer never asks what his Zionism entails—what he believes about ethno-nationalism, sovereignty, Jewish self-determination, Palestinian self-determination, or whether the ethnic principle he accepts in Israel has any analogue in his conception of Britain. Gender identity must undergo ceaseless metaphysical examination; this immensely consequential political identity is permitted to appear as a charming biographical constant, adopted at seventeen and apparently requiring no subsequent thought.

Zionism supplies the hard spine of Young’s politics while the interview treats it as a buttonhole. One wonders where his father stood on Israel. Young concludes by paraphrasing Andy Warhol: in the future, everyone will be cancelled for fifteen minutes. He does not perceive that universal fame and universal cancellation have already become the same condition. Cancellation is one of the principal means by which public personalities reproduce their visibility; indignation becomes attention, attention becomes membership, membership becomes institutional power, and institutional power becomes a seat in the Lords. Lord X, on receiving the coronet upon his noble and very middle brow, has not preserved an older public world against this machinery, because he cannot see anything outside it. He is mind-child and man-child of an England that cannot assimilate the web-world and therefore mistakes frantic activity within it for resistance to it.

Acton may be his territorial designation, but the web is his true peerage: Lord X of the Counter-Mob, Baron of the Search Return, standing nowhere athwart history, and twittering constantly ‘Stop the world!’, while sitting comfortably in the business-class lounge of the attention economy—just as he no doubt does in business class once airborne, complaining without cease about the other passengers. The spectacle would be amusing—especially to those of us who recall his Lilliputian grandstanding of old—were it not that Lord X of Acton and his ilk, with every flap of their lips, bring this floating isle of ours, this Laputa of once-lapidary minds, closer to the parched earth of civilisational ruin. His father helped build a society. Toby Young has spent years playing with it. Soon it will be broken altogether, while Lord X and the other aristocrats of egotism stand there staring at the shit they and the rest of us are in.

No British filmgoer—or, indeed, film fan throughout the world—can be in any doubt that the visual spectacular of 2026 is Andy Burnham’s The Labour Odyssey, a vastly expensive production filmed for the first time in the British IMAXimised Imagination. This will, its director hopes, make plausible the myth of soft, woolly, worsted, socialist, cuddly inclusion, and thereby convert an Industrial Age epic struggle into a summer popcorn movie that everybody can compulsively truffle up while ignoring the reality of… I dunno: the ongoing war, the climate emergency, the rise of machines that easily outthink political imaginations remaining in a reverie of the recent past.

Like Christopher Nolan, the organic component of the Burnham (Starmer) entity—who we must, perforce, call ‘Andy’—has aimed above all to provide a spectacle mediated not merely by computer-generated effects, but by physical presences imbued with emotional sincerity, regional authenticity and wounded decency—the warm, fibrous stuff of solidarity, one afforded British government by mano-a-mano warfare and contact football alike. Nolan’s imaginative vision required 5,300 costumes, six countries, ninety-one days’ filming and a 35-foot Trojan Horse weighing 8,000 pounds to make the very Ur-text of the Western Logos appear even remotely plausible to today’s cinema-going illiterates. Andy has had to make do with Westminster, a red tie and the unreconstructed personnel of the Starmer administration.

Inside his own beached horse are crammed John Healey, Ed Miliband, Shabana Mahmood, Louise Haigh, Angela Rayner, Dame Angela Eagle, Matthew Pennycook and—struggling to keep his own empty, wooden head above the water being pumped into the hollow prop—Wes ‘down your’ Streeting. Thus the Burnham (Starmer) entity’s production triumphantly achieves the same effect as Nolan’s: you’ve all superficially heard the story of the horse—but have you heard it from the inside, deep inside? The crucial difference between The Odyssey, and The Labour Odyssey, is that nob-head Nolan packed his contraption with Greek warriors armed not just with swords and spears, but a common and executable plan of action. In stark contrast, the immense and creakily ageing apparatus of the Burnham (Starmer) entity’s political end-of-the-pier production is required to persuade us that the figures packed its wooden cabinet are even aware of a common destination.

Frankly, I don’t blame them: it would take a harder man than I to cope with being part of a human sandwich constituted by these distinctly unappetising, fatty ingredients. Sadly… predictably, the British right has failed altogether to appreciate the wondrous Labour Odyssey. Y’know, sometimes I just think they don’t really want to be entertained! Because rather than receive this divine dithyramb for what it is, their purblind commentariat refuses the spectacle in favour of football as a master narrative: Andy is a character in a 1970s comic strip: the doughty but dumb manager of a failing side, who has simply swapped the positions of the same old players, then sent them out for what—given the country has seen seven premiers in a decade—can only be figured as the second half.

Presumably the win against France means Britain is now content to imagine itself neither punching above its weight, nor volleying fantastic goals on the world stage, but putting in a respectable performance and finishing runner-up. Yet neither the Bronze Age epic nor the footballing analogy survives contact with the hard realities of governing Britain in 2026. The manager no longer possesses the game: the fixture list, broadcasting rights, betting markets, security cordons, data systems, fiscal constraints and geopolitical exposures have constituted the match before he ever chooses his formation. In recent years, every incoming British Prime Minister has looked—like a canny hotel guest—to tip the electorate immediately, given they’re only too aware of their colleagues’ incapacity to provide anything like good customer service.

The abolition of VAT on household energy bills was a perfect miniature of what to expect from the remodelled entity’s sovereignty. Here, on Andy’s first day, was the sovereign act itself: a tax removed by command of the new leader, relief delivered to the household, the warm puffa jacket of government gently draped around the shoulders of the ageing voters of that embiggened Makerfield which is the Burnham (Starmer) entity’s true heartland—and its bigoted Achilles’ heel. For, strange to relate, the money was to be found by abolishing expenditure the previous administration had announced but, duh!, never funded. The Burnham (Starmer) entity has financed an actual tax remission with the cancellation of a counterfactual expenditure: seeming intentionality was here being paid for out of failed intentionality.

Badenoch and Jenrick may be right about the arithmetic, but their larger presumption—that exposing the trick will cause sovereign government to reappear—is as fatuous as the new entity’s gesture. It’s been a blow for Andy, obviously, but it must also be acknowledged that it was sustained by a warrior hunched inside a prop-horse on a foreign shore, that is itself being speedily washed away and replaced by an overseas infrastructure fund. Poor old Andy, he’s been cast by his directorial entity as the wily hero of The Odyssey; now, before the title sequence has finished, he’s discovering that the new administration is more likely, in filmic terms, to resemble a Wallace and Gromit production, animated in stop-motion using plasticine figures of politicians.

The jolly little Russian warship that bobbed along in the Channel then opened fire forty nautical miles south of Plymouth, supplies the charming anachronism required by the genre: a sinister naval presence drifting into English wateriness from some earlier, harder-edged sovereign melodrama. It looks bad, but hey, it’s perfectly consonant with the Burnham (Starmer) entity’s own mouldable conception of the people’s will. Caught up in his new role as Wallace (it’s hard to smile winningly when you’ve got a sleeveless Fair Isle woolly wrapped round your plasticine mush), Andy contemplates turning Gromit on the Russian warship: in the form of sanctioned tankers, insurance arrangements, naval escorts, Royal Marine seizures, surveillance aircraft, and warning shots in the form of many rounds of Babybel. But the very cosiness of the imagery discloses the stark situation it’s intended to swaddle.

I’ve stated this uncomfy fact in earlier SITREPS, ones not directed by Nick Park (Cartoonist of the British Empire); namely: that the Russian frigate’s very real and rigid guns did not announce the possibility of war; they made audible the war already under way. The battlespace through which this war is being waged, runs through the Channel, along tanker routes, across maritime-insurance markets, through satellite constellations, sanctions databases, flags of convenience, ports, undersea cables and financial clearing systems. To interpret the exercise simply as Vladimir Putin (the organic element of the Putin entity) ‘challenging’ a new prime minister, is to end the charming, animated film and restore the summer blockbuster: Vlad-the-Impaler threatens—lion-hearted Andy must respond. The reality is less box office and far more terrifying: neither actor truly plays the role whose momentary facial expression he supplies.

Christopher Nolan may make much of the fact that he personally doesn’t have a mobile phone or an email address, but the fact of the matter is that his vast cinematic productions require all the technological apparatus of modernity—the international travel, plant, the filming equipment, the machine intelligences coordinating the whole circus—and therefore his drama replicates precisely that hubris which was so central to the Ancient Greek conception of human tragedy. For, the invisible constraints these economically operationalised logistical systems impose on human intentionality foreclose on historical causation quite as much as they do visual imagination, thereby transforming the bloody flux of contemporary politics into an entertainment that can be safely watched throughout Britain’s air-conditioned multiplexes.

At least until the electricity bill falls due—alright, it’ll be 5% less, but who would’ve thought all those optimistically optimised cameras used quite so much? And then there is Wes Streeting, an unusually squishy little Plasticine figure whom we have already described as doom-scrolling his own popularity ratings for what feels like many years. (To him.) Streeting is precisely the appointment through which the Burnham (Starmer) entity’s failure to understand the vitiation of intentionality by bidirectional digital media ceases to be merely foolish and becomes absurd. Defence is the department in which the sovereign conceit—that the minister intends, commands and obtains—is least plausible.

Its nominal head presides over procurement chains, satellite systems, autonomous platforms, software dependencies, private contractors, intelligence-sharing agreements, American export permissions and weapons containing components manufactured across multiple jurisdictions by corporations with valuations exceeding the GDP of medium-sized countries, and not far off that of, gulp, Blighty. Streeting is emotionally and performatively equipped to wear a sleeveless woolly and cut up bits of Cheddar for tea but unfitted by handyman Wallace in the brain-box department, so wholly unable to see the entity of which ‘the Ministry of Defence’ is merely a disguise. The organic component of the newly moulded Defence Minister can be briefed on capabilities, deployments and readiness; it cannot apprehend the distributed intentionality of the logistical formation it has been installed to personify.

Streeting’s characteristic skills—rhetorical velocity, conspicuous responsiveness, personal visibility and rapid repositioning (easy enough if you’re squishy)—are themselves products of the mediatized environment that makes executive agency increasingly fictitious. When you stop believing that comfort food can ever really comfort you, you’ll see that the fictious nature of British sovereignty in June, 2026, lies in the relationship between the Magnificent Seven’s market capitalisation, the empty aspiration to create ‘AI sovereignty’, and the Trump entity’s oscillating conviction that Britain—like the British Army’s establishment—remains interoperable with the American military-industrial complex.

Britain’s defence policy, foreign policy and domestic policy cannot be disarticulated like a yummy roast chicken, because the same computational systems that allocate hospital beds and theatre time also order military supplies, analyse intelligence, police borders and determine what ministers are able to perceive as reality, given they aren’t big readers. I mean, I know he likes a little Alan Hollinghurst of an evening, but no line of beauty is going to lassoo you and pull you out of this quicksand, Andy. Hence the argument over Palantir. The Burnham (Starmer) entity’s left imagines that national intentionality might be recovered by cancelling a contract with an ideologically contaminated American corporation and procuring a clean British substitute. Sir Jeremy Fleming calls instead for British champions, British resilience and British control, before conceding that complete sovereignty is not really an option.

The concession, Jerry-baby, abolishes the proposition—so get back in your Chubb-armoured Silver Cross pram. A British Palantir would not necessarily constitute British sovereignty; it might—no! Scratch that: will merely be a domestically incorporated node in the same transnational computational formation, using American chips, American cloud architecture, American capital and American security protocols while presenting a Union Jack on its user interface, to much the same effect as Union Jack livery on a Mini-bloody-Countryman. Meanwhile, the growing capability of Chinese open-weight AI models casts an eldritch glow over all this futile filmic posturing. If powerful models can be downloaded, distilled, adapted and deployed at a fraction of the cost of their closed American equivalents, Britain cannot obtain sovereignty merely by choosing its favoured contractor.

But the American response—export bans, pre-release inspections, blacklists and warnings about Chinese models—is inseparable from the commercial interests of companies whose immense valuations depend upon preserving a capital-intensive closed-model dispensation. AI safety, national security and regulatory capture begin to resemble not competing explanations but different views of the same logistical process which, since it’s deemed a priori to be unstoppable, cannot by that fact alone be controlled... The incoming administration therefore confronts an impossible task: it cannot govern without AI-mediated logistical systems; it cannot safely entrust those systems to American corporations; it cannot manufacture technological sovereignty by buying British substitutes; and it cannot exclude cheap Chinese open models without further entrenching American corporate power.

Nor can it regulate the field through ordinary ministerial intentionality, because the permanent officials, parliamentary committees, technical advisers, security-cleared contractors and commercial actors through whom regulation must pass are themselves technologically dependent and commercially penetrated: so many dumb actors, hunched up in the horse, and waiting for Andysseus to give them their lines. However, he reaches for the levers of power to open the horse’s hatch, only to discover they are graphical representations of operations occurring elsewhere! Such a shame: he wanted to make a real film, with a real cast, not these oxymorons. Still, the show must go on: amplified music was prohibited around Number 10, lest some grimy rhythm dubstep its way into the solemn transfer of vapid intentionality.

The Starmer entity’s organic component entered the constitutional mechanism; the organic component of the new Burnham (Starmer) entity travelled to Buck House for its audience with Chucky III, then returned to Downing Street as if contact with the monarchical film franchise had completed the circuit and charged the new administration with sovereign current. Britain’s constitution is commonly represented by Big Ben, but Big Ben only tells the time; the cuckoo clock tells the truth. Its Gothic little house contains the monarch, the prime minister, the Cabinet, the opposition, Black Rod and all the carved and painted figures who emerge in sequence to strike their appointed attitudes. One organic component withdraws into the clock; another pops out, bows to Chucky III, announces the hour and is acclaimed as the motive force of the mechanism. This happens now—as I’ve observed above—with such regularity, why, you could set your iWatch by it.

Or could, if it weren’t a graphical representation as well. Because the cuckoo clock isn’t just an image: it’s obsolete. Behind it—and passing straight through the wall on which it hangs for a year or five waiting to chime—the real machinery of government runs continuously: data centres, fibre-optic cables, satellites, financial markets, procurement platforms, cloud services, shipping routes, insurance syndicates and military interoperability agreements. These systems neither recognise the accession nor hear the clock strike. They do not applaud the Burnham (Starmer) entity, oppose it or wish it success. They simply operationalise whatever can pass through them. At the appointed hour the little door opens. Andy comes out, warm, woolly and woundedly decent, to tell us what time it is in his quaint, going-to-get-a-loaf-of-Hovis accents.

Behind him, unheard, the machinery has already set all the clocks, and they’re running far, far faster than even Nick Park could animate them.

Originally published as SITREP No. 020 on X on 21 July 2026. Read the original on X.
