Among Jordan Peterson’s self-styled ‘12 Rules for Life’ is his notorious injunction to set your house in perfect order before criticising the world. What a house constitutes, quite as much as a rule, can vary. I well remember asking one of my younger acquaintances why he was having his child baptised as a Catholic, given he himself manifestly didn’t believe in the Ten Commandments; he thought for a fraction of a second, before replying by channelling Ireland’s most famous spiritual leader, the hebephrenic Father Dougal: ‘They’re just guidelines.’ Given the creator of the show in which this moral latitudinarianism was proposed—and one may assume the writer of these lines—has gone on to be a social media addict, and a crazed bigot, it would seem Grahan Lineham, at least, is no hypocrite.

But the Daily Telegraph should know: it’s been drifting progressively rightwards for years now, tacking into anfractuous and emphatically non-ideological waters, there to cruise about, all its paper sails set, so as to pick up whatever available afflatus there is—racist zephyrs, transphobic gusts, misogynist mistrals, even fascistic fohns—that might be required so as to propel its shareholders into a beneficent future of ‘adaptation’ to our warming world. So it’s no surprise that under its new German proprietor and with jejeune Associate Comment Editor Harry Howard apparently officiating, this Fighting Temeraire of journalism has invited the Canadian psychologist to set the atmosphere in order for us. Peterson’s article, ‘Climate change catastrophism is a Leftist weapon to destroy capitalism’, begins with air conditioning.

This is appropriate, as air conditioning is the perfect technology for Petersonian man: it preserves his personal climatic envelope while warming everybody else’s. Inside, the upstanding patriarch remains cool, dry and potently individuated; outside, the machinery emits the heat—and hopefully the stench—it’s extracted from his immediate surroundings. Never mind that the electricity powering the dinkus has to be generated somewhere, or that the refrigerants may themselves be potent greenhouse gases. The significant question is: who dares lay a hand on Jordan’s thermostat? Titter-ye-not: this is what the climate emergency has come down to, Peterson says: ‘something as personal as home or workplace temperature’ being subjected—pass the ammunition, the revolution begins here!—to state regulation.

Setting aside the fact that I, personally—as well as many millions of others—would rather the Earth’s thermostat wasn’t dialled way up—one might say much the same about the lavatory, the kitchen, the fuse box and the bedroom. I mean, no one wants the state interfering with these spaces and their intimacies, do they? So, let’s follow Peterson’s Rule and rescind regulations against human waste being discharged into the water supply; abolish dumb rules that stop rats being served for dinner; cancel safety codes preventing lethal wiring from installation in nurseries—and while we’re at it, both legal and moral prohibitions on children being employed for sexual purposes. Now, that’s what Jordan—in common with, say, Jimmy Savile—presumably calls political freedom.

The distinction between the personal and the political is not a law of nature, Jordan—not that you’re a conspicuous believer in those rules, either, especially the Second One of thermodynamics. Rather, it’s an ever-permeable barrier: an always provisional settlement devised by human societies to prevent the exercise of one person’s freedom from becoming another’s electrocution, poisoning or death. Listen I sympathise: there you are, a perfectly respectable academic, working on a subject so diffuse—personality—it can hardly condense into power. You work systematically, to produce serious empirical research, thereby acquiring a clinical practice… Then, little by little—the normalcy of this creeping up on you—you persuade yourself that the patterns you've discerned in individuals can be scaled up… and up… to explain not just, say, the large corporates other clin’ psychs shill for, but entire civilisations! Jungian archetypes!

Biblical symbolism! Evolutionary psychology! Political controversy! Everything begins to arrange itself into a single explanatory mosaic—it’s vaunting thought, always the telltale sign of equally vaunting ambition. And before long, every passing dispute appears as another skirmish in an eternal battle between Order and Chaos, which is why what’s needed is someone to tell Chaos to tidy up its concupiscent bedroom… Then destiny arrives in its most self-confirmatory form: celebrity. But Peterson should remember André Malraux’s aperçu, given the Frenchman knew a thing or two about both fame and political power: ‘The worst thing about death is that it turns life into destiny.’ Not the other way round, Jordan. So, the now notorious Peterson does all the podcasts and the lecture tours; he works those socials big time, so entrains millions of followers; he accepts the invitations into the antechambers of power.

Before long he’s mano a mano with Viktor Orbán, and Benjamin Netanyahu, exchanging ideas with leaders who increasingly regard him, he hopes, less as a psychologist than as an ally. This is now, he feels, his destiny, because the temptation is no longer simply to interpret events but to become an actor within them—and Jordan, being an expert in personality, is adept when it comes to donning the persona, or tragicomic mask of Ancient Greek drama. I mean, how could he resist being an icon wearing a mask? Like so many distal members of the Trump entity, Peterson has been caught by a new oscillation: the shifting relation between thought and sovereign power. Once the intellectual’s task was to scrutinise power from an awkward distance; now the rewards lie in synchronising oneself with its real-time deformations.

At that point the psychologist risks becoming less an observer of personality than a fame-junky in search of history—reading every event as confirmation of the grand narrative that has, by happy coincidence, also become the engine of his own success. In the Telegraph essay, Peterson’s supposed subject is climate science, but his real agon is restraint: he cannot bear it in any way, shape or form; while the notion that the exercise of a personal preference might have cumulative consequences is, for him, not merely disagreeable but unthinkable. If what we drive, eat, burn and cool contributes to atmospheric heating, he asks, ‘what freedoms can possibly remain?’ Quite a few, Jordan: the freedom to walk, the freedom to enjoy beauty, the freedom to speak, associate, and participate politically; the freedom to eat less meat, or not fly, Jordan—because surely, there’s a right not to consume?

Even the freedom to live amid other people without confusing every limitation upon appetite with castration is a freedom to be devoutly desired, because without it social existence of any sort at all is, to adopt a somewhat redundant idiom, unsustainable. Then there’s the freedom, even, to accept that you cannot have everything you want merely because someone can devise a machine that supplies it—a machine that in a sense manufactures the desire by manufacturing its object, such is the on-demand nature of contemporary consumer capitalism. So it goes—and Peterson has been pogoing around the world for years now on the steadily diminishing priapism of Western patriarchy, making ready cash dispensing advice to anxious young men—the sort formerly available from gym masters, scout leaders and the better class of provincial barber: stand up straight, tidy your room, marry a woman who was born with a vagina and stop whining.

And by the way, sir, would you like something for the weekend? Sure, as long as it isn’t a copy of the Telegraph: I don’t need to read adverts for Viagra just yet. The erection difficulty is obviously a speculation on my part. I possess no intelligence concerning the present condition of Peterson’s penis, nor do I wish you to approach me if you’ve been his whistleblower, because what concerns me is the libido of his thought: hierarchy as tumescence, division as penetration, the entire social order arranged so that somebody is always on top and somebody else supplies the hole. Drill, Jordan, drill! Peterson’s own difficulties deserve more compassion than his public philosophy generally extends to others. But he won’t get it here. He developed a severe physical dependence upon prescribed benzodiazepines, and in 2020 travelled to Russia for an extraordinarily hazardous detoxification involving a medically induced coma.

Illness and dependence are not contemptible; I know rather too much about both, um, personally, to suggest they are. But great hilarity, as well as bleak incongruity, is present in the spectacle of the prince of self-mastery outsourcing consciousness itself to a Russian anaesthetist. The man who commands the young to impose order upon chaos had to have his mighty brain switched off while chaos was extracted from his bloodstream. Just to give a comparator: I had an allogenic stem cell transplant for secondary myelofibrosis in 2024, a procedure the mortal odds for which were equivalent to playing Russian roulette with a five-chambered revolver. Chronic nausea, pain, acute discomfort, insomnia and anxiety led to dependence on benzodiazepeines and opiates while hospitalised. Once home, and settled, I detoxed in a few weeks, albeit with considerable discomfort, but no Russians save an illuminating reading of ‘War and Peace’.

Since his own detox, my fellow recovering addict has suffered further serious ill health. He’s the same age as me: 64. It therefore occurs to me that among his twelve rules—and the twelve further rules he produced after those, funny that—one remains conspicuously absent; and it’s one he could well do with understanding properly himself: learn how to die. I wouldn’t claim to be a past master at it yet—only time will tell—but my experience of severe ill-health hasn’t been to sublimate my fear of death into an absurd form of faith. Because that’s what the denial of anthropogenic climate change is: a new credo with absolutely no factual basis whatsoever; a revealed religion of nothing but rich people’s and wannabe rich people’s ressentiment. In a way, climate change denial is a metaphor, the metaphrand for which would have to be a flower that never lost its petals.

And it’s this eternal metaphrand that Peterson and all others of his ilk, clutch to their withering bosoms. To them, restraint is anathema, because to say goodbye to anything is to die a little, while they’re so little themselves, such a diminutive death would altogether annihilate them. But I’m not suggesting you kill yourself, Jordan—or despair or surrender to fatalism. Learning how to die is confronting the fact right now that one day (in yours and my case, one day fairly soon in all likelihood), without your agreement and at a moment you cannot choose, the world will continue without you—which means other puckish Canadian clinical psychologists will have your followers, and quite possibly be tidying up your room. But if you don’t confront this plenipotent reality, you’ll never even attain a scintilla of moral seriousness either. Why?

Because only scrupulous attention to the ethical realm discloses the difference between restraint and extinction. It is precisely the person who cannot imagine his own ending who experiences every curtailment of appetite as a little death—and consequently insists upon the endless continuation of every little thing that sustains him, however destructive it may be to everybody else. Peterson’s refusal of climate science proceeds from this ethical incapacity. He does not deny that atmospheric carbon dioxide has risen; he does not quite deny that human activity has caused the warming; instead he suspends the observed increase inside a vaguely specified ‘epoch of natural warming’, as if the planet were turning within some immense geophysical gyre whose rotations conveniently absolve the internal combustion engine of any wrongdoing.

This conceit (it cannot be deemed a theory) is a wheel within a wheel: Peterson’s head gyroscopically mounted inside another gyroscope, thereby preserving its ideological orientation, however violently the physical world moves around it. Climate is too complex, he says, for anthropogenic causation to be disentangled from natural variability without models. However, by pleasing contrast—since it yields such a rich, explanatory-cum-financial dividend—the politics of climate is miraculously simple! According to Jordan, a single documentary made by that consummate influencer, Al Gore, in 2006 explains the convictions of millions, the policies of hundreds of governments and perhaps $10–15 trillion of expenditure. You get the picture formed by the Rorschach blot, Jordan: incomprehensible complexity for atmospheric physics; pellucid monocausality for everything else!

The scientific position is considerably less addled, which goes a long way towards explaining why you don’t, personally, adopt it. Human activities, principally the emission of greenhouse gases, have unequivocally caused global warming. The best estimate is not that humans caused ‘most’ of the increase—as Peterson asserts, and the Telegraph implicitly endorses—but that they caused all the net long-term warming observed since the nineteenth century. Natural variations continue: El Niño, La Niña, volcanic activity and solar fluctuations modulate individual years and regions; however not a single sainted scientific member of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) believes they explain the sustained accumulation of heat in the oceans, the warming lower atmosphere and cooling stratosphere, the retreat of glaciers, the rise in sea level or the fossil-carbon signature of the additional CO₂.

The untidy room is emphatically not caused by staring at it through blurred spectacles. Because this is not merely the opinion of a majority: the IPCC’s assessment—produced by 234 scientists from 65 countries, and drawing on more than 14,000 scientific papers, while also being subjected to 78,007 expert and governmental review comments—is the most comprehensive and exactingly reviewed statement of physical climate knowledge available. Perhaps Jordan—and Harry—should actually parse it: it makes for sobering reading, which in turn encourages restraint, duh. The Report finds unequivocally that human influence has warmed the atmosphere, “sigh”; the ocean, “glug”; and the land, “snuff”.

There exists no credible body of climate science in which Peterson’s miscellaneous natural causes constitute a rival explanation: only isolated dissenters whose possession of scientific credentials cannot confer evidential standing upon claims the evidence itself has excluded: all they do is summon a false mob to oppose them—false, both because it’s a straw man argument in the first place, and also because the real body of cod-environmentalist keyboard-warriors it calls forth are in equally if opposite bad faith to Peterson. Nice: two armies equipped with helmets made from tin foil. Nor does the Medieval Warm Period offer an alternative baseline, as Peterson suggests. It was neither globally synchronous nor an instrumental period that can simply be substituted for 1850–1900.

This is not abstruse: one cannot assess the Earth’s feverishness by hearing an anecdote about how warm the Mondial patient felt eight centuries before the thermometer was inserted into its rectum in the form of a deep-bore geology core-sampler. Ouch. Being Jungian-adjacent, I’m not at all surprised, that hierophantic Jordan fixates on the Mediaeval Warm Period. It sounds archetypal, doesn’t it? I mean, it sounds old, that’s the mediaeval bit; it sounds warm—and everyone likes warm. At least they used to: if only the Period could’ve continued indefinitely, together with its happily organic social relations, and its instinctive—because morally-mandated by Big Daddy—patriarchal ideology.

But tin-foil-helmed Peterson’s strongest ‘evidence’ is another phenomenon with a suggestion of the ancient and the archetypal: ‘global greening.’ It’s also the clearest demonstration of his confabulating obscurity; for, while satellite observations do indeed show a substantial increase in leaf area since the early 1980s, and a major study attributed about 70 per cent of the trend to CO₂ fertilisation, this shouldn’t surprise anyone—even Jordan, as he slumps sleepily to the fridge to get the necessary for another sandwich—since carbon dioxide is plant food; so much so that many plants photosynthesise more efficiently when given more of it, just as more sandwiches make Jordan pontificate…more. Commercial greenhouses therefore enrich their atmosphere with CO₂: it’s—if you’ll forgive the allusion—effective. A greenhouse, however, also regulates water, temperature, nutrients, pests and humidity.

Clearly, the increasingly muggy atmosphere does not: far from regulating anything in particular at a particular time, it changes everything at once: heat sears crops above specific thresholds; drought throttles growth; excessive rainfall inundates roots; fires scorch vegetation; elevated CO₂ can leech the protein, iron and zinc from staple foods, not just celeriac; and plants themselves may transpire more water in aggregate, because there are more leaves doing the transpiring; thereby adding a lot more mugginess—or global sweat, as I prefer to think of it—to humanity’s changing room. Mind where you flick that jockstrap, Jordan!

‘Greening’ describes an optical measurement of leaf area; to seize on this as evidence of increased biodiversity, secure water supplies, nutritious crops or stable ecosystems takes purblindedness, it pains me to say, into the realms of a ‘personality disorder’, which is presumably the sort of epithetic psychiatry Peterson would like to avoid having practiced on him. This does, of necessity, make the whole Russian induced-coma-Xanax-clucking-avoidance look even more perverse—almost risqué; but, hey, let’s not get carried away: I once stayed in a friend of my wife’s parents’ miniature villa, wedged on to a hillside opposite Porquerolles on the French Riviera.

If you think this sounds glamorous, you’re as credulous as Jordan: we’re talking the Sunbelt stretched and attenuated until it’s a sort of retirement garotte: our infinitesimal chateau had an entirely artificial garden, but not like Des Esseintes’ in Huysmanns’ Á Rebours (the decadent novel that’s seduced many a pretty Dorian such as yourself , Jordie-baby, with the decaying perfume of immortality’s dead-on-arrival dream), but a tablecloth-sized bit of Astroturf, surrounded by plastic plants implanted in macadamised mini-berms the like of which seemed the stuff of nightmarish miniature funerary rites envisaged by some mutant Edgar Allen Poe… …All of which is by way of saying, you poor Romantic consumptive fool, willing the entire world on to your sick denial of death: to infer a healthy biosphere from greater leaf area is the vegetable equivalent of mistaking a feverish consumptive’s flush for rude health.

Peterson employs the ‘fact’ of growing agricultural production in the same fanciful way. Yields have, in point of fact, risen spectacularly during the period of anthropogenic warming; therefore, he implies, warming has benefited agriculture. But yields also rose because of plant breeding, fertiliser, irrigation, pesticides, mechanisation, refrigeration, international trade and the expansion of cultivated land. The relevant comparison is not between agriculture now and agriculture in 1960; it’s between the food produced now and the food that would have been produced using the same technology without the additional climatic stress. On that comparison, climate change has already considerably—if not exactly quantifiably—slowed the growth of agricultural productivity.

But anyway, any counterfactual at all that isn’t summoned simply and clearly to emphasise the reality of the situation, is by that by summoning alone able to elicit denial concerning that very reality. There’s nothing paradoxical about this at all—as any remotely competent clinical psychologist could tell you—given the historical counterfactual simply scales up wishful thinking to a civilisational level. The climate has not prevented every harvest—so Peterson declares crop failure a fantasy; the patient has not died—therefore putting them in a coma has worked! The same pollyannaish prestidigitation governs Peterson’s attack upon Gore.

Gore always struck me as a tool in an empirical not a satirical way; so I was pleasantly surprised by his percipience on the climate emergency; be that as it may, he made crass errors, notably his 2009 Nostradamus-alike prediction that the Arctic might be effectively ice-free in summer within five to seven years. As for An Inconvenient Truth’s bruiting of a possible 20-foot sea-level rise, while this did give an accurate order of magnitude for the loss of a major ice sheet, it left the timescale in this instance impressionistically vague. This is where the toolishness showed: anyone who views their own being as intrinsically a component of large-scale social and economic processes which appear to them as inexorable, has, by the fact alone, surrendered themselves to the very abnegation of intentionality they would require to address the dread phenomenon.

Gore left the vice-presidency worth less than $2 million and is now estimated to possess between $300 million and $500 million—at 78, Al-baby, you’ll have to spunk-off fast on a load of Gucci loafers to really feel you’ve earned it. His fortune derives chiefly from his partnership in Generation Investment Management, early and exceptionally lucrative Apple share options, and the roughly $100-million gross proceeds attributed to his stake in Current TV, supplemented by venture-capital investments, speaking fees, books and films. Wealth on this scale is not a thing or things in any meaningful sense, but a system that must be continually reproduced: by global capital flows, data centres, telecommunications networks, energy-intensive computation, mineral extraction and the ceaseless manufacture, distribution and replacement of technological goods.

Gore is therefore no longer merely an environmentalist compromised by personal extravagance; he has become a node in the very logistical entity whose expansion is driving the emergency he deplores: in a compound word, a technotool. His fortune can be consistently regenerated only by operationalising a future that is more technologically dependent, more materially extractive and more energetically voracious than the present. The contradiction is not that Gore preaches restraint while privately consuming too much, but that his environmental authority and his immense private wealth now arise from opposite descriptions of the same future: one publicly condemned as ecologically insupportable, the other privately owned as a growth prospect.

Be that as it may be, a failed deadline may be evidence of bipolar, but it doesn’t reverse a physical trend, and you don’t have to be a climate scientist to know with certainty Arctic summer sea ice has declined drastically: just call someone in Baffin-bloody-Bay, and they’ll tell you: ‘“Glug-glug-glug” sea levels are rising…’ And along with this, ocean heat is accumulating, heat extremes are intensifying, glaciers and ice sheets are losing mass. To move from ‘Al Gore exaggerated certain claims’ to ‘anthropogenic warming is a Leftist plot’ is like dismissing lung cancer because an anti-smoking advertisement misstated the date upon which a particular smoker would die. It’s defective reasoning—not an argument at all.

Then comes the truly comic causal inflation: Gore’s film, Peterson tells us, transformed environmental concern into partisan dogma, compromised the authority of science, demoralised a generation, crippled energy production and caused trillions to be squandered. These claims are presented more or less sans phrase, in marked contrast to the evidential demands Peterson has just imposed upon climatology. Evidently the atmospheric effect of billions of tonnes of carbon requires exquisite modelling, while the psychological effect of one American politician’s slide show can simply be intuited by a Canadian psychologist. Way to go, Jordan—and I wish you would. But before you amscray, let’s consider a potential Rule 13—if you can monetise this as effectively as the other twelve, you won’t need to worry about footing the bill for the next deep sleep.

Personally, although I suffer not so much from insomnia, as experience every night the hard truth that Somnia has left the building altogether, my settled policy remains: I’ll sleep when I’m dead. In the meantime, how about this for a new rule: when several facts inconvenience your argument, put them in a sack together and beat Naomi Klein—or any available leftist—with it. Klein appears in the Jordanian inner-space, because he requires the climate emergency to be a Left-wing conspiracy to allow him to turn up his air con’ while maintaining his conception of a—don’t laugh—clean conscience. If she wants degrowth, public ownership and redistribution, then the physical phenomenon must have been fabricated to produce those preferred remedies by driving good, honest hardworking people into a Mondial tizzy.

This is equivalent to saying that because a dietician recommends taking off a few pounds, the patient must have been hypnotised into believing they’re coated with a thick slather of avoirdupois. One may contest the proposed treatment without denying what you see in the mirror. Peterson is right about one important thing: many supposed technological remedies to the climate emergency are inadequate, ecologically damaging or fraudulent. Renewable systems require storage, backup and enormous quantities of mined material; carbon markets have, by and large, turned into theatres of accountancy—even setting aside (!) the underlying morally centrifugal tendency of such schemes.

Remarking on the burgeoning carbon credit market some years ago now, an emphatically former friend thought he’d amuse me with his conception of the underlying mechanism: ‘Every time I book a seat, someone runs into an African village and cries “Turn the generator off, the big man is taking a flight!”’ Needless to say, this self-appointed ‘big man’ is a very small individual if he imagines flying high makes him, or anyone at all in 2026, anything much besides a monkey, pogoing to nowhere using a stick of its own burning shit. I’m one of those people who remember the Stern Review of the economic consequences of global heating, which was published in 2006 with much fartfare. Unsurprisingly, given its entirely Panglossian prediction of a beneficent technology transfer that would both reduce those pesky greenhouse gases and allow for a vast emergent market in… well, what precisely?

What the eponymous author of the Review conveniently forgot—besides the increasingly fissiparous geopolitics evident even then—was that electric cars still require roads, tyres, lithium, cobalt and power; while reliably producing, in direct proportion to their rate of manufacture, more drivers, who in turn beget more cars. For years nuclear energy was damned by the environmental movement: how many millions, one wonders, of non-biodegradable Atomkraft? Nein danke!stickers were there manufactured? Towards the end of his long and illustrious life, James Lovelock actively campaigned for a serious resumption of research into nuclear power, and building the building of more reactors. Again, unsurprisingly: given he’d saved the world once from the hole in the ozone layer, and developed the most compelling account of its biosphere, he had to come up with something.

But the problem with the nuclear option is that the infrastructure required is necessarily extensive, while the allied industries are equally so; a phenomenon well attested to by the numerous raids on such facilities undertaken by all sides since the Gulf War flared up again in February and began once more to cast its sinister glow—compounded of many, many burning wellheads—over the rest of the gas-guzzling world. The environmental movement’s historical hostility to it has only been obtuse in so far as it hasn’t itself channelled the necessary inner-Peterson. Because what not just Peterson, but almost the entirety of the world­—including Naomi Klein and Al Gore—cannot admit, is that no change of energy source will redeem endless consumption. A civilisation cannot technologise its way out of the consequences of technology while retaining its governing commitment to perpetual expansion.

Greater efficiency has repeatedly enabled greater aggregate use. This is because the new machine does not abolish appetite—whether for oil, or oat milk—it industrialises it, and the industrialisation goes deep… deep into the irritable tract of the soul-bowel. Because moral loop-the-loop isn’t confined to the hot-aerialists of the climate-denial industry. Al Gore has apparently traversed at least twenty intercontinental flight sectors during the past five years, many of them to explain the climate emergency at Davos and successive COPs; while Naomi Klein’s seven-week ‘Doppelganger’ tour seems to have required a minimum of a dozen flights; quite possibly she should’ve sent one instead, in the form of a digitised eidelons.

One of the most curious things about the faux-environmentalists is that they not only tweet as if garden birds were going extinct (which they are), but when the tweeting fails to get them a mate, or a sale, or another CEO to be starstruck by, they take to the air, hoping thereby to be able to locate one, Either way, with all such boosters, they all have a unique dispensation to avoid restraint—aka, leaving the world-bedroom to become filthy and foetid with the evidence of their, gulp, unsustainable adolescent desires—and need to be told to tidy up their portion of it, not go gadding about on the aforementioned flammable flying turd: the atmospheric carbon molecule, regrettably, cannot distinguish between a journey undertaken to deny its effects and one undertaken to lecture us about them.

Meanwhile, Peterson gets dizzy opposing wind turbines because they require destructive mining, then proposes 11,000 nuclear power stations as if they might be assembled from lumber and good intentions. This is where the Telegraph enters the battle royale on the banks of everyone’s Acheron. I suspect regular SITREP readers may quite reasonably think that I have some sort of personal agon with the Telegraph. I don’t, apart from regarding it as a slightly more malevolent dying—and hence lashing out—beast than other corporately-owned legacy media entities. That being said, having paid for an online subscription, I find that I can’t scan the first panel of the site without immediately going to an article that I then find to be not simply ethically dubious, but a complete abandonment of the editorial nous that once conveyed respect not just for a political hierarchy, but an intellectual one as well.

My grandfather, Sir Henry Self exhibits, by means of both his person and career, the fatuity of projecting the ‘values’ (I use the term advisedly) of the present on to the past. A lifelong Tory voter, a fervent reader of the Daily Telegraph, knighted for his civil services to the defence and energy industries; nevertheless, as the holder of numerous extramural degrees from the University of London, including a doctorate in philosophy, I suspect he would find the current editorial line not merely sketchy but straightforwardly irrational. Until, that is, Axel Springer, its new German owner was brought to his attention. The publisher of every German publication you’ve ever heard of if you aren’t a German-speaker, in the 21st century it’s become a vast logistics entity, which is what the biggest of the former paper-producers have media-morphosed into.

Obviously,‘Dids’, as the family called him, knew sod-all about global heating, although all the family liked drinking ‘bombshells’, a very, very dry Martini—six parts gin to one of vermouth—and these were indubitably locally warming. So Grandad wouldn’t—couldn’t obv’—have cavilled at Axel Springer having a material carbon footprint running—even before its recent restructuring—into hundreds of thousands of tonnes annually. Being a true establishmentarian, he would’ve paid heed to its respectable corporate climate targets. But let’s drop the piloting counterfactuals: Axel Springer’s controlling chief executive, Mathias Döpfner, has been known to (I learnt these weasel words from a well-known newspaper) express enthusiasm for an additional two degrees of global heating, on the ground that warmer epochs may prove more productive. Hm… I am, in the demotic favoured around my little patch of the inferno, gobsmacked. Productive for whom?

Certainly not for anybody who has to do anything that involves them not having anyone else to do it for them, which is curiously enough not a category of humanity for whom the corporate class have any empathy whatsoever. I personally know this to be a fact: I’m not proud of having known very rich people—it was filthy being around that lucre, but somebody had to do it; just as they had to hang around with junkies, criminals… even real scum, like politicians. It used to be called journalism, now it’s mostly sycophancy. I digress—but not much: the substance of it all being that I’ve witnessed many, many people in my life who, faced with an essential and preventing contradiction between the mendacity of their means, and the supposed morality of their ends, are quite unable to avoid hypocrisy, except by being mutually-reassured of their probity by many more of their kind.

The deeply sad truth of the matter is that this circle jerk of denial is a ring-a-ring-a- roses until we all fall down dead. Inasmuch as the elite has any primacy, it’s in the form of its own oscillation resonating through the crumbling pyramid of the now subsiding hierarchy of what once passed for political power. Anyone who in any way participates in corporate capitalism then begins oscillating, jerking and climate-emergency-denying as well; which, in the West at least, means everyone. Yes, an entire civilisation is now compelled by their own miniature gyre to exhibit the same flickery succession of Janus faces: thus, denial perfuses our steadily stagnating society. How long will it be before everything clots up? And here ‘clot’ is meant in the nounal form as well.

Because if there’s one thing, that Harry Howard’s commissioning of Jordan Peterson as a Telegraph columnist exhibits more than anything else it’s that the German shepherd is wagging the old English sheepdog, Springer’s German titles have repeatedly converted rational climate policy into irrational culture war: the heat pump, the bicycle, the reduced speed limit and the insulated home will become in the eyes of the world—or so they hope—assaults upon prosperity and freedom. The newly acquired Telegraph is to be Springer’s space probe into the vacuity of the American hypercapitalist market. Stolid but newly feisty Germans, sensing their own political settlement rearranging itself, have purchased a legacy British newspaper and are now plugging it into the North American grievance grid: that great network of bi-directed venom that poisons every possibility of truth and justice getting in the American way.

Hence Peterson: a Canadian pop psychologist, trafficked like, um, fictitious fentanyl, over the border, through the Barren Lands, and now having toxified North America, is blown around the world by the old British commentariat. On the same day Peterson’s intellectually and morally indefensible essay appeared, as many as seventy thousand people crossed from Morocco into the Spanish enclave of Ceuta. A viral rumour attached itself to a real legal ruling in the Spanish Supreme Court; this engendered a flash mob: arguably the only organised political formation that still exists in our wired world of cyborgs. When this mostly Moroccan—rather than recent, sub-Saharan migrant—multitude tested the frontier simultaneously, border enforcement either failed or stood aside.

About a hundred people died over the two days of the incursion; now, at the end of the week, most entrants have returned; and Ceuta is left with several thousand people, a large child-protection crisis and the possibility of another organised attempt. It would be fatuous to declare each person a climate refugee—their motives will have been economic, political, familial and personal; human movement is never produced by a single variable. But it would be more fatuous still not to recognise the image, given the society of the spectacle laps them up, then spews out more bigotry. For here is the repressed nightmare of the North European propertarian made flesh: a torrent of humanity moving out of the Maghreb hinterland and overrunning the barrier separating African poverty from European property.

Not an ‘invasion’ in a pleasingly symmetrical military sense, but a breach in the imaginative fortification by which wealthy societies preserve the illusion that the consequences of their consumption will remain elsewhere. As desperate swimmers were drowning in the sea off Ceuta, immense wildfires burned around Madrid and through south-western France. Smoke covered Bordeaux; hundreds of thousands were evacuated across France and Spain. The fires had physical causes—heat, dryness, wind, vegetation and ignition—and no responsible person would claim that climate change struck each individual match. But warming creates the psychic as well as the physical conditions: it increases the frequency and intensity of the fire weather through which a spark becomes a landscape. The firestarters are of course sociopaths—in my opinion: all of them, including those who merely make the weather by emitting contrails.

The Château de Montaigne, east of Bordeaux, was not reported to be in the fire’s path. Nonetheless, the proximity supplies the correct counter-image. Montaigne—the great irenic anatomist of mortality, who wrote that to philosophise is to learn how to die—sits in his tower while the horizon smokes. Across the Channel, Peterson philosophises in order not to learn how to die at all. This is the homological face-off for the summer of unlimited fire- rather than cage-fighting: an inferno pressing upon the national capital, a conflagration of people pressing upon the continental border, and the ideological drumbeat insisting that the only emergency is the threatened freedom of the air-conditioned consumer.

Behind it, the rim shots continue sounding across the tautened human-skin-drum of Ukraine, Gaza and the Middle East; drones and missiles consume the critical materials extracted, refined and circulated through the same world system whose climatic consequences we are invited to regard as merely the nightmares of utopian socialist dreamers-of-a-new-day. What is it like to shill for hyper-extractive capitalism while the smoke crosses the vineyards? Comment Editor Harry Howard might ask his new star columnist—Telegraph editor, Tom Welsh might ask Harry Howard. Boss-man Döpfner might ask them both. What precisely do you tell yourself while the last accessible oil is sucked up, the last tarry patch scraped from the sand, the last fragment of deep coal tweezered from the seam and the last conflict mineral smelted into a capacitor?

Presumably, that somewhere a vegetarian with a secure job is behaving hypocritically—before, that is, pouring yourself a lovely glass of Château Malartic-Lagravière Rouge, 2026, assuming, that is, one’s available in 2036. Of course, environmentalists are hypocrites: they fly, drive, stream, heat and cool; they incontinently purchase electronics containing materials whose origins they do not know, and they take to the waves to expel their hypocritical afflatus with best of the right-wing bloviators. Because so do socialists, conservatives, liberals, fascists, monarchists and emeritus professors of psychology: hypocrisy is not an economic system—consumption is.

Nor is facing this fact conventionally Left-wing: the old Left placed its faith in production, technology and abundance quite as ardently as the Right—Marxism is a philosophy that sees human consciousness itself as a function of materially productive processes; its utopia is a machined dream quite as much as the tech’ barons’. But what we require now is realism about the end of any possibility that people can technologise their way out of the consequences of technology. That realism may tactically favour nuclear power, public transport and strict carbon limits; but in order to warrant the name of strategy, it will also have to control markets, impose rationing and civic obligation, enact local discretion, and in particular forms of restraint for which the established political vocabulary has no adequate name. So let’s get coining!

It shouldn’t be too hard, what with every single major religious and ethical movement in the world espousing just that. Moreover, unlike Petersonism, the ethical beginning is simpler: you don’t have to have an induced coma to know you’re going to die. I am going to die soon enough, odds-on Peterson will, too. The editors who commissioned him will die—even Harry Howard, who’s ‘spiritual home’ is a Christian church, St Bartholemew-the-Great. This magnificent, Romanesque hulk has lasted a thousand years, but it definitely won’t continue this Reich unless he and his generation—the precocious crisis-manager is only in his early thirties—evince a little more asceticism along with their, um, undoubted piety. Döpfner will die, Gore will go to the grave, Klein and every reader of the Telegraph will kark it as well.

This does not render human action pointless: it’s what gives action its point—and inaction: you can’t emit much in the way of GHGs sitting quietly alone in a room—unless you buy your nosh at Diddly-Squat Farm Shop. Finitude makes possible proportion, discretion, sacrifice and most importantly: care. It allows us to distinguish what we need from what we merely fear to relinquish. A morality that takes its inspiration from the fact of human mortality can—and should—be scaled up not just to confront us with fragility of collective life on Earth but help us comprehend it. In the process, it needn’t mean that life contracts into hair-shirted punishment: properly understood, restraint makes life thicken, and experience inspissate. A city with fewer cars necessarily offers the opportunity for more and less impactful encounters—a city full of driverless ones, offers none at all.

A life with fewer flights will be more grounded, by definition: I’d argue that it’s precisely lift-off that loops even infrequent flyers into the oscillating go-round of climate change denial. Whereas us rooted folk possess more nous: we understand that it’s only the imagination that can make you believe you can fly, doing it is strictly for the declining population of birds. A culture released from the compulsive consumption of space, may discover forms of pleasure in placemaking that cannot be measured by throughput. The limit is not the enemy of freedom, Jordan, it’s what gives freedom shape—so go clean all those blister packs up off the floor of your fucking room. Even bobbing on the surface, rather than being drawn into the depths in a vortex of downers, Peterson’s head has no such ethical equilibrium.

It spins within its ideological gimbals, remaining fixed upon the decaying hierarchy that’s its gnomon, while the physical world oscillates around it. Donald J Trump’s own oscillating semi-consciousness has snagged him: Drill! Burn! Extract! Dominate! Construe every restraint as weakness! Interpret that weakness as feminisation! Yuck! Then figure Gaia herself as the passive object of an infinitely renewable male potency. But the Earth is not a hole waiting for you to fill it, Jordan; it’s the maternal and material condition of your existence—and your existence, like mine, was only ever temporary, while soon our time will be up. So, tidy your room by all means, my boy. Then turn off the air conditioner, open the window and smell the rich smoke produced by barbecuing long pig.

Yesterday afternoon, on one of the hottest days of the year, I found myself standing in the almost preternatural cool of St Peter and St Paul at Peasmarsh, talking to two strangers about Nigel Farage. The church is largely Norman, its nave and western chancel dating from around eleven hundred, the aisles and tower added later in the twelfth century, the roofs renewed towards the end of the fifteenth. It stands a little apart from the village on the ridge between the Tillingham and the Rother, and inside it has that peculiar hush of an old English parish church in which architecture doesn’t so much contain history as arrest it.

The nave feels extraordinarily broad; above it the old timbering produces something of the same effect as the crown-post construction of the Wealden hall house: an integral sense of Englishness, domestic and ecclesiastical simultaneously, so that you might imagine yourself standing in a proto-, transhistorical semi-detached house of the Lord. And, perhaps, semi-detached from the reality of what politics used to be. The two men were father and son. The father was balding, had evidently suffered some ill health, and was dressed in the khakis and beiges of the Boden-catalogue English middle class. He was personable, relaxed, a little younger than me. His son, probably in his late twenties, was an electrician who had emigrated to Western Australia and taken citizenship there.

He worked in extractive mining and talked intelligently about its contradictions: lithium, the environmental damage attendant on extraction, relations with Indigenous Australians, the extraordinary distances involved in a mineral economy whose workers themselves become components in a vast logistics system. He flew in and out of the mines from Perth. He understood perfectly well that what he was participating in was ecologically problematic. But what could he do? Somebody had to do it. There, in five words, is the political philosophy of the dromodronological era: somebody has to do it. Not I believe this should be done, nor we have collectively decided that it should be done, nor even the benefits outweigh the costs. The system requires it and I occupy the place in the system where it gets done. All intentionality has drained out.

We had been down at Dungeness earlier, looking through a telescope across the shingle near Derek Jarman’s Prospect Cottage to see whether there were small boats offshore. Experimentalism confronting harsh reality: no England’s dreaming here, Derek. And now, in this hushed Norman church, the conversation turned to immigration, assimilation, Reform and Farage. The father was by no means ranting. On the contrary, he seemed moderate, thoughtful, almost painfully ordinary. But when I asked what would happen if Farage actually won a general election, he said the establishment would never allow him to take power. I asked him what he meant by the establishment. “The BBC,” he said. And I felt cold. Because this, rather than the loudmouth racist, the tattooed thug or the swivel-eyed conspiracist, is one of the faces extremism can wear in contemporary England. It wears beige trousers. It goes sightseeing with its adult son.

It talks civilly to a bearded old writer in an ancient church. It may possess no coherent theory whatsoever of how the BBC, the courts, Parliament, the civil service, the police, the intelligence agencies, universities, banks and regulators could conceivably combine their contradictory purposes into a single political will. It simply feels that somebody must be preventing politics from working. This is the stab in the back returned in domesticated form: not the dagger of the Dolchstoßlegende, but something bought at B&Q on Sunday afternoon for carving the joint from Sainsbury’s. The historical distinction matters. Farageism is not National Socialism. But the morphology bears examination. The original stab-in-the-back myth converted Germany’s defeat into evidence that the authentic national will had been thwarted by internal enemies.

The contemporary version performs a related operation on the experience of political impotence: we no longer experience ourselves as possessing political agency, therefore somebody must have taken it from us. Which brings us to Clacton. Farage has regained the seat he voluntarily vacated, receiving 22,239 votes, while Count Binface received the extraordinary total of 9,455. Thirty-four candidates stood, the largest field in British parliamentary electoral history; the established major parties declined to participate. Farage himself did not appear at the count. British elections have always had their licensed fools. Screaming Lord Sutch stood more than forty times and eventually founded the Official Monster Raving Loony Party.

He was part of the theatre of election night: the man in the absurd costume standing beside the Prime Minister while the returning officer read out the figures, a little eruption of carnival reminding the powerful that democratic authority remained faintly ridiculous. But Sutch’s story itself ended terribly. Suffering from depression, he killed himself in 1999. The coroner called him “a comedian with tragedy in his heart”. The joke wasn’t funny any longer for him, and it isn’t terribly funny now. Because Count Binface didn’t merely provide punctuation to an electoral process. He became, with 9,455 votes, its principal opposition. Satire has ceased commenting upon politics and begun occupying the space vacated by it. We wrote earlier this year about the failure of satire; here is the phenomenon in almost laboratory conditions.

When twenty-seven per cent of those voting choose the man with the bin on his head, it is tempting to call the decision rational because the election itself was absurd. But this merely completes the circuit: the evacuation of political intentionality is answered by the evacuation of political seriousness. And hovering over this entire spectacle is Christopher Harborne’s £5 million. The legacy press will naturally pursue Farage’s hypocrisy. It is what the legacy press knows how to do. Farage received £5 million from Harborne shortly before reversing his decision not to stand in the 2024 general election; the Parliamentary Commissioner for Standards is investigating whether the gift should subsequently have been registered. Farage says it was a personal gift, originally explained in terms of his security. But Farage’s hypocrisy is the least interesting thing about Nigel Farage.

Ten years ago, on Question Time in Theresa May’s constituency, I called him a grubby little opportunist riding on the coattails of history. I see no particular reason to revise the description. The interesting object is the £5 million itself: a financial drogue attached to a political aircraft which can no longer navigate by its old instruments. Harborne is an almost indecently apposite figure. He founded an aviation-fuel business, became enormously wealthy through cryptocurrency investments and is a substantial shareholder in QinetiQ, the defence-technology company descended from the state’s Defence Evaluation and Research Agency. Defence and crypto make suggestive bookends to Harborne’s political role. Harborne doesn’t have to possess an ideology of non-intentionality. He inhabits an economy increasingly constituted by it. And then he gives Nigel Farage £5 million for, among other explanations, security.

A politician whose programme promises the recovery of national sovereignty apparently requires the private fortune of an immensely wealthy man to secure his own person while practising democratic politics. That claim, if taken seriously, is more interesting than the accusation. For what sort of recovered polis is this, if its tribune requires five million quid merely to move through it? And so the establishment acquires intentionality at precisely the historical moment when our actual institutions appear increasingly incapable of exercising it. When the state acts, it is tyrannical. When one institution contradicts another, the state is broken. When a regulator investigates Farage, the establishment is persecuting him. When the electorate returns him, the people have repudiated the establishment.

And when the investigation resumes regardless, its refusal to accept the electoral verdict can itself be presented as further evidence of establishment obstruction. This is why the comparison with Marine Le Pen is worth making, briefly. The legal circumstances are profoundly different: Le Pen’s difficulties arise from a criminal conviction and continuing appeal, Farage’s present problem from parliamentary standards regulation. What they share is the attempt to make electoral legitimacy answer a question belonging to another jurisdiction altogether. An election can determine whether voters want you to represent them. It cannot determine whether financial rules were complied with. Yet across Western democracies the distinction is being subjected to attrition: the court, commissioner, regulator or prosecutor becomes another contestant against “the people”. The modern stab in the back.

The young electrician had responded to lost intentionality by accepting it: somebody has to do it. His father responded by hallucinating intentionality back into the world: somebody is stopping us doing it. Count Binface offers a third possibility: nobody can do anything, so let’s laugh. What happened in Clacton isn’t principally a story about whether Nigel Farage is a hypocrite, and the torrent of scuttlebutt now passing through the media processors should not distract us from its geopolitical significance. The tail of populism wags the body politic ever more violently, while those experiencing the resulting vertigo become increasingly convinced that the movement must be caused by an invisible hand. Standing in that beautiful old church, in the heat outside and the ancient cool within, I suddenly found the prospect frightening. We shouldn’t reassure ourselves with Nigel Farage’s vulgarity.

We shouldn’t reassure ourselves with Count Binface’s wastepaper basket either. The joke isn’t funny any more.
